modules.title: Kickoff: recruiter screen and why you're a strong PS asset
objectives: Deliver your pitch in 30 seconds, 90 seconds and 3 minutes, from evidence only
Answer the logistics questions (salary, availability, travel, English, location) cleanly
Explain the Netskope exit and the return to Fortinet in a neutral, confident way
Position yourself as a strong PS consultant with proof points and honest gaps
Ask the recruiter questions that move the process forward
sources: Your evidence: super-cv (roles, dates, achievements, certifications)
Your Cato cheatsheet: answer frameworks (technical, behavioural, 'why us')
Verizon 2026 DBIR and IBM Cost of a Data Breach 2026: business context

units.title: What the recruiter is really screening for
units.body:
A recruiter screen is a **filter**, not a technical exam. In 20–30 minutes the recruiter checks five things, and the hiring manager trusts their notes:

1. **Fit to the role on paper:** can you explain, simply, why your background fits professional services?
2. **Motivation:** why Fortinet, why now, why PS?
3. **Logistics:** location, availability, travel, salary range, English level.
4. **Red flags:** gaps, short tenures, how you talk about previous employers.
5. **Communication:** clear, structured, friendly, concise.

Your situation has two strengths to lead with: you're a **former Fortinet TAC P3 engineer** (2022–2024), so you know FortiOS and the support side from inside, and you're **referred by the PS manager**. Mention the referral early and naturally: *"I was referred by [name] from the PS team, and I'm very excited about this role."*

## Rules for this call

- Answers of **30–60 seconds**. Stop, and let them ask more.
- Every claim comes from your real experience. No numbers you can't back up.
- Positive about every former employer. Never vent.
- Have your CV, the job description and your notes open, and your salary range written down.

:::recall
Q: Five things a recruiter screens for?
A: Fit on paper, motivation, logistics, red flags, communication.
:::

:::tip
Smile while you talk; it changes your voice on a call. Stand up for the pitch if it helps your energy.
:::

units.title: Your pitch, three lengths
units.body:
Use the **behavioural skeleton** from your Cato notes: context → specific actions → measurable results, and a "why us" close (company strength → your skills → contribution).

## 30 seconds

> "I'm a network security engineer with five years in customer-facing security roles. I was a Technical Support Engineer P3 at Fortinet, one of the escalation points for North American and Brazilian enterprise customers, with more than 2,000 cases closed. Then I spent two years at Netskope as a Customer Success Manager owning enterprise accounts. I want to bring both sides, the FortiOS depth and the customer ownership, to Fortinet's professional services team."

## 90 seconds: add proof

- **Fortinet (2022–2024):** escalation point for NAM and Brazil, 2,000+ cases with a CSAT above 4.7; FortiOS end to end: NAT (the team's go-to), SD-WAN designs, IPsec and FortiClient VPN, HA including AWS and Azure, debug flow and captures; defects escalated to development with reproduction steps.
- **Netskope (2024–2026):** about 60 named enterprise accounts, then a 2,000+ account scale book; finished partners' half-delivered PS projects in stages; rollouts (one account from below 50 % to 70 % utilisation); kept more than USD 900k in contract value through a hostile escalation.
- **Before that:** Cisco TAC (via SYKES) on ISE, AAA and 802.1X.
- **Close:** "PS is where those two meet: designing and changing things safely, and keeping the customer aligned. I work in English, Spanish and Portuguese, and I can travel anywhere."

## 3 minutes: add one story

Add **one** story with a result, for example the partner PS completion, or the escalation you turned into a license exchange. End with why Fortinet PS, now.

:::pitfall
The Cato cheatsheet contains figures that your super-cv does not support ("four years", "$50M", "153 %", "85 %"). Don't use them unless you can confirm them.
:::

:::recall
Q: Your two lead proof points in the 30-second pitch?
A: Former Fortinet TAC P3 escalation point (2,000+ cases, CSAT above 4.7) and two years owning enterprise accounts at Netskope.
:::

units.title: Logistics and the tricky questions
units.body:
## Salary

Give a **range**, as a total monthly package, and stay flexible on structure: *"Based on my research for this kind of role in Colombia, I'm looking at [your range] per month as a total package, and I'm flexible on how it's structured."* Prepare your range before the call and confirm it with your referrer if you can. Don't give a number below your real floor; the first number anchors the rest.

## Availability, location, travel, English

- **Availability:** immediately.
- **Location:** Santa Marta, Colombia, working remotely; open to relocating or travelling for customers.
- **Travel:** "As much as the role needs, including international. I have a current US visa."
- **English:** full professional proficiency; you worked daily with North American enterprise customers and executives. Spanish native, Portuguese professional (you supported Brazil).

## Why did you leave Netskope?

Keep it **short, neutral and forward-looking**. Don't give details you'd rather keep private, and never criticise them:

> "My time at Netskope ended in September. It was a great two years owning enterprise accounts, and it gave me a clear view of what I want next: to go back to hands-on Fortinet work, on the delivery side."

## Why come back to Fortinet?

> "I know the product deeply from TAC, I liked the people and the culture, and PS lets me use both the technical depth and the customer skills I built at Netskope. Coming back on the delivery side is the natural next step."

## "You've been in support and CS, not PS"

Own it, then bridge: the pieces you've done (designs, rollouts, recoveries, partner PS completion) and how you'd ramp up.

:::recall
Q: The three-sentence Netskope answer: what does each sentence do?
A: States the fact neutrally, says something positive about the experience, and points forward to why this role.
:::

:::why
Q: Why give a range as a total package instead of one base number?
A: It anchors the conversation on your real expectations while leaving room to negotiate structure (base, bonus, benefits).
:::

units.title: Why you're a strong PS asset, and the threat story
units.body:
## Positioning lines (all evidenced)

- **Inside knowledge:** ex-Fortinet TAC P3. You know how FortiOS behaves under stress and how TAC and development work, so your escalations will be fast and clean.
- **Delivery mindset:** at Netskope you completed partially delivered partner PS projects in stages, ran health checks and proofs of concept, and planned rollouts with partners such as Cloudrise, AccessIT Group, CDW and Deloitte.
- **Design from requirements:** SD-WAN steering and failover, SSL deep inspection rollouts with the CA pushed by Group Policy, HA in AWS and Azure, Terraform labs to test before changing production.
- **Executive communication:** QBRs with C-level and VPs; turning telemetry into business evidence.
- **Certifications:** NSE 7, NSE 5 FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer, NSE 4, SD-WAN Architect, plus OSCP for an attacker's view. They expired, and you're re-studying on 7.6/8.0 right now.
- **Field-ready:** English, Spanish, Portuguese; travel anywhere.

## Use the threat landscape for the "why it matters"

The recruiter won't test you on it, but a line of business context makes you memorable:

- Exploiting vulnerabilities is now the **top initial access vector at 31 %** of breaches (Verizon DBIR 2026), and only **26 %** of known-exploited vulnerabilities were fully fixed in 2025. Firewalls with IPS and virtual patching buy customers time.
- The average breach costs **USD 4.99 million**, **USD 11.5 million** in the US (IBM 2026). Getting deployments right and fast is real money for customers.

## Questions to ask the recruiter

- "What does success look like in the first six months for this role?"
- "How is the PS team organised in LATAM, and what kind of projects are most common?"
- "What are the next steps and the timeline of the process?"
- "Is there anything in my background you'd like me to clarify for the hiring manager?"

:::recall
Q: One-line business reason why firewall PS matters in 2026?
A: Vulnerability exploitation is now the top way in (31 %, DBIR 2026) and breaches average USD 4.99M (IBM 2026); deploying controls correctly and fast directly reduces that risk.
:::

scenarios.title: The salary push-back
scenarios.situation: You give your range. The recruiter says: "That's a bit above what we had in mind for this level. Would you consider something lower?"
scenarios.ask: What do you say?
right_thinking: Don't drop your number immediately
Ask about the full package and the level they have in mind
Restate the value you bring to this specific role
Show flexibility on structure, not on your floor
scenarios.what: Keep the conversation open without anchoring lower.
scenarios.why: The first concession sets the offer; understanding the package and level gives you room.
scenarios.model_answer: "I appreciate you telling me. Could you share the range you have for this level, and how the package is structured, bonus and benefits? I'm coming in with Fortinet TAC experience, so I'd ramp up fast. I'm flexible on how the package is built, and I'm sure we can find something that works once I understand the full picture."
scenarios.best_way: Help me understand the full package and the level; I'm flexible on structure, and I'll ramp up fast because I know the product.

scenarios.title: 'Why did it end at Netskope?' - the follow-up
scenarios.situation: You gave your neutral answer. The recruiter asks: "Was it your decision?"
scenarios.ask: How do you answer without oversharing or lying?
right_thinking: Stay truthful and brief
Don't volunteer private details
Pivot to what you learned and what you want next
scenarios.what: A short, truthful, forward-looking answer.
scenarios.why: Recruiters screen for red flags in how you talk about exits; calm and brief reads as mature.
scenarios.model_answer: "[One truthful sentence in your own words; no details.] I'm at peace with it, and I'm proud of what I did there: enterprise accounts, partner projects and a big escalation I turned around. And it made me choose deliberately what I want next, which is hands-on Fortinet delivery."
could_have_added: Keep it to two or three sentences, then stop and smile
scenarios.best_way: One truthful sentence, then: I'm proud of the work, and it made me choose this path on purpose.

scenarios.title: The English check
scenarios.situation: Halfway through, the recruiter switches to English: "Could you describe a technical problem you solved recently, in simple words?"
scenarios.ask: Pick a story and say it in about a minute.
right_thinking: Choose a story you can tell without jargon
Problem → what you did → result
Speak slowly and finish with the impact
scenarios.what: A simple, clear one-minute technical story.
scenarios.why: They test clarity and fluency, not depth.
how: Pick the MTU or debug-flow story
scenarios.model_answer: "A customer's users could open small web pages over a new VPN, but big downloads froze. The VPN adds extra headers, so large packets no longer fit and were being dropped. I proved it with a packet capture, then told the firewall to make the connections use slightly smaller packets. Downloads worked again, and I added that test to the customer's checklist so it wouldn't happen again."
scenarios.best_way: Small pages worked, big downloads froze; the packets were too big for the tunnel. I made them smaller and it worked.

interview.question: Tell me about yourself.
interview.framework: Who you are → two proof points → why this role
interview.model_answer: "I'm a network security engineer with five years in customer-facing security roles. I was a Technical Support Engineer P3 at Fortinet, one of the escalation points for North American and Brazilian enterprise customers, with more than 2,000 cases closed and a CSAT above 4.7. Then I spent two years at Netskope as a Customer Success Manager owning enterprise accounts, where I also finished partners' half-delivered professional-services projects. I was referred by [name] from your PS team, and this role is where my FortiOS depth and my customer work come together."
interview.best_way: Fortinet TAC depth plus two years owning enterprise customers: PS is where they meet.

interview.question: Why do you want to come back to Fortinet?
interview.model_answer: "I know FortiOS from the inside: two years of escalated cases taught me how it behaves and how to fix it. I liked the people and the pace. Coming back on the delivery side, in PS, lets me use that depth together with the customer skills I built at Netskope: planning rollouts, executive reviews and finishing projects others had left half done."
interview.best_way: I know the product from inside, and PS lets me use that with the customer skills I built since.

interview.question: Why did you leave Netskope?
interview.model_answer: "My time at Netskope ended in September. It was a great two years owning enterprise accounts and working with partners, and it gave me a clear view of what I want next: to go back to hands-on Fortinet work, on the delivery side."
interview.best_way: It ended in September; great two years; now I'm choosing hands-on Fortinet delivery on purpose.

interview.question: What are your salary expectations?
interview.model_answer: "Based on my research for professional services roles like this in Colombia, I'm looking at [your range] per month as a total package. I'm flexible on how it's structured between base, bonus and benefits."
could_have_added: If they share their range first, react to it instead of repeating yours
interview.best_way: [Your range] per month, total package, flexible on structure.

interview.question: When could you start?
interview.model_answer: "Immediately. I'm available now."
interview.best_way: Immediately.

interview.question: This role requires customer travel. How do you feel about that?
interview.model_answer: "Happy to. I can travel as much as the role needs, including internationally, and I have a current US visa. I've worked with customers across North America and Latin America, including Brazil, so I'm used to different time zones and cultures."
interview.best_way: As much as you need, including international. Current US visa.

interview.question: Where are you based? Would you relocate?
interview.model_answer: "I'm in Santa Marta, Colombia, and I work remotely. I'm open to relocating or spending time on-site if the role needs it."
interview.best_way: Santa Marta, remote, open to relocating or on-site time.

interview.question: How would you rate your English?
interview.model_answer: "Full professional proficiency. For five years I've worked every day in English with enterprise customers and executives in North America, including escalations and business reviews. Spanish is my native language and I work professionally in Portuguese too; I supported Brazilian customers at Fortinet."
interview.best_way: Full professional: five years of daily escalations and executive reviews in English, plus Spanish and Portuguese.

interview.question: What do you know about professional services at Fortinet?
interview.framework: What PS does → why it matters → your fit
interview.model_answer: "PS turns what the customer bought into a working deployment: design, implementation, migrations and knowledge transfer, usually on FortiGate with FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer, and increasingly SD-WAN, ZTNA and the Security Fabric. From TAC I saw the other side: many cases were implementations that would have gone better with a solid design and change plan. That's the part I want to own."
could_have_added: Ask the recruiter what kind of projects are most common in LATAM
interview.best_way: PS makes the purchase work: design, implement, migrate, transfer knowledge. I've seen from TAC what happens when that's done poorly.

interview.question: What's your experience with FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer?
interview.model_answer: "I worked with both in Fortinet support cases, customer deployments and labs, and I was NSE 5 certified on both. Those certifications expired, and I'm re-studying them right now on the current versions."
interview.best_way: Support cases, deployments and labs; NSE 5 on both, now refreshing on current versions.

interview.question: Why are your Fortinet certifications expired?
interview.model_answer: "They lapsed during my two years at Netskope, where I worked on a different platform. I'm already re-studying with the FortiOS 8.0 and FortiManager 7.6 guides, and I plan to re-certify as soon as possible."
interview.best_way: They lapsed while I was at Netskope; I'm already re-studying on the current versions.

interview.question: What's your biggest strength?
interview.framework: Strength → proof → value for this role
interview.model_answer: "Turning tense technical situations into progress. At Fortinet I was an escalation point and handed development clean reproductions of real defects. At Netskope I turned a hostile escalation into a license exchange by fixing the underlying technical issue first, keeping more than 900 thousand dollars in contract value. In PS, that's the calm in a hard change window."
interview.best_way: I turn tense technical situations into progress, with evidence: fix the real problem, and the trust follows.

interview.question: What's a weakness you're working on?
interview.model_answer: "Early in my customer roles I let work scatter across email, chat and the CRM. I fixed it by building my own Python and AI workflows that consolidate account activity into one view and turn notes into action items. Now I set up one tracker and a weekly status from day one."
interview.best_way: I used to let tasks scatter; now I build systems so nothing slips.

interview.question: Are you interviewing elsewhere?
interview.model_answer: "Yes, I have a few processes open, but Fortinet PS is my first choice, because it's the role that fits my background best and I was referred by the team."
interview.best_way: A few processes, but this is my first choice.

interview.question: Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult customer.
interview.model_answer: "At Netskope an enterprise account escalated and was ready to leave. I treated it as a technical problem, not just a relationship one: I diagnosed the underlying issue, fixed it, and with that credibility we restructured the agreement as a license exchange instead of a cancellation. We kept more than 900 thousand dollars in contract value."
interview.best_way: I fixed the real technical problem first; the relationship and over 900k in contract value followed.

interview.question: Why should we move you to the hiring manager?
interview.model_answer: "Three reasons. I know FortiOS from the inside, as a former TAC escalation engineer. I know how to own customers and finish delivery work others left half done. And I'm ready for the field: three languages, travel anywhere, available immediately, and already re-studying the current versions."
interview.best_way: Inside product knowledge, proven customer ownership, and ready to go now.

interview.question: What questions do you have for me?
interview.model_answer: "What does success look like in the first six months? How is the PS team organised in LATAM, and what projects are most common? And what are the next steps and timeline? Also, is there anything in my background you'd like me to clarify for the hiring manager?"
interview.best_way: Success in six months, the LATAM team and projects, next steps, and anything to clarify.

interview.question: In one minute, why does a firewall consultant matter to a CFO in 2026?
interview.testing: Business framing (often asked by HM or panels)
interview.model_answer: "Because the front door changed. Exploiting vulnerabilities is now the most common way attackers get in, 31 % of breaches in Verizon's 2026 report, and the average breach costs about 5 million dollars, over 11 in the US, according to IBM. A well-designed and well-deployed FortiGate, with IPS, segmentation and good logging, buys time while systems get patched and shortens incidents. My job as a consultant is to get that right the first time, without disrupting the business."
interview.best_way: Attackers now walk in through unpatched systems, and a breach costs about 5 million dollars. Good deployments buy time and cut that cost.

modules.title: Hiring manager: prove you can deliver, own customers and ramp fast
objectives: Know what a PS hiring manager is deciding and what they worry about
Map every likely competency question to a real, evidenced story
Answer the hard questions (no end-to-end PS projects yet, the Netskope exit, expired certs) honestly and confidently
Present a 30-60-90 day plan for your first months in the role
Ask questions that show you think like a consultant
sources: Your evidence: super-cv achievements (Fortinet TAC P3, Netskope CSM and Scale CSM, SYKES)
M11.01 STAR bank (I2.s01–I2.s12) for the core stories
Cato cheatsheet: answer frameworks only (behavioural skeleton, 'why us' close); its unverified figures stay out

units.title: What the hiring manager is deciding
units.body:
The recruiter checked fit on paper. The **PS manager** decides whether to put you in front of their customers, alone, soon. Under the questions are four worries:

1. **Can you deliver?** Will a FortiGate, FortiManager or SD-WAN deployment be designed, executed and handed over properly, inside the hours sold?
2. **Will customers trust you?** On a kickoff call, in a tense change window, in an escalation.
3. **How fast will you ramp?** How much hand-holding before you're billable and independent.
4. **Will you make the team better?** Documentation, templates, helping colleagues, honest status.

## How PS makes money

PS sells **hours or fixed-price projects** under a **statement of work (SOW)**. The manager watches **utilization** (billable time), **scope** (what's in the SOW, and what's a **change request**), **milestones** and **customer acceptance** (sign-off). Show you understand that delivering what was sold, on time, with a signed acceptance, is the job; extra work goes through a change request, not a favour.

## Your angle

You are the rare candidate who has seen both sides: **inside Fortinet support** (you know how FortiOS fails and how TAC and development work) and **owning customers** at Netskope (rollouts, health checks, executive reviews, finishing a partner's half-delivered PS project). Your answers should keep connecting those two.

:::recall
Q: Four worries under the hiring manager's questions?
A: Can you deliver, will customers trust you, how fast will you ramp, will you make the team better.
:::

:::tip
Answer in **STAR-L**: Situation, Task, Action, Result, and one line of Learning. 60–90 seconds. Most of the time goes on Action.
:::

units.title: Your story bank, mapped to competencies
units.body:
Use only evidenced stories. The core twelve are in M11.01; this table tells you which one answers which question.

| Competency asked | Best story | Proof point |
|---|---|---|
| Delivery, finishing work | Partner PS project left half done, finished in stages | You acted as the QA layer on partner PS work |
| Rollout without disruption | Account below 50 % utilisation | One-month planned rollout, 70 % utilisation, nothing got out of hand |
| Hostile customer | Escalation turned into a license exchange | More than USD 900k contract value kept |
| New stakeholders | Whole security team replaced | Health check first; over half the seats in use within six weeks |
| Value and renewals | Book from red to green | Around 60 % of ~60 named accounts moved to green |
| Technical depth | SD-WAN packet duplication over three ISPs | Traced to SLA settings; about two months with development |
| Hard recovery | Cloud HA split brain | Recovered by comparing checksums, reachable only via heartbeat; others escalated these |
| Test before production | Shared Terraform templates | Reproduced customer scenarios before recommending fixes |
| Proactive risk | CVE advisory to every account | The one late adopter contained a small compromise quickly |
| Executive communication | QBRs with C-level and VPs | Eased most renewals; in three languages |
| Teamwork, mentoring | Onboarded new CSMs; mentored engineers | Without a formal reporting line |
| Building tools | Python and AI workflows | Health-check generator, license analysis, activity trackers |

## Rules for numbers

- Say exactly what's in your evidence. "Around 60 %", "more than half within six weeks", "more than 900 thousand dollars".
- The telemetry model for 2,000+ accounts was **co-built with your team**: say "with my team".
- "Near-zero unsanctioned AI" applies to **a couple of accounts**, not dozens.
- Leave out the unverified Cato cheatsheet figures.

:::pitfall
Don't tell three stories in one answer. One story, told well, with a number and a learning, beats a list of achievements.
:::

units.title: Hard questions, your 30-60-90, and your questions
units.body:
## The three hard questions

- **"Have you led full Fortinet implementations end to end?"** Honest no, then bridge: you've done every piece (designs from requirements in TAC, rollouts and health checks at Netskope, finishing partner PS work, change-window recoveries), and you're refreshing the current versions. Don't claim projects you haven't run.
- **"Why did you leave Netskope?"** The same short, neutral, forward-looking answer as with the recruiter. Keep private details private.
- **"Your certifications expired."** They lapsed while you worked on another platform; you're re-studying FortiOS 8.0, FortiManager 7.6 and FortiAnalyzer now, with a re-certification plan.

## Bring a 30-60-90 plan

You built 30-60-90 plans for customers at Netskope. Show one for yourself:

- **30 days:** onboarding, internal tools and templates, shadow two projects, labs on the current FortiOS, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer, first re-certification booked.
- **60 days:** lead parts of projects with a senior consultant reviewing (design document, MOP, change window); contribute one template improvement.
- **90 days:** run smaller projects independently from kickoff to acceptance; customer feedback and utilization on target.

## Questions to ask the hiring manager

- "What does a typical project look like here: size, products, on-site versus remote?"
- "How do you measure a consultant in the first six months? Utilization, CSAT, certifications?"
- "Where do projects usually go wrong, and what would you want me to do differently?"
- "How do PS and TAC work together on escalations during a project?"

:::recall
Q: What does your 90-day milestone promise?
A: Running smaller projects independently from kickoff to customer acceptance, with feedback and utilization on target.
:::

scenarios.title: "Walk me through your first week on a project"
scenarios.situation: The hiring manager says: "You're assigned a FortiGate HA pair and FortiManager rollout for a bank. Walk me through your first week."
scenarios.ask: Answer in about 90 seconds.
right_thinking: Start from the SOW and pre-sales handoff, not from the CLI
Kickoff: stakeholders, scope, success criteria, change process, access
Discovery: current design, constraints, banking change windows and approvals
End the week with an agreed plan and design draft
scenarios.what: A structured first-week plan.
scenarios.why: It shows you think about scope, people and risk before configuration.
scenarios.model_answer: Day one, I'd read the SOW and the pre-sales handoff so I know exactly what was sold and the success criteria. Then the kickoff: who the stakeholders are, the scope, how changes are approved in a bank, maintenance windows and remote access. The next days are discovery: current topology, policies to migrate, HA and FortiManager requirements, logging and compliance needs. I'd raise risks early, like change-freeze dates. By the end of the week the customer has an agreed plan and a first design draft to review. From TAC I know where these deployments go wrong, so I'd build those checks into the plan.
scenarios.best_way: SOW and handoff, kickoff, discovery, risks, and an agreed plan with a design draft by Friday.

scenarios.title: "What would you do if you were behind schedule?"
scenarios.situation: The manager asks: "You're two days behind on a fixed-price project because the customer's team didn't provide access. What do you do?"
scenarios.ask: Answer with action and communication.
right_thinking: Escalate early and in writing, with facts
Show impact on dates and hours
Propose options; don't absorb unbilled time silently
Keep the relationship positive
scenarios.what: An early, factual escalation with options.
scenarios.why: Surprises at the end hurt both the customer and the PS margin.
how: Offer options: replan, parallel tasks, change request
Confirm the new plan in writing
scenarios.model_answer: I'd raise it the same day, in writing: what access was needed, when we asked, and the impact on the plan. I'd tell my manager or the PM, and the customer's sponsor, with options: work on tasks that don't need the access, move the dates, or if the delay adds hours, a change request. Then I confirm the agreed plan by email. I did this kind of escalation at Netskope with a support backlog before a rollout: going early to the right person with facts got it moving.
scenarios.best_way: Raise it the same day with facts and options, and confirm the new plan in writing.

scenarios.title: What if the manager pushes on the CSM background?
scenarios.situation: "Customer success is relationship work. PS is hands-on engineering. Aren't you more of an account manager now?"
scenarios.ask: Respond without being defensive.
right_thinking: Agree on the distinction
Show the hands-on parts of your CSM work and your TAC base
End with why PS is the natural next step
scenarios.what: A confident reframe with evidence.
scenarios.why: It's the core doubt about your profile.
how: Evidence: health checks auditing live config, rollouts, finishing partner PS, TAC escalations
scenarios.model_answer: That's a fair distinction. My CSM work was unusually technical: I audited live configurations in dozens of health checks, planned rollouts with partners, and finished a partner's half-done PS project. Before that I spent over two years as a TAC escalation engineer on FortiOS, working from packet captures and debugs. PS is where I combine both: hands-on delivery, with the customer skills to keep the project on track.
scenarios.best_way: Fair point, but my CSM work was hands-on, and my base is two years of FortiOS escalations. PS combines both.

interview.question: Tell me about the most technically complex problem you solved.
interview.model_answer: "At Fortinet, a customer had packet duplication across three ISPs over VPN with SD-WAN. Situation: intermittent application problems nobody could pin down. I reproduced it, analysed captures and SD-WAN behaviour, and traced it to specific SLA settings. Because it was a product defect, I worked with development for almost two months with clean reproductions. Learning: clean, reproducible evidence is what gets development to move."
interview.best_way: SD-WAN packet duplication over three ISPs, traced to SLA settings, fixed with development.

interview.question: Tell me about a time you had to win over new stakeholders.
interview.model_answer: "An account's whole security team was replaced. The previous team wanted Netskope out over DLP problems and had gone silent for months. I opened with the new team with a health check of their live configuration, then followed its recommendations with them. Within six weeks more than half the seats were in use. Learning: start with something useful to them, not with a sales conversation."
interview.best_way: New team, health check first, more than half the seats in use within six weeks.

interview.question: How do you make sure a customer sees value from what they bought?
interview.model_answer: "I tie the platform to their own objectives with a 30-60-90 plan, measure progress, and review it at a regular cadence. At Netskope I did that across about 60 named accounts and moved around 60 % of them from red to green, mostly because customers who had had no contact beyond support finally had someone setting the why and the how."
interview.best_way: Objectives first, a measurable plan, a cadence. Around 60 % of my book went from red to green.

interview.question: Tell me about a time you prevented a problem before it happened.
interview.model_answer: "When a critical CVE affected our customers' environments, I sent every account the remediation steps proactively instead of waiting for tickets. The one account that adopted late had a couple of endpoints compromised, but contained it quickly because the steps were already in hand. Learning: proactive communication pays off even with the customers who don't act immediately."
interview.best_way: Sent CVE remediation to every account proactively; even the late adopter contained it fast.

interview.question: How do you test changes before you apply them to production?
interview.model_answer: "I reproduce first. At Fortinet I used shared Terraform templates to stand up environments matching the customer's scenario, so the fix I recommended had been validated. In PS I'd do the same with a lab or the customer's test environment, and every change has a MOP with pre-checks and a rollback."
interview.best_way: Reproduce in a lab first, then a MOP with pre-checks and rollback.

interview.question: Tell me about a recovery under pressure.
interview.model_answer: "Cloud FortiGate HA clusters in split brain, where the only path in was the heartbeat interface. Others on my team escalated those straight away; I recovered them by comparing configuration checksums and re-syncing manually, step by step with the customer. Learning: a calm method and clear communication matter as much as the commands."
interview.best_way: Recovered cloud HA split-brain clusters via the heartbeat path by comparing checksums and re-syncing.

interview.question: How do you communicate with executives?
interview.model_answer: "In their terms: where they're heading, risk and value, not features. I ran QBRs with C-level and VPs at Netskope, in English, Spanish and Portuguese, built around their roadmap, and that eased most renewals. I also turned log data into compliance evidence for SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI-DSS that a board could read."
interview.best_way: Their roadmap, risk and value; QBRs with C-level in three languages.

interview.question: How do you work with partners?
interview.model_answer: "As a second customer layer, usually more technical. At Netskope I planned technical initiatives and health-check proposals with partners like Cloudrise, AccessIT Group, CDW and Deloitte across NAM and LATAM, and when a partner's PS project was left half done, I finished it in stages. At Fortinet PS I'd expect to deliver alongside partners, so I'd agree roles and quality checks up front."
interview.best_way: Partners are a second, more technical customer: agree roles and quality checks up front.

interview.question: What do you do when you don't know the answer in front of a customer?
interview.model_answer: "I say so, tell them when they'll have the answer, and follow through. Then I use the right resources: documentation, a lab, colleagues, or TAC. Customers trust a consultant who says 'I'll confirm that by tomorrow' far more than one who guesses."
interview.best_way: Admit it, commit to a time, and follow through.

interview.question: How do you organise your work across several projects?
interview.model_answer: "One tracker, a weekly status, and automation for the repetitive parts. At Netskope I built Python and AI workflows: a health-check report generator, a license-analysis tool and an activity tracker that summarised every account touched in a week. In PS I'd keep one view of milestones, risks and hours per project."
interview.best_way: One tracker, weekly status, automation; I built my own tools for it.

interview.question: Tell me about a time you used data to change a decision.
interview.model_answer: "A customer planned to cut half their web gateway licences for budget reasons. After a value QBR showing what they were actually using and what they needed next, they kept the budget and moved it into ZTNA instead of dropping it. With my team, I also co-built the telemetry model that decided which of 2,000+ accounts needed hands-on time."
interview.best_way: A value QBR turned a budget cut into a licence exchange into ZTNA.

interview.question: Why should I hire you over someone with more PS years?
interview.model_answer: "Three reasons. I know FortiOS from the inside, as a former TAC escalation engineer, so I'll prevent the problems I used to fix. I've owned customers and finished delivery work others left half done, so the customer side won't need coaching. And I build tools and templates that make a team faster. Add three languages and full travel availability, and I think the ramp-up is short and the upside is high."
interview.best_way: Inside FortiOS knowledge, proven customer ownership, and I make teams faster.

interview.question: What would your first 90 days look like?
interview.model_answer: "First 30 days: onboarding, your templates and tools, shadowing two projects, labs on the current FortiOS, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer, and my first re-certification booked. By 60: leading parts of projects with a senior consultant reviewing my designs and MOPs. By 90: running smaller projects from kickoff to acceptance myself. I built plans like this for customers at Netskope; this one's for me."
interview.best_way: Shadow, then lead with review, then independent projects by day 90.

interview.question: How do you handle feedback that you disagree with?
interview.framework: Listen → understand → act or discuss with evidence
interview.model_answer: "I listen first and ask for an example, because I may be missing context. If it's right, I change it and say so. If I still disagree, I bring evidence and discuss it privately, then commit to the decision. That's how I worked with development at Fortinet: evidence, not opinions."
interview.best_way: Listen, ask for an example, act on it, or disagree with evidence and then commit.

interview.question: What questions do you have for me?
interview.model_answer: "What does a typical project look like here, size, products, on-site versus remote? How will you measure me in the first six months? And where do projects usually go wrong, and what would you want me to do differently?"
interview.best_way: Typical project, how I'm measured, and where projects go wrong.

units.title: How a technical panel works
units.body:
A PS technical panel usually has three parts: **rapid-fire questions** (concepts and commands), a **whiteboard design** (draw a solution for a scenario) and a **troubleshooting walk-through** (here's a symptom, find the cause). They're testing three things at once: **knowledge**, **method** and **how you'd sound in front of a customer**.

## Five habits that score

1. **Clarify before you draw.** Ask 3–4 questions: users and sites, bandwidth, availability target, compliance, what exists today. Panels often hide a requirement to see if you ask.
2. **Think out loud.** Silence reads as stuck. Narrate: "First I'd confirm… then…".
3. **State assumptions.** "I'll assume two ISPs per branch and a hub in each data centre."
4. **Justify and give trade-offs.** "A-P rather than A-A because it's simpler to operate and the throughput fits."
5. **Say what you'd verify.** "I believe the default is X; I'd confirm in the release notes before the change." Honest beats confident and wrong.

## Your edge

You've seen how these designs fail from TAC: asymmetric routing with SD-WAN, NAT order, HA split brain, MTU over VPN. Mention the failure mode you'd design out: it's what separates a consultant from someone who memorised the guide.

:::recall
Q: First thing to do when given a whiteboard scenario?
A: Ask clarifying questions and state assumptions before drawing.
:::

units.title: The packet flow, your troubleshooting map
units.body:
Explain the life of a packet in a FortiGate at a high level, then use it to place any problem:

1. **Ingress** on an interface (with DoS policy checks if configured)
2. **IPsec decryption** if it arrives on a tunnel
3. **Destination NAT** (VIP)
4. **Routing** decision (policy routes, SD-WAN rules, then the routing table)
5. **Firewall policy** lookup and session creation
6. **Security profiles** (flow or proxy inspection)
7. **Source NAT**
8. **IPsec encryption** if leaving through a tunnel
9. **Egress**

`diagnose debug flow` shows the same story: *received a packet* → *allocate a new session* → *find a route* → *DNAT/SNAT* → *Allowed by Policy-N* or *Denied by forward policy check*.

## A method you can say in one breath

**Define → isolate → prove → fix → verify → document.**

- **Define:** who, what, since when, what changed, one or all users.
- **Isolate** with the layers: is the packet arriving (sniffer)? Is it allowed and routed (debug flow)? Is the session there and offloaded (session list)? Is the reply coming back?
- **Prove** with output, not opinion.
- **Fix** in a window with a rollback; **verify** with the user; **document** the cause.

:::pitfall
Debug flow shows only the first packets of a session that's offloaded to the NPU. If you need to see the whole flow in a lab, disable offload on that policy temporarily, and say so to the panel.
:::

units.title: Whiteboard patterns to have ready
units.body:
## Branch SD-WAN with a hub

Two ISPs per branch, IPsec overlays to one or two hubs, **BGP over the overlays**, SD-WAN zones (Underlay, Overlay), health checks to the hub and to SaaS, rules: voice **Best Quality**, business apps **Lowest Cost (SLA)**, backups **Maximize Bandwidth**. Managed from **FortiManager** templates, logs to **FortiAnalyzer**. Risk to mention: asymmetric routing and SLA probes that don't reflect the application path.

## Data-centre HA pair

**FGCP A-P**, two back-to-back heartbeat links, session pickup for long-lived sessions, monitored uplinks, reserved management interfaces, uninterruptible upgrades. Risk: split brain if heartbeats share a switch; override behaviour surprising the customer.

## Remote access

**IPsec dial-up with FortiClient** (IKEv2, EAP, MFA via FortiToken or SAML), split or full tunnel by policy, or **ZTNA** for application-level access with posture checks. Risk: VPN gateways are top targets: patch cadence and restricting IKE exposure.

## Security operations stack

FortiGates with tuned security profiles → **FortiAnalyzer** (logs, reports, incidents) → **FortiSIEM** for multi-vendor correlation, **FortiEDR** on endpoints, automation stitches for response. Risk: logging everything without retention planning.

## Answer shape for any design

**Requirements → diagram → key choices with reasons → failure modes and how you designed them out → operations (management, logging, upgrades) → acceptance tests.**

:::ps
End every design with "and here's how we'd prove it works": the acceptance tests. It's what customers sign, and panels love it.
:::

scenarios.title: Whiteboard: 40 branches, 2 data centres
scenarios.situation: "We have 40 branches with two internet links each, two data centres, Microsoft 365 and an on-prem ERP. Design the network security and WAN."
scenarios.ask: Talk through it as you would at the whiteboard, in 3–4 minutes.
right_thinking: Clarify: availability, voice, compliance, team skills, existing gear
Hub-and-spoke overlays to both DCs, BGP, SD-WAN rules per app
HA pairs in the DCs, FortiManager templates, FortiAnalyzer logs
Failure modes and acceptance tests
scenarios.what: A structured design with reasons and risks.
scenarios.why: It's exactly what you'd do in a design workshop.
scenarios.model_answer: I'd start with questions: uptime target, voice at branches, compliance like PCI, and who operates it. Assuming two ISPs per branch: each branch FortiGate builds IPsec overlays to both data centres, with BGP over the overlays so the DCs are reachable over either. SD-WAN zones for underlay and overlay; health checks to the hubs and to Microsoft 365; rules: voice on Best Quality, ERP over the overlay with Lowest Cost (SLA), Microsoft 365 straight out locally using the Internet Service Database. In each DC an FGCP active-passive pair with two heartbeat links and session pickup. Everything is templated in FortiManager, logs go to FortiAnalyzer. Failure modes I'd design out: asymmetric routing between the two hubs, probes that don't reflect the app path, and split brain in the DCs. Acceptance tests: pull each ISP at a pilot branch, fail over each hub, and fail the DC primary during a call.
scenarios.best_way: Clarify, overlays to both DCs with BGP, SD-WAN rules per app, HA pairs, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer, failure modes, acceptance tests.

right_thinking: Define: which apps, since when, what changed
Tunnel state and counters
Small works, large fails → MTU/MSS
Prove, fix, verify
scenarios.what: A narrated, evidence-based diagnosis.
scenarios.why: Panels judge method and communication as much as the answer.
how: get vpn ipsec tunnel summary / diagnose vpn tunnel list
scenarios.model_answer: First I'd define it: is it all branch users, since when, did anything change, and does browsing small pages work while uploads fail? Then I'd check the tunnel: summary and tunnel list, phase 2 up and counters moving both ways. If small requests work and big transfers fail, I suspect MTU: ESP overhead means full-size packets don't fit, and if ICMP 'fragmentation needed' is blocked, hosts never adjust. I'd prove it with pings with the don't-fragment bit at decreasing sizes and a sniffer showing retransmissions. The fix is clamping TCP MSS on both tunnel policies. Then I'd verify with the users and document it, and add the MSS setting to the VPN template so the next site doesn't repeat it.
scenarios.best_way: Define it, check the tunnel, small-works-big-fails means MTU, prove with DF pings, clamp MSS, verify, template it.

scenarios.title: What if the panelist challenges your answer?
scenarios.situation: You say SD-WAN rules come after policy routes. A panelist says, "Are you sure? I think SD-WAN rules win."
scenarios.ask: How do you respond?
right_thinking: Stay calm; it may be a test
Explain your reasoning and how you'd verify
Offer the evidence: the commands that show the decision
scenarios.what: A confident, respectful correction with evidence.
scenarios.why: Customers will challenge you too.
scenarios.model_answer: I'd say: "My understanding is that policy routes are checked first, then SD-WAN rules, then the routing table. I've seen it in migrations, where a leftover policy route bypassed a new SD-WAN rule. To confirm on a live unit, diagnose firewall proute list shows the policy routes and SD-WAN rules in the order they're applied, and diagnose ip proute match shows what a given packet would use. Happy to be corrected if a newer version changed it."
scenarios.best_way: Respectfully hold your position with the reasoning and the command that proves it.

interview.question: Walk me through what happens to a packet entering a FortiGate.
interview.framework: Ordered steps → how you use it
interview.model_answer: "It arrives on an interface, DoS checks apply if configured, it's decrypted if it came through a tunnel, then destination NAT if it matches a VIP. Then the routing decision: policy routes, SD-WAN rules, routing table. Then the firewall policy lookup and session creation, security profiles, source NAT, encryption if it leaves through a tunnel, and egress. I use that order when troubleshooting: debug flow shows exactly where a packet stops."
interview.best_way: Ingress, decrypt, DNAT, route, policy, profiles, SNAT, encrypt, egress, and debug flow shows where it stops.

interview.question: A user can't reach a server through the FortiGate. Go.
interview.framework: Define → sniffer → debug flow → session → fix
interview.model_answer: "First the facts: source, destination, port, one user or all, what changed. Then the sniffer on the ingress and egress interfaces to see whether the packet arrives and leaves. If it arrives and doesn't leave, a filtered debug flow tells me the route and the policy decision, or the drop reason. If it leaves and nothing returns, I look downstream and at the return route. Then fix in a window and verify with the user."
interview.best_way: Facts, sniffer, debug flow, then downstream; fix and verify.

interview.question: How does FortiGate choose between policy routes, SD-WAN rules and the routing table?
interview.model_answer: "Policy routes first, then SD-WAN rules, then the routing table. And by default an SD-WAN rule is only consulted if the best route for the destination points to an SD-WAN member. In migrations, leftover policy routes or more specific static routes are the classic reason a new SD-WAN rule seems to be ignored."
interview.best_way: Policy routes, SD-WAN rules, routing table, with the FIB check for SD-WAN.

interview.question: Explain the order of NAT and policy matching with a VIP.
interview.model_answer: "Destination NAT happens before routing and the policy lookup, so the policy for a VIP matches the VIP object or the mapped address depending on configuration, and VIP policies take priority. Source NAT is applied after the policy. I was my TAC team's go-to for NAT, and the common customer mistake was writing the policy against the public IP instead of the VIP."
interview.best_way: DNAT before routing and policy, SNAT after; most errors are policies written against the wrong address.

interview.question: Design remote access for 500 users with MFA.
interview.model_answer: "Two options: IPsec dial-up with FortiClient, IKEv2 with EAP and MFA via FortiToken or SAML to their identity provider, or ZTNA if they want per-application access with device posture. For 500 users I'd usually start with IPsec dial-up for full-tunnel needs and plan ZTNA for sensitive apps. Either way: patch the gateway fast, limit who can reach IKE, and log to FortiAnalyzer."
interview.best_way: IPsec dial-up with IKEv2 and MFA now, ZTNA for sensitive apps, and harden the gateway.

interview.question: How would you migrate a customer from another firewall vendor to FortiGate?
interview.framework: Discover → convert → clean → test → cut over
interview.model_answer: "Discover the current config and what's actually used, convert with FortiConverter or a scripted approach, then clean up: unused objects, shadowed and overly broad rules, NAT semantics that differ between vendors. Test in a lab, write a MOP with a rollback, cut over in a window, and validate with the customer's application owners. The NAT translation is where most migrations break, so I review it line by line."
interview.best_way: Discover, convert, clean, lab-test, MOP with rollback, cut over, validate. NAT is where they break.

interview.question: What's the difference between FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer, and why deploy both?
interview.model_answer: "FortiManager is central configuration: devices, policy packages, templates, installs and revisions. FortiAnalyzer is central logging and analytics: log storage, FortiView, reports, incidents and automation. Together: you change many FortiGates consistently and you can prove what happened afterwards."
interview.best_way: FortiManager changes things consistently; FortiAnalyzer proves what happened.

interview.question: A customer's FortiGate is in conserve mode. What does that mean and what do you do?
interview.model_answer: "Memory is under pressure: by default it enters red conserve mode at 88 % memory, recovers below 82 %, and extreme at 95 %. Proxy-based inspection may stop accepting new sessions that need it. I'd check memory consumers and sessions, and look at proxy usage. At Fortinet I reduced memory pressure for customers by moving policies from proxy to flow inspection where proxy wasn't needed, which also kept more traffic on the NPU."
interview.best_way: Memory pressure at 88 %. Find the consumers; move proxy policies to flow where proxy isn't needed.

interview.question: How do you deploy SSL deep inspection without breaking users?
interview.model_answer: "Use a CA from the customer's PKI, push it by Group Policy and MDM before enabling anything, pilot with IT, exempt banking, health and pinned apps, then roll out by department with a rollback to certificate inspection. I taught customers exactly this, pushing the CA through Group Policy."
interview.best_way: CA first via GPO and MDM, pilot, exemptions, phases.

interview.question: What do you check after a cluster upgrade?
interview.model_answer: "Both units on the target version, get system ha status showing in sync with heartbeats up, the expected primary, routing and VPN tunnels up, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer connectivity, and the customer's own application test list. Then a short report. I've guided customers through HA upgrades step by step, including a manual console upgrade when the online one failed, so I always have the backup and console ready."
interview.best_way: Versions, HA in sync, routing and VPNs, FMG/FAZ, the customer's test list, then a report.

interview.question: Tell us about a Fortinet issue you escalated to development.
interview.model_answer: "SD-WAN with three ISPs over VPN was duplicating packets. I reproduced it, traced it to specific SLA settings with captures, and worked with development for almost two months with reproductions until the fix."
interview.best_way: Packet duplication over three ISPs traced to SLA settings; clean reproductions to development.

interview.question: Which logs and reports would you set up for a new deployment?
interview.model_answer: "Traffic logs on the policies that matter, all security events, and system events, sent to FortiAnalyzer with retention sized to the customer's compliance needs. Then scheduled reports for the security team and executives, and alerts for critical events. I've turned log data into SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI-DSS evidence for boards, so I start from what they need to prove."
interview.best_way: Log what matters to FortiAnalyzer, size retention to compliance, scheduled reports and alerts.

field_reports.title: The edge is the target
field_reports.body: Vulnerability exploitation was the top initial access vector in the 2026 DBIR (**31 %**). Panels like candidates who design for that: patchable, segmented, logged, with IPS covering the patch gap.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR

modules.title: Transport, state and NAT theory
objectives: Explain TCP setup, teardown and reset, and what a stateful firewall remembers about each flow
Explain how UDP and ICMP get "state" on a firewall even though they have none themselves
Tell SNAT, DNAT, PAT and hairpin NAT apart and say when each is used
Explain MTU, MSS and why large transfers stall over tunnels while small pages work
Explain why some protocols (FTP active mode, SIP) need a session helper or ALG to survive NAT
