FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: IP pool types (pp. 2166–2170), Hairpin NAT (pp. 2229–2231)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Asymmetric routing (pp. 653–655)
RFC 9293 (TCP), RFC 768 (UDP), RFC 3022 (NAT) — general knowledge

units.title: TCP from SYN to FIN, as a firewall sees it
units.body:
TCP gives applications a reliable, ordered byte stream on top of IP, which is happy to lose, duplicate or reorder packets. It does this with **sequence numbers**, **acknowledgements**, a **receive window** and a strict **connection life cycle**. A firewall engineer doesn't need to memorise every RFC detail, but must be able to read that life cycle in a capture and explain it to a customer.

## Setup: the three-way handshake

1. **SYN**: the client picks an initial sequence number and asks to open a connection. Options travel here too, most importantly the **MSS** (the largest segment it can receive).
2. **SYN/ACK**: the server answers with its own sequence number and acknowledges the client's.
3. **ACK**: the client acknowledges the server. The connection is now *established* and data flows.

If the server port is closed, the server (or a firewall in between) answers the SYN with a **RST**. If nothing answers at all, the client retries the SYN with growing back-off: that is the classic "connection timed out" a user sees when a firewall silently drops traffic.

## Teardown: FIN versus RST

A graceful close uses **FIN** in each direction, each acknowledged. The side that closes first waits in **TIME_WAIT** so late packets from the old connection can't pollute a new one. A **RST** tears the connection down immediately with no goodbye. RSTs are normal in small doses (a browser abandoning a tab) but a burst of them points at a middlebox or an application crashing.

## What a stateful firewall remembers

A stateful firewall evaluates the **first packet** of a flow against the policy table. If a policy allows it, the firewall creates a **session** keyed by the 5-tuple: source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port and protocol. Every later packet, in both directions, is matched against that session instead of the whole policy table. That is why you only write a policy for the direction that *starts* the conversation: replies ride the session.

FortiOS can also check that TCP packets make sense for the session's state. The **anti-replay** option checks TCP flags per policy, so a stray ACK that doesn't belong to a known handshake is dropped.

:::recall
Q: Why does a firewall only need a policy for the direction that opens a TCP connection?
A: The first packet creates a session (5-tuple). Replies match the session, not the policy table, so the return direction is allowed automatically.
:::

:::why
Q: Why is "connection timed out" usually a silent drop while "connection refused" is usually a RST?
A: A drop gives the client nothing back, so it keeps retrying the SYN until it gives up. A RST is an explicit answer that the port is closed or the connection was rejected.
:::

:::tip
On a support call, ask "timed out or refused?" first. It tells you whether to look for a drop (routing, policy, RPF) or for an active reject (closed port, server firewall, IPS reset).
:::

units.title: UDP, ICMP and session timers
units.body:
**UDP** has no handshake, no acknowledgements and no teardown. DNS, NTP, syslog, SNMP, RADIUS, voice media (RTP) and QUIC all run on it. A firewall still builds a session for UDP: the first packet that matches a policy creates a 5-tuple entry, and the reply matches it. The difference is how the session ends. With no FIN, the firewall relies on a **timer**: if the session sees no packets for its time-to-live, it is removed.

**ICMP** is the network's messenger: echo request and reply (ping), destination unreachable, time exceeded (traceroute), and "fragmentation needed" (path MTU discovery). Firewalls track echo using the ICMP identifier so a reply can match its request.

## Session TTL

Every protocol has a session time-to-live: how long an idle session stays in the table. FortiOS lets you change it globally and **per policy** with `set session-ttl <seconds>` (or `never` for a few special cases). Two classic problems come from TTLs:

- **Too short:** a database or ERP client keeps an idle TCP connection open for an hour. The firewall drops the idle session after its TTL, the next packet arrives with no session and is dropped, and users see "the app freezes after lunch".
- **Too long:** huge numbers of dead UDP sessions fill the table on a busy gateway.

:::recall
Q: How does a firewall know a UDP "conversation" is over?
A: It doesn't get a signal. The session expires when it has been idle for longer than its TTL.
:::

:::pitfall
Raising the TTL for one application is fine on its own policy. Raising it globally to fix one app can bloat the session table for everyone.
:::

:::cli
config firewall policy
    edit 12
        set session-ttl 7200
    next
end
:::

:::why
Q: Why might a VoIP phone lose incoming calls after a few minutes of quiet even though outgoing calls always work?
A: The phone's registration and the pinhole for incoming SIP live in a UDP session. If the session expires before the phone re-registers, inbound INVITEs find no session and are dropped.
:::

units.title: NAT, PAT and hairpin NAT
units.body:
**Network Address Translation** rewrites addresses as packets cross the firewall, and the session remembers the rewrite so replies can be translated back.

| Type | What changes | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **SNAT** | Source IP (and often port) | Users going out to the internet |
| **PAT** (overload) | Source IP *and* port, many users share one IP | Almost every office internet edge |
| **Static 1:1** | One inside IP always maps to one outside IP | A server that must always appear from the same address |
| **DNAT** | Destination IP (and optionally port) | Publishing an internal server (FortiOS calls this a VIP) |
| **Hairpin** | Both, for inside users reaching an inside server by its public address | Bookmarks with public names that must work in the office too |

## How many users fit behind one IP?

PAT distinguishes sessions by the translated source port. FortiOS documents **60,416 usable ports per IP** in an overload IP pool. The limit applies **per destination service** (same protocol, destination IP and port), so a single public IP supports far more than 60,416 total sessions as long as they go to different destinations. When many users hammer the *same* service, a pool with more IPs, or a fixed-port-range / port-block-allocation pool, is the answer.

## Hairpin NAT

A user inside the office types `portal.company.com`, which resolves to the public IP. The packet goes to the FortiGate, which sees its own external address as the destination, applies the VIP (DNAT) **and** must make the server reply back through the firewall. FortiOS's hairpin example uses a VIP plus a policy for the DNAT and a SNAT policy so the return traffic comes back through the FortiGate. Split DNS (an internal answer with the private IP) is the alternative that avoids hairpinning.

:::recall
Q: Why does PAT need to change the source port, not just the source IP?
A: Many inside hosts share one outside IP. The translated source port is what lets the firewall tell their sessions apart and send replies to the right host.
:::

:::why
Q: Why do inside users sometimes fail to reach their own published web server by its public name, while internet users can?
A: Without hairpin NAT (or split DNS) the inside user's packet to the public IP is either not translated or the server replies directly to the inside client, bypassing the firewall, so the session breaks.
:::

:::threat ref=dbir-2026-vuln-exploitation-31pct
Every DNAT/VIP publishes a service to the internet. Exploiting vulnerabilities is now the top initial access vector at 31 % of breaches (Verizon DBIR 2026). Each VIP you configure for a customer needs an owner, a patch plan and IPS on its policy.
:::

units.title: MTU, MSS and protocols that fight NAT
units.body:
## MTU and MSS

The **MTU** is the largest IP packet a link carries: 1500 bytes on standard Ethernet. The **MSS** is the largest TCP payload: MTU minus the IP header (20) and TCP header (20), so **1460** on plain Ethernet. Each side announces its MSS in the SYN.

Tunnels and encapsulations add headers: PPPoE adds 8 bytes, GRE 24, IPsec ESP typically 50–80 depending on cipher and NAT-T. If a full-size packet no longer fits and the sender set "don't fragment", a router should send back **ICMP fragmentation needed** so the sender lowers its packet size (path MTU discovery). When that ICMP is blocked somewhere, small exchanges work but full-size packets vanish. Users report: **"the page half-loads", "small emails send but attachments hang", "SSH works but file copy stalls"**.

## The fix: MSS clamping

The firewall rewrites the MSS option in the SYN so both ends agree to smaller segments that fit the tunnel. In FortiOS you can clamp per policy:

:::cli
config firewall policy
    edit 10
        set tcp-mss-sender 1350
        set tcp-mss-receiver 1350
    next
end
:::

You can also set `tcp-mss` on an interface. Clamping only helps TCP; UDP-heavy apps over tunnels still need a correct MTU.

## Protocols that carry addresses inside the payload

NAT rewrites headers. Some protocols also write IP addresses and ports **inside the payload**:

- **FTP active mode**: the client tells the server, in the PORT command, which IP and port to connect back to. Behind NAT that is a private address the server can't reach.
- **SIP** (VoIP signalling): SDP bodies carry the IP and ports for the RTP media streams.

Firewalls solve this with **session helpers / ALGs**: they read the control channel, rewrite the embedded addresses and open the expected secondary connection (a pinhole). When helpers fight with a phone system that already handles NAT itself, you get **one-way audio** or calls that drop at 30 seconds, and the fix is to decide which side does NAT traversal, not both.

:::recall
Q: What MSS does a host announce on a standard 1500-byte Ethernet link, and why?
A: 1460: 1500 MTU minus 20 bytes of IP header and 20 bytes of TCP header.
:::

:::why
Q: Why do large downloads stall over an IPsec tunnel while web pages with small objects still load?
A: Full-size packets exceed the tunnel MTU after ESP overhead. If the ICMP "fragmentation needed" messages are lost, the sender keeps sending packets that are dropped. Small packets fit and pass. MSS clamping fixes it for TCP.
:::

:::ps
In a cutover plan, add an MSS test (a large file copy and an HTTPS download through each new tunnel) to the acceptance checklist. It catches the problem before users do.
:::

cards.front: Name the three packets of the TCP handshake in order.
cards.back: SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK.

cards.front: Which TCP option, sent in the SYN, announces the largest segment a host can receive?
cards.back: MSS (maximum segment size).

cards.front: What five fields identify a firewall session?
cards.back: Source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port, protocol (the 5-tuple).

cards.front: A user says 'connection refused'. What did the client most likely receive?
cards.back: A TCP RST: the port is closed or something actively rejected the connection.

cards.front: Which TCP state does the side that closes first wait in, and why?
cards.back: TIME_WAIT, so late packets from the old connection can't be mistaken for a new one.

cards.front: What does the FortiOS per-policy `anti-replay` option check?
cards.back: TCP flags, so packets that don't fit the session's TCP state are dropped.

cards.front: How does a UDP session leave a firewall's session table?
cards.back: When it is idle longer than its session TTL; UDP has no FIN.

cards.front: FortiOS CLI to give one policy's sessions a 2-hour TTL?
cards.back: `set session-ttl 7200` under that policy in `config firewall policy`.

cards.front: Symptom of a session TTL that is too short for an app with long idle connections?
cards.back: The app freezes after being idle; the next packet finds no session and is dropped.

cards.front: Which ICMP message drives path MTU discovery?
cards.back: Destination unreachable – fragmentation needed (DF set).

cards.front: SNAT vs DNAT in one line each.
cards.back: SNAT rewrites the source (users going out). DNAT rewrites the destination (publishing a server inside).

cards.front: What does FortiOS call a DNAT object?
cards.back: A virtual IP (VIP).

cards.front: How many usable ports per IP does FortiOS document for an overload IP pool?
cards.back: 60,416 per IP, per destination service (protocol, destination IP and port).
Letting inside users reach an inside server through its public address: DNAT to the server plus SNAT so replies return through the firewall.

cards.front: Alternative to hairpin NAT for inside users?
cards.back: Split DNS: inside resolvers answer with the server's private IP.

cards.front: MSS on a standard 1500-byte Ethernet link?
Classic user symptom of an MTU/MSS problem over a tunnel?
cards.back: Small things work, large transfers stall: half-loaded pages, hanging attachments, stuck file copies.

cards.front: FortiOS policy options to clamp TCP MSS?
cards.back: `set tcp-mss-sender <n>` and `set tcp-mss-receiver <n>`.

cards.front: Why does FTP active mode break behind NAT without a helper?
cards.back: The PORT command carries the client's private IP and port inside the payload; the server can't connect back to it.

cards.front: Classic sign that SIP ALG and the phone system are both doing NAT traversal?
cards.back: One-way audio or calls that drop after about 30 seconds.

quiz.stem: A firewall allows HTTPS from LAN to WAN. Why doesn't it need a second policy for the server's replies?

options.text: The reply packets match the session created by the first packet
Replies on port 443 are always allowed by default
options.why_wrong: There is no blanket rule for 443; replies are allowed because they match an existing session.

options.text: The implicit deny only applies to UDP
options.why_wrong: The implicit deny applies to all traffic that matches no policy and no session.

options.text: NAT automatically opens the return path for any protocol
options.why_wrong: NAT rewrites addresses; the session is what permits the reply.

quiz.explanation: The first packet is checked against policies and creates a session keyed by the 5-tuple. Replies match the session.

quiz.stem: Put the TCP connection setup in order.
items: Client sends SYN with its MSS
quiz.explanation: SYN, SYN/ACK, ACK, then data.

quiz.stem: What MSS (in bytes) will a host announce on a plain 1500-byte Ethernet link with no IP or TCP options?
Users can browse small pages over a new IPsec tunnel, but large downloads stall. Most likely cause?

options.text: Packets larger than the tunnel MTU are dropped and path MTU discovery isn't working
The IPsec phase 2 selectors are wrong
options.why_wrong: Wrong selectors would break all traffic, not only large transfers.
Slow DNS delays the start of every connection, small or large.

options.text: The session TTL is too long
options.why_wrong: A long TTL keeps idle sessions longer; it doesn't affect packet size.

quiz.explanation: The size-dependent symptom is the clue. ESP overhead lowers the usable MTU; clamp MSS or fix PMTUD.

quiz.stem: What does a FortiOS virtual IP (VIP) do?

options.text: Destination NAT: maps an external address (and optionally port) to an internal one

options.why_wrong: That is an IP pool or the outgoing interface address.
Loopbacks are interfaces, not NAT objects.
VIPs can load-balance servers, but their core job is DNAT.

quiz.explanation: VIPs are FortiOS's DNAT objects.

quiz.stem: An app freezes whenever users leave it idle for about an hour, then works after a restart. What do you check first?

options.text: The session TTL for that traffic

options.why_wrong: IPS wouldn't cause an idle-time pattern.
A lease renewal doesn't break an open TCP connection to a server.
Duplex problems cause errors under load, not after idle time.

quiz.explanation: Idle-then-broken is the signature of a session expiring before the app sends its next packet.

quiz.stem: Which of these protocols carry IP addresses or ports inside their payload, and so often need a session helper (ALG) to cross NAT? Select all that apply.

options.why_wrong: HTTPS carries no IP/port pairs that the firewall must rewrite.
SSH runs over one TCP connection with no embedded addresses.

quiz.explanation: FTP's PORT command and SIP's SDP body embed addresses; helpers rewrite them and open pinholes.

quiz.stem: In a capture you see SYN, SYN, SYN from the client with growing gaps and nothing back. What does it mean?

options.text: Something is silently dropping the SYN or the reply

options.why_wrong: A closed port answers with RST.

options.text: The handshake completed but data is lost
options.why_wrong: There was no SYN/ACK, so the handshake never completed.

options.text: The client's MSS is too high
options.why_wrong: MSS problems appear after the handshake, with full-size data packets.

quiz.explanation: SYN retransmissions with no answer mean a drop somewhere: routing, policy, RPF or the server's own firewall.

quiz.stem: Why can one public IP support far more than 60,416 simultaneous PAT sessions?

options.text: The port limit applies per destination service, so sessions to different destinations can reuse ports

options.why_wrong: There is no port compression; ports are reused per destination.
UDP uses ports exactly like TCP for PAT.

options.text: It can't; 60,416 is a hard total limit
options.why_wrong: The guide states the figure per service (protocol, destination IP and port).

quiz.explanation: FortiOS documents 60,416 ports per IP for the same service, so the real total depends on how many destinations users reach.

quiz.stem: Inside users can't open the company portal by its public name, but internet users can. The portal is published with a VIP. What do you propose?

options.text: Hairpin NAT (VIP plus a SNAT policy for inside users) or split DNS

options.why_wrong: Timers are unrelated; the issue is the return path.

options.text: Disable the VIP for inside traffic
options.why_wrong: Inside users still resolve the public IP and would hit nothing.

options.text: Add a static route to the public IP
options.why_wrong: The public IP is the FortiGate's own; routing isn't the gap.

quiz.explanation: Inside users need either hairpin NAT so replies come back through the FortiGate, or an internal DNS answer with the private IP.

quiz.stem: A PPPoE link has an MTU of 1492. What MSS should hosts use for TCP without options?
Which FortiOS configuration clamps MSS for traffic matching policy 10?

options.why_wrong: MTU override is an interface setting, not a policy option.
That sets a 1350-second timer, not a segment size.
Anti-replay checks TCP flags; it doesn't change MSS.

quiz.explanation: FortiOS policies support tcp-mss-sender and tcp-mss-receiver.

quiz.stem: After a firewall migration, VoIP calls connect but the caller hears nothing. The PBX already handles NAT traversal. Best first move?

options.text: Check whether the firewall's SIP ALG is also rewriting the signalling and test with it disabled for that traffic

options.why_wrong: SIP media is RTP over UDP; MSS is irrelevant.

options.text: Move the PBX to a different VLAN
options.why_wrong: Doesn't address the double NAT traversal.
A reboot won't stop the SDP being rewritten twice.

quiz.explanation: One-way audio is the classic sign of two components fighting over NAT traversal. Decide who does it.

quiz.stem: Order the life of a TCP session through a stateful firewall with SNAT.
items: First SYN is checked against the policy table
A session is created with the original and translated 5-tuples
The source is rewritten to the outside IP and port
The reply matches the session and is translated back
The session is removed after FIN/RST or the TTL
quiz.explanation: Policy lookup happens once, at the first packet. Everything after rides the session.

quiz.stem: Sniffer on the inside interface shows SYN → SYN/ACK → ACK, then the client's 1460-byte data segments repeat every few seconds with no ACK from the server. The path crosses an IPsec tunnel. What is the most likely root cause?

options.text: Full-size segments exceed the tunnel MTU and are dropped; MSS isn't being clamped
The firewall policy denies the traffic
options.why_wrong: The handshake completed through the firewall, so the policy allowed the session.
With asymmetry the handshake itself would usually fail at the firewall.

quiz.explanation: Handshake fine, full-size data lost, tunnel in the path: MTU/MSS. Clamp MSS (for example 1350) and retest.

quiz.stem: A customer raised the global session TTL to 24 hours to fix one ERP app. A week later the firewall is close to its session limit. What do you recommend?

options.text: Restore the default globally and set a longer session-ttl only on the ERP policy

options.why_wrong: The root cause is configuration, not capacity.
Unrelated to how long idle sessions live.

options.text: Turn on NAT for the ERP policy

quiz.explanation: Scope the change to the policy that needs it. Global timers affect every session in the table.

quiz.stem: What is the common name for 'NAT loopback' / 'U-turn NAT' in the FortiOS guide? (two words)
quiz.explanation: The FortiOS guide calls it Hairpin NAT.

quiz.stem: Which statement about UDP sessions on a stateful firewall is correct?

options.text: The first packet creates a session; it ends when idle longer than its TTL
UDP is never tracked; every packet is checked against policies
options.why_wrong: Stateful firewalls track UDP with sessions too.

options.text: UDP sessions end with a FIN packet
options.why_wrong: UDP has no FIN; timers end its sessions.

options.text: UDP replies always need their own policy
options.why_wrong: Replies match the session like TCP.

quiz.explanation: UDP gets pseudo-state from the 5-tuple and a timer.

quiz.stem: A retail customer will put 9,000 users behind one public IP, all hitting the same SaaS endpoint on 443 at peak. What do you design?

options.text: An IP pool with more public IPs (or port block allocation) because one IP gives 60,416 ports per destination service
One IP is enough; PAT has unlimited ports
options.why_wrong: Ports per destination service are finite: 60,416 per IP.

options.text: Disable NAT and route private IPs to the internet
options.why_wrong: Private addresses aren't routable on the internet.

quiz.explanation: With one SaaS destination the per-service port budget matters. Size the pool from peak concurrent sessions per user to that service.

quiz.stem: Which symptom best fits an FTP active-mode transfer through NAT with no session helper?

options.text: Login works, but directory listings and transfers fail
The control connection on port 21 can't be opened
options.why_wrong: The control connection is a normal outbound TCP session and works.
That points to MTU, not to FTP data channel setup.

options.text: DNS lookups for the server fail
options.why_wrong: Name resolution is unrelated to the data channel.

quiz.explanation: The control channel works; the data channel fails because the embedded address in PORT is private and no pinhole is opened.

labs.title: Clamp MSS for a site-to-site tunnel
labs.goal: Traffic from branch LAN to HQ over the IPsec tunnel `to-HQ` stalls on large transfers. Clamp MSS to 1350 on the policy that allows it.

worked.config:
config firewall policy
    edit 21
        set name "LAN-to-HQ"
        set srcintf "lan"
        set dstintf "to-HQ"
        set srcaddr "BRANCH-LAN"
        set dstaddr "HQ-NETS"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
        set service "ALL"
        set tcp-mss-sender 1350
        set tcp-mss-receiver 1350
    next
end
notes: tcp-mss-sender rewrites the MSS in SYNs from the original sender; tcp-mss-receiver does the same for the other side.
1350 leaves room for ESP, NAT-T and possible PPPoE overhead; tune after testing.
Clamping only affects TCP. Test with a large file copy before closing the change.

solo.prompt: Write the CLI to clamp MSS to 1380 on existing policy 7.
solo.solution:
config firewall policy
    edit 7
        set tcp-mss-sender 1380
        set tcp-mss-receiver 1380
    next
end

labs.title: Watch a handshake with the sniffer
labs.goal: Prove whether SYNs to 10.0.10.20:443 reach the FortiGate and leave toward the server.

worked.config: # diagnose sniffer packet any 'host 10.0.10.20 and tcp port 443' 4 20 l
notes: Format: diagnose sniffer packet <interface> '<filter>' <verbose> <count> <tsformat>.
Interface `any` shows the packet arriving on one interface and leaving on another; verbose 4 prints the interface name.
Count 20 stops after 20 packets; `l` prints local absolute time.
Seeing the SYN in on `lan` but never out on `dmz` means the FortiGate dropped it: next step is debug flow.

faded.template: # diagnose {{sniffer}} packet {{any}} 'host 10.0.10.20 and tcp port 443' {{4}} 20 l

solo.prompt: Sniff 50 packets on port1 for traffic to or from 192.168.1.10 on UDP 53, showing headers with the interface name.
solo.solution: # diagnose sniffer packet port1 'host 192.168.1.10 and udp port 53' 4 50
solo.notes: Verbose 4 = headers with interface name. The filter goes in single quotes. Stop early with Ctrl+C.

scenarios.title: The file shares are 'slow' after the SD-WAN cutover
scenarios.situation: You led the cutover of 12 branches to IPsec overlays last weekend. Monday 9:00 the customer's IT lead calls: browsing and Teams are fine, but copying files from the HQ file server "never finishes" and the ERP report export times out. It started after the cutover.
constraints: Change freeze for the rest of the week except emergency changes
stakeholders: CFO (needs the ERP exports for month-end)
scenarios.ask: What do you think is happening, how do you prove it, and how do you fix it safely?
right_thinking: Clarify: size-dependent? Only through the tunnels? All branches or some? Since exactly when?
Hypothesis from the pattern: small works, large stalls, new tunnels in the path → MTU/MSS
Prove: sniffer shows handshake fine and full-size segments retransmitted; a ping with DF and large size fails while small passes
Fix with lowest risk: emergency change to clamp MSS on the branch-to-HQ policies (or tunnel interfaces), one branch first
Validate with the IT lead: large file copy and ERP export from the pilot branch, then roll to all
Communicate and document: root cause, fix, and add an MSS test to the cutover acceptance checklist
scenarios.what: MSS clamping on the overlay policies, piloted on one branch first.
scenarios.why: ESP overhead lowered the usable MTU and PMTUD isn't working end to end, so full-size TCP segments are dropped. Clamping makes both ends agree on segments that fit.
how: Sniffer to confirm retransmitted full-size segments
set tcp-mss-sender / tcp-mss-receiver 1350 on the overlay policies
pitfalls: Changing all 12 branches at once during a freeze
Blaming the file server or the WAN provider without evidence
Forgetting that UDP-based apps need the MTU fixed, not MSS
scenarios.model_answer: "This looks like an MTU problem the new tunnels introduced: small packets pass, full-size ones don't. I'd confirm it in ten minutes with a sniffer and a large DF ping from one branch. If confirmed, I'd raise an emergency change to clamp MSS to 1350 on that branch's overlay policy, test a large file copy and the ERP export with you, and then apply it to the other eleven. Afterwards I'll send the root cause and add an MSS test to our cutover checklist so it can't happen again."
could_have_added: Offer the CFO an interim workaround timeline for month-end
Check whether the hub side also needs clamping for HQ-initiated transfers
scenarios.best_way: Small works, big stalls, new tunnels: that's MTU. I'll prove it on one branch, clamp MSS, test with your team and then roll it out, all inside an emergency change.

scenarios.title: Legacy FTP vendor can't send files anymore
scenarios.situation: After replacing the customer's old firewall with a FortiGate, a supplier says they can log in to the customer's FTP server (published through a VIP) but listings and uploads fail.
scenarios.ask: What is going on and what are your options, from best to quick-fix?
right_thinking: Clarify: active or passive mode? Which side initiates the data channel?
Recognise the pattern: control channel works, data channel fails → embedded addresses in FTP
Check the FTP session helper / protocol options are applied and the VIP maps the passive port range if passive
Best long-term option: move the supplier to SFTP or FTPS with a defined port range
Validate with the supplier on a call; document the passive range in the VIP and policy
scenarios.what: Make the FTP data channel work through NAT (helper or passive range) and plan the move to SFTP.
scenarios.why: FTP carries IPs and ports in its payload; without a helper or a published passive range the data connection has nowhere to go.
how: Confirm the mode with the supplier
Publish the passive range in the VIP or rely on the FTP helper
Propose SFTP as the target state
pitfalls: Opening a huge port range to any source
Leaving clear-text FTP as the permanent answer
scenarios.model_answer: "Login works and transfers don't, so the control channel is fine and the data channel isn't getting through NAT. I'll confirm whether they use active or passive mode, make sure the FTP helper is doing its job or publish a small passive port range limited to the supplier's IPs, and test with them on a call. Then I'll recommend moving them to SFTP, because FTP sends credentials in clear text."
could_have_added: Restrict the VIP policy source to the supplier's public IPs
Log the policy so you can show the supplier's attempts
scenarios.best_way: Control works, data doesn't: that's FTP fighting NAT. I'll fix the data path today with a tight rule, and propose SFTP so we stop sending passwords in clear text.

scenarios.title: Raid: one-way audio at the call centre
scenarios.situation: 08:05. The customer's 200-seat call centre went live on the new FortiGate at 07:00. Agents can call out and the customer hears them, but agents hear silence. The voice vendor says "it's your firewall". The call centre manager is on the bridge, angry.
scenarios.ask: Walk the bridge through your first 15 minutes.
right_thinking: Stabilise the room: acknowledge impact, give a time-boxed plan and the next update time
Gather: which direction fails (inbound RTP), all agents or some, since the cutover only
Hypothesis: SIP ALG on the firewall and the PBX/SBC both handling NAT, so the SDP advertises the wrong address/ports for return media
Test on a pilot: disable the SIP ALG for the voice traffic (or the PBX's NAT handling), place a test call
If audio returns, apply to all voice traffic; if not, roll back and look at the RTP port range policy and session timers
Document the decision of who owns NAT traversal; update the design
scenarios.what: Pick one owner for SIP NAT traversal and make the media path explicit.
scenarios.why: When two devices rewrite SIP/SDP, return media goes to the wrong address or port, which is the classic one-way audio pattern.
how: Pilot test with ALG off for voice
pitfalls: Arguing with the vendor on the bridge
Making several changes at once so you can't tell which fixed it
scenarios.model_answer: "First I tell the bridge: 'Outbound audio works, inbound doesn't; that's a NAT traversal pattern. Give me 15 minutes on one agent, next update at 08:20.' Then I test one change only: SIP ALG off for the voice traffic, one test call. If the audio comes back, we apply it to all agents; if not, we roll back and check the RTP policy and timers. After the incident I'll document who owns NAT traversal so this design can't regress."
could_have_added: Ask the voice vendor to confirm on the bridge whether their SBC does NAT traversal
Capture one call before and after the change for the report
scenarios.best_way: One change at a time, one agent first, next update in 15 minutes. One-way audio is two devices fighting over NAT; we'll make it one.

interview.question: Explain what a stateful firewall does with the first packet of a connection and with the rest.
interview.testing: Fundamentals, and whether you can say them simply
interview.framework: Anchor definition → mechanism (session, 5-tuple) → why it matters
interview.model_answer: "A stateful firewall checks the first packet of a flow against its policy table, top to bottom. If a policy allows it, it creates a session keyed by the 5-tuple: source and destination IP, source and destination port, and protocol, plus any NAT it applied. Every later packet in both directions is matched against that session, not the policy table, which is faster and is why you only write policies for the side that starts the conversation. FortiGate adds checks on top, like TCP flag validation with anti-replay and timers per protocol."
could_have_added: Mention that the session also carries the security profile decisions and offload state
interview.best_way: First packet: policy lookup. Everything after: session lookup. That's what 'stateful' means.
follow_ups: How would asymmetric routing affect this?

interview.question: A customer says: 'Small web pages load, big downloads hang, only since we added the VPN.' What do you tell them?
interview.model_answer: "That pattern, small works and big stalls after adding a tunnel, is almost always MTU. The VPN adds headers, so full-size packets no longer fit, and if the ICMP messages that tell the sender to shrink them are blocked, those packets just disappear. I'd prove it with a sniffer and a large ping with don't-fragment set, then clamp the TCP MSS on the VPN policy, for example to 1350, and test a big download with them before closing."
could_have_added: Mention you'd add it to the acceptance checklist for future tunnels
interview.best_way: Small works, big hangs after a VPN: MTU. I'll prove it in minutes and clamp MSS.

interview.question: What is the difference between SNAT, DNAT and PAT, and how does FortiGate implement each?
interview.framework: Define each → FortiOS object → typical use
interview.model_answer: "SNAT rewrites the source, usually so private users can go out to the internet. PAT is SNAT where many users share one IP and the firewall uses the source port to keep their sessions apart. On FortiGate that's NAT on the policy with the outgoing interface address or an IP pool, or central SNAT if central NAT is enabled. DNAT rewrites the destination to publish an internal server, and FortiGate does it with a virtual IP, optionally with port forwarding."
could_have_added: The 60,416 ports per IP per destination service figure, and when you need more IPs in the pool
interview.best_way: SNAT changes who's talking, DNAT changes who you're talking to, PAT lets a crowd share one address. On FortiGate: IP pools for the first, VIPs for the second.

interview.question: Why do protocols like SIP and FTP give firewalls trouble with NAT?
interview.model_answer: "Because they put IP addresses and ports inside the payload, not just in the headers NAT rewrites. FTP active mode tells the server where to connect back; SIP's SDP tells the other side where to send the audio. Behind NAT those embedded addresses are private, so the secondary connection fails. Firewalls use session helpers or ALGs to rewrite them and open pinholes. The catch is when the PBX or SBC also does NAT traversal; two rewrites give you one-way audio, so you pick one owner."
interview.best_way: They hide addresses inside the payload. Helpers fix it, unless someone else is fixing it too.

interview.question: How would you size NAT for 9,000 users going to the same SaaS service?
interview.model_answer: "PAT gives about 60,416 ports per public IP per destination service, according to the FortiOS guide. If 9,000 users each open several concurrent connections to the same SaaS endpoint, one IP can run out at peak. I'd estimate peak concurrent sessions to that service, divide by 60,416 with headroom, and build an IP pool with that many public IPs, or use port block allocation if they need predictable per-user ports for logging. Then I'd watch pool usage in the first week."
could_have_added: Ask whether the SaaS rate-limits per source IP, which also argues for more IPs
interview.best_way: Ports per IP per destination are finite: 60,416. Measure peak, add headroom, size the pool.

field_reports.title: The front door is now the vulnerability
field_reports.body: For years stolen credentials were the top way in. In the Verizon 2026 DBIR, **exploiting vulnerabilities** took first place at **31 %** of breaches with a known initial access vector, while credential abuse fell to 13 %. Only **26 %** of CISA KEV vulnerabilities were fully fixed in 2025, with a median of **43 days** to fix. Every VIP you publish is a door: put IPS on it and agree on who patches what behind it.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR, Key topics and findings

field_reports.title: Ransomware is half the story
field_reports.body: Ransomware appeared in **48 %** of breaches in the 2026 DBIR, up from 44 %. The good news: **69 %** of victims didn't pay. Segmentation and tight NAT/VIP design are what keep one compromised host from becoming every host.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR, Key topics and findings

modules.title: Routing fundamentals and the FortiGate route lookup
objectives: Subnet quickly and pick the route a packet takes with longest-prefix match
Explain how FortiOS chooses between routes - prefix, distance, priority, ECMP - and where policy routes and SD-WAN rules fit
Explain the routing database vs the routing table, and floating routes
Explain RPF (feasible vs strict) and why asymmetric routing breaks a stateful firewall
Read `get router info routing-table` output and configure static and policy routes
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Static routing (pp. 644–674): routing table, distance, priority, RPF, asymmetric routing, policy routes, ECMP
General knowledge: IPv4 subnetting, longest-prefix match

units.title: Subnetting at interview speed
units.body:
Every design and every troubleshooting call starts with "which network is this address in?". You need to answer in seconds, without a calculator.

## The fast method

A prefix `/n` means the first *n* bits are the network. The **block size** in the "interesting" octet is `256 − mask value` in that octet.

| Prefix | Mask | Block size | Usable hosts |
|---|---|---|---|
| /24 | 255.255.255.0 | 256 | 254 |
| /25 | 255.255.255.128 | 128 | 126 |
| /26 | 255.255.255.192 | 64 | 62 |
| /27 | 255.255.255.224 | 32 | 30 |
| /28 | 255.255.255.240 | 16 | 14 |
| /29 | 255.255.255.248 | 8 | 6 |
| /30 | 255.255.255.252 | 4 | 2 |
| /22 | 255.255.252.0 | 4 in the 3rd octet | 1,022 |

**Example:** `10.20.37.140/27`. Block size 32 in the last octet: networks start at 0, 32, 64, 96, 128, 160. 140 is in the **128** block, so the network is `10.20.37.128`, the broadcast is `.159`, and usable hosts are `.129–.158`.

Usable hosts = 2^(32 − n) − 2. A /31 is the exception used on point-to-point links (2 addresses, no broadcast).

:::recall
Q: Network and broadcast for 172.16.5.77/28?
A: Block 16: networks …64, 80. 77 is in 64. Network 172.16.5.64, broadcast 172.16.5.79.
:::

:::why
Q: Why does a customer who summarises 10.10.0.0/22 cover 10.10.0.0 to 10.10.3.255?
A: /22 leaves 2 bits of the third octet for hosts, so the block in the third octet is 4: 0, 1, 2, 3.
:::

units.title: How FortiOS picks a route
units.body:
Routers keep candidate routes from every source (connected, static, OSPF, BGP) in a **routing database**. Only the best become the **routing table** (the RIB), which is what forwarding uses. FortiOS follows this order (FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide, p. 647):

1. **Most specific prefix wins.** A /28 beats a /24 beats the default route, whatever the source.
2. Same prefix: **lower administrative distance** wins and is injected into the table. FortiOS shows it as `[distance/metric]`, for example `[20/0]` for an eBGP route.
3. Same distance: all are injected, and **priority** decides (lower is preferred; static routes default to priority 1).
4. Still equal: **ECMP** shares traffic across them.

Typical FortiOS distances: connected 0, **static 10**, eBGP 20, OSPF 110, iBGP 200. A default route learned by **DHCP gets distance 5**, which beats a static default of 10. That catches people who leave "Retrieve default gateway from server" enabled on a second WAN.

## Floating routes

A backup static route with a **higher distance** stays in the routing database, not the table. It only becomes active when the better route disappears (interface down, or a **link monitor** declares the gateway dead). That is a "floating" route, and it is how simple dual-WAN failover works without SD-WAN.

## Reading the table

:::cli
# get router info routing-table all
S*      0.0.0.0/0 [10/0] via 203.0.113.1, wan1
C       10.0.10.0/24 is directly connected, lan
B       192.168.0.0/24 [20/0] via 172.31.0.1, MPLS, 00:31:43
O       10.50.0.0/16 [110/20] via 10.0.0.2, port3, 01:12:09
:::

`get router info routing-table database` shows **all** candidates, including inactive floating routes.

:::recall
Q: Two static routes to 0.0.0.0/0 have distance 10. One has priority 5, the other priority 1. Which is used?
A: Both are in the table (same distance). The one with priority 1 is preferred.
:::

:::pitfall
Enabling DHCP on a backup WAN with "Retrieve default gateway from server" adds a default route with distance 5. It silently beats your static default (10) and can send all traffic out the backup link.
:::

units.title: Policy routes, SD-WAN rules and ECMP
units.body:
Sometimes the destination alone isn't enough: "FTP from this VLAN must leave through the MPLS link". **Policy routes** (PBR) match on incoming interface, source, destination, protocol, ports or ToS, and send matches to a gateway and/or interface.

How FortiOS evaluates them (Admin Guide, pp. 659–664):

- Policy routes are checked **top-down, before the routing table**.
- A policy route only matches if FortiOS can resolve it: with only an interface it looks up the gateway in the routing table; with only a gateway it looks up the interface; with both, it still needs a route that makes the gateway reachable on that interface.
- No match: it falls through to the routing table.
- Precedence among the policy-route family: **policy-based routes > ISDB routes > SD-WAN routes**.
- **ECMP is considered after policy routing.** ECMP needs the same destination and the same costs (for static routes: distance and priority) from the same protocol.
- The ECMP algorithm is `set v4-ecmp-mode` under `config system settings` (default **source-ip-based**; also weight-based, usage-based, source-dest-ip-based). When SD-WAN is enabled, use `load-balance-mode` under `config system sdwan` instead.

:::cli
config router policy
    edit 1
        set input-device "port1"
        set src "0.0.0.0/0.0.0.0"
        set dst "0.0.0.0/0.0.0.0"
        set protocol 6
        set start-port 21
        set end-port 21
        set gateway 172.20.120.23
        set output-device "port4"
    next
end
:::

:::recall
Q: A packet matches a policy route and an SD-WAN rule. Which wins?
A: The policy route: policy-based routes > ISDB routes > SD-WAN routes.
:::

:::why
Q: Why might a policy route "do nothing" even though its match fields are right?
A: FortiOS also needs a route that makes the gateway reachable through the chosen interface. If it can't resolve that, the policy route doesn't match and the packet falls through to the routing table.
:::

:::ps
SD-WAN designs fail in production when someone has an old policy route nobody remembers. In a migration discovery, export `config router policy` and ask about every entry.
:::

units.title: RPF, asymmetric routing and the session table
units.body:
## Reverse path forwarding (anti-spoofing)

When a packet arrives, FortiGate asks: "could I reach this **source** back through the interface it came in on?" If not, it drops the packet. It's a cheap defence against spoofed sources (Admin Guide, p. 653).

- **Feasible** (default): there is at least one active route back to the source through the incoming interface.
- **Strict** (`set strict-src-check enable` under `config system settings`): the **best** route back to the source must use the incoming interface.
- `set src-check disable` on an interface removes RPF checks there. Fortinet documents it as less secure and meant for troubleshooting.

In debug flow, an RPF drop shows up as a reverse-path check failure. The usual cause is a **missing route** for a remote subnet, typically a new VPN or a second WAN.

## Asymmetric routing

If the request crosses the FortiGate but the reply takes another path, the session never sees a full TCP handshake (Admin Guide, pp. 653–654):

- PC1 starts TCP to PC2: the SYN passes, the SYN/ACK bypasses the FortiGate, and the **ACK is blocked** because it matches no established session.
- PC2 pings PC1 when only the reply crosses the FortiGate: no session matches, and the reply is **dropped as invalid**.

`set asymroute enable` makes FortiGate permit it, but then it **can't inspect all traffic**, and Fortinet says to use it only when the routing itself can't be fixed. The real fix is routing: make both directions cross the same firewall (or the same HA cluster / FGSP peers).

:::recall
Q: Default RPF mode on FortiGate, and what it checks?
A: Feasible path: at least one active route back to the source through the incoming interface.
:::

:::why
Q: Why is "turn on asymroute" a bad permanent fix?
A: The firewall stops seeing whole conversations, so it can't enforce state or inspect all traffic. You trade a routing bug for a security hole.
:::

:::threat ref=dbir-2026-third-party-48pct
In the 2026 DBIR, breaches involving a third party reached 48 %, up 60 % from the year before. Partner and vendor links are where "temporary" routing hacks like disabled RPF checks tend to survive for years. Make every exception an expiring, documented change.
:::

cards.front: Block size and usable hosts of a /27?
cards.back: Block 32; 30 usable hosts.
6 (8 addresses minus network and broadcast).
Longest prefix (most specific) wins, regardless of route source.

cards.front: Default distance of a FortiOS static route?
Distance FortiOS gives a default route learned via DHCP?
cards.back: 5, which beats a static default route (10).

cards.front: Two routes, same prefix and same distance. What decides?
cards.back: Priority (lower preferred); both are in the table. If priority is also equal, ECMP.
Database: every learned candidate. Table: only the best routes, used for forwarding.

cards.front: What is a floating static route?
cards.back: A backup route with a higher distance; it stays in the database and only becomes active when the better route is lost.
20 = administrative distance, 0 = metric.

cards.front: Are policy routes checked before or after the routing table?
cards.back: Before; no match falls through to the routing table.

cards.front: Precedence among policy-based, ISDB and SD-WAN routes?
cards.back: Policy-based routes > ISDB routes > SD-WAN routes.
source-ip-based (`set v4-ecmp-mode` under config system settings).

cards.front: With SD-WAN enabled, where do you set the load-balancing algorithm?
cards.back: `set load-balance-mode` under `config system sdwan`.
Feasible: any active route back via the incoming interface. Strict: the best route back must use the incoming interface.
`config system settings` → `set strict-src-check enable`.

cards.front: TCP through FortiGate, reply bypasses it. Which packet gets blocked?
cards.back: The client's ACK (third packet), because no established session matches.
FortiGate can't inspect all traffic; malicious traffic may pass. Fix the routing instead.

quiz.stem: What is the network address of 192.168.10.200/26?
How many usable host addresses does a /28 have?
Routes to 10.1.0.0/16 (OSPF) and 10.1.5.0/24 (static) exist. Where does traffic to 10.1.5.9 go?

options.text: Via the static /24, because it is more specific
Via OSPF, because dynamic routes are preferred
options.why_wrong: Prefix length is checked before route source or distance.

options.text: Via the static route only if its distance is lower
options.why_wrong: Distance only matters between routes with the same prefix.

quiz.explanation: Longest-prefix match comes first.

quiz.stem: A branch FortiGate has a static default via WAN1 (distance 10). Someone enables DHCP on WAN2 with 'Retrieve default gateway from server'. What happens?

options.text: The DHCP default route (distance 5) becomes the active default, sending traffic out WAN2

options.why_wrong: Lower distance wins and DHCP routes get distance 5 by default.
Different distances: only the lower one goes into the table.

options.text: The FortiGate rejects the DHCP route
options.why_wrong: It installs it unless you disable the option or change its distance.

quiz.explanation: The guide warns about exactly this. Disable gateway retrieval or set the DHCP distance higher.

quiz.stem: Which is checked first for a new session on FortiGate?

options.why_wrong: The routing table is used when no policy route matches.
ECMP is considered after policy routing.
Forwarding uses the routing table, not the protocol database.

quiz.explanation: Policy routes are evaluated top-down before the routing table.

quiz.stem: What does FortiGate's default reverse path check verify?

options.text: That at least one active route back to the source uses the incoming interface
That the best route back to the source uses the incoming interface
options.why_wrong: That is strict mode, not the default.
RPF checks the source, not the destination.

options.text: That the source MAC is in the ARP table

quiz.explanation: The default is feasible-path RPF.

quiz.stem: Broadcast address of 10.0.4.0/23?
quiz.explanation: /23 spans two /24s in the third octet: 10.0.4.0–10.0.5.255.

quiz.stem: How many /27 subnets fit in one /24?
Order FortiOS route selection between candidate routes.
items: ECMP between the remaining equal routes
quiz.explanation: Prefix, then distance, then priority, then ECMP.

quiz.stem: Where would you see a floating backup route that isn't active?

options.why_wrong: That shows only the active routing table.

quiz.explanation: The database holds all candidates, including inactive ones.

quiz.stem: Policy route: input port1, protocol 6, ports 21–21, output port4, gateway 172.20.120.23. FTP still leaves via wan1. Most likely reason?

options.text: FortiOS can't find a route making 172.20.120.23 reachable via port4, so the policy route doesn't match
Policy routes only work for UDP
options.why_wrong: They work for any protocol you specify.

options.text: SD-WAN rules always override policy routes
options.why_wrong: It's the opposite: policy-based routes > SD-WAN routes.
A missing firewall policy would drop traffic, not send it out wan1.

quiz.explanation: With both gateway and interface set, FortiOS still needs a route that makes the gateway reachable on that interface; otherwise it falls through to the routing table.

quiz.stem: Which command sets FortiGate's ECMP algorithm when SD-WAN is NOT enabled?

options.why_wrong: That's the setting when SD-WAN is enabled.
There's no such static route option.

quiz.explanation: v4-ecmp-mode lives in system settings at VDOM level.

quiz.stem: Which configuration gives simple dual-WAN failover without SD-WAN?

options.text: Primary default route distance 10, backup default route distance 20, plus a link monitor on the primary
Two default routes, both distance 10, priority 1
options.why_wrong: That's ECMP: both are used at once.

options.text: One default route with two gateways
options.why_wrong: A static route has one gateway.

options.text: A policy route to each WAN
options.why_wrong: Policy routes don't fail over on their own.

quiz.explanation: The higher-distance route floats in the database and takes over when the primary is withdrawn; a link monitor withdraws it when the gateway is dead but the interface stays up.

quiz.stem: A new site-to-site VPN comes up. Pings from HQ to the branch fail and debug flow on the HQ FortiGate shows the branch's replies dropped by the reverse path check. Best fix?

options.text: Add a route for the branch subnet via the VPN interface
Disable src-check on the WAN interface
options.why_wrong: Fortinet describes it as less secure, for troubleshooting; the root cause is a missing route.
Hides the problem and disables full inspection.
Stricter checking would drop even more.

quiz.explanation: RPF drops mean FortiGate has no route back to the source through the incoming interface. Add the route.

quiz.stem: TCP from PC1 → PC2 crosses the FortiGate; the reply returns through another router. What does the user see and why?

options.text: The connection fails: the client's ACK is blocked because the FortiGate never saw a SYN/ACK

options.why_wrong: FortiGate blocks the ACK; it doesn't just slow it down.

options.text: It works fine because sessions are stateless
options.why_wrong: FortiGate is stateful; that is the problem.
TCP is the one that breaks clearly in this scenario.

quiz.explanation: Asymmetric routing breaks stateful TCP tracking at the third packet.

quiz.stem: Which conditions must hold for FortiOS to ECMP between two static routes? Select all that apply.

options.why_wrong: ECMP is about different next hops, usually on different interfaces.

quiz.explanation: Same destination and costs (distance and priority for static), from the same protocol.

quiz.stem: Which route does FortiOS prefer between eBGP (distance 20) and OSPF (distance 110) for the same /24?

options.text: eBGP, because its distance is lower
OSPF, because link-state is more accurate
options.why_wrong: Route source quality isn't considered; distance is.
ECMP needs the same protocol and costs.

quiz.explanation: Same prefix, so lower distance wins.

quiz.stem: A customer wants all traffic from the guest VLAN to always use the cheap broadband link, while corporate traffic follows normal routing with failover. Which design is simplest and most robust?

options.text: A policy route (or SD-WAN rule) for the guest VLAN source to the broadband link, with normal routes plus failover for the rest
Make broadband the default route for everyone
Use asymroute so guest replies can return any way
options.why_wrong: Doesn't steer traffic and weakens security.

options.text: Put the guest VLAN in its own /16
options.why_wrong: Address size doesn't choose an exit link.

quiz.explanation: Steer by source with a policy route or SD-WAN rule; keep the default routing for everything else. Document that policy routes beat SD-WAN rules.

quiz.stem: A customer disabled RPF checks on an interface 'temporarily' two years ago for a partner link. What's your PS recommendation?

options.text: Find the missing or asymmetric route that caused it, fix it in a change window, re-enable the check, and document the exception if one must stay
Leave it; it's been fine for two years
options.why_wrong: It removes an anti-spoofing control on a third-party path.

options.text: Disable RPF on all interfaces for consistency

quiz.explanation: Fix the routing, restore the control, and keep exceptions documented with an expiry.

labs.title: Dual-WAN failover with a floating default route
labs.goal: WAN1 (gateway 203.0.113.1) is primary; WAN2 (gateway 198.51.100.1) takes over only if WAN1 fails.

worked.config:
config router static
    edit 1
        set gateway 203.0.113.1
        set device "wan1"
        set distance 10
    next
    edit 2
        set gateway 198.51.100.1
        set device "wan2"
        set distance 20
    next
end
notes: No dst means 0.0.0.0/0, the default route.
Route 2 stays in the routing database until route 1 is withdrawn.
If WAN1's interface stays up while the ISP is dead, add a link monitor to withdraw route 1.
Verify with `get router info routing-table all` and `... database`.

faded.template:
config router {{static}}
    edit 2
        set gateway 198.51.100.1
        set {{device}} "wan2"
        set {{distance}} 20
    next
end

solo.prompt: Add a floating default route via 192.0.2.254 on interface "lte" with distance 30.
solo.solution:
config router static
    edit 0
        set gateway 192.0.2.254
        set device "lte"
        set distance 30
    next
end
solo.notes: `edit 0` picks the next free sequence number.

labs.title: Policy route for FTP
labs.goal: Send FTP (TCP 21) arriving on port1 out port4 to next hop 172.20.120.23 (the FortiOS guide example).

worked.config:
config router policy
    edit 1
        set input-device "port1"
        set src "0.0.0.0/0.0.0.0"
        set dst "0.0.0.0/0.0.0.0"
        set protocol 6
        set start-port 21
        set end-port 21
        set gateway 172.20.120.23
        set output-device "port4"
    next
end
notes: protocol 6 = TCP; start/end port = destination port range.
FortiOS needs a route that makes 172.20.120.23 reachable via port4, or the policy route won't match.
Policy routes beat ISDB and SD-WAN routes.

faded.template:
config router {{policy}}
    edit 1
        set {{input-device}} "port1"
        set protocol {{6}}
        set start-port 21
        set end-port 21
        set gateway 172.20.120.23
        set {{output-device}} "port4"
    next
end

solo.prompt: Write a policy route: traffic from source 10.30.0.0/24 arriving on "vlan30" goes out "wan2" via 198.51.100.1 (any protocol).
solo.solution:
config router policy
    edit 2
        set input-device "vlan30"
        set src "10.30.0.0/255.255.255.0"
        set dst "0.0.0.0/0.0.0.0"
        set gateway 198.51.100.1
        set output-device "wan2"
    next
end

scenarios.title: 'The internet goes out the backup link'
scenarios.situation: A customer with two ISPs (fibre primary, broadband backup) says their monthly broadband bill tripled and speed tests show broadband speeds. Nobody changed "anything important". Last month their IT intern set up the backup WAN.
scenarios.ask: How do you find and fix it, and how do you prevent it?
right_thinking: Clarify: when did it start, what exactly changed on the backup WAN
Check the routing table: which default route is active and its [distance/metric]
Suspect the DHCP-learned default (distance 5) beating the static (10)
Fix: disable 'Retrieve default gateway from server' or raise the DHCP distance; keep the backup as a floating route with a link monitor
Validate failover in a window: pull the primary, check traffic moves, restore
Prevent: config review checklist and change control for edge devices
scenarios.what: Restore the intended route preference and make failover deliberate.
scenarios.why: FortiOS gives DHCP default routes distance 5, which beats a static default of 10.
how: Fix the DHCP setting or distance
pitfalls: Deleting the backup route entirely
Testing failover in business hours without warning users
scenarios.model_answer: "I'd start with the routing table: if the active default shows distance 5 via the broadband interface, it was learned by DHCP. That beats the static default of 10, so everything leaves through the backup. I'll turn off gateway retrieval on that interface, or raise its distance, keep broadband as a floating route with a link monitor, and test failover with them in a maintenance window. Then I'd suggest a simple change process for the edge."
could_have_added: Show Finance the date the route changed from the logs to close the billing question
scenarios.best_way: Your backup link learned a default route that outranks the primary. One setting fixes it, and we'll prove failover still works.

scenarios.title: Raid: the new VPN pings one way
scenarios.situation: Friday 17:30. You just brought up a site-to-site IPsec tunnel between HQ and a new plant. Phase 1 and 2 are up. Plant can ping HQ servers; HQ can't ping the plant. The plant manager wants it working before the night shift at 22:00.
scenarios.ask: Walk through your diagnosis and fix.
right_thinking: Tunnel up means crypto is fine; think routing and policy
Run debug flow on the HQ FortiGate for a ping to the plant subnet
Look for: no route (traffic leaves the wrong way), policy deny (policy 0), or reverse path check failure on replies
Most likely: HQ lacks a route for the plant subnet via the tunnel, or there is no HQ→plant policy
Add the route/policy, retest both directions, save the debug output for the handover
scenarios.what: Complete the routing and policy for the HQ → plant direction.
scenarios.why: Phase 2 up only proves the tunnel; each side still needs routes and a policy for traffic it initiates.
how: Add static route via the tunnel interface
pitfalls: Disabling RPF to 'make it work'
Changing the plant side when the evidence points to HQ
scenarios.model_answer: "The tunnel is up, so crypto isn't the issue. I'd run a debug flow on HQ for a ping to the plant: it will tell me in one line whether it's a missing route, a policy deny or a reverse-path drop. My bet is HQ has no route to the plant subnet through the tunnel, or no policy for that direction. I'll add what's missing, test both directions, and leave the debug output in the handover notes."
scenarios.best_way: Tunnel up, one direction broken: that's routing or policy, not crypto. Debug flow tells me which in one line.

scenarios.title: Asymmetric routing in the data centre
scenarios.situation: In discovery for a firewall migration, you find the customer's core switch has two default paths: one through the old firewall, one through a WAN optimiser that bypasses it. Their admin says "it's fine, we enabled asymmetric routing on the old firewall years ago".
scenarios.ask: What do you tell them, and what goes into the design for the new FortiGate?
right_thinking: Name the risk plainly: with asymroute the firewall can't inspect whole sessions
Map flows: which traffic actually needs the optimiser path
Design: make both directions cross the FortiGate (or place the optimiser behind it); use FGSP if two firewalls must share sessions
Plan the migration step and a validation test for return paths
Get the CISO to sign off on any exception, with an expiry
scenarios.what: A design where every flow's two directions cross the same inspection point.
scenarios.why: Stateful inspection needs both directions; Fortinet states asymroute should be used only when routing can't be fixed because traffic can't be fully inspected.
scenarios.model_answer: "I'd be direct: with asymmetric routing allowed, the firewall can't see whole conversations, so some traffic is effectively uninspected. In the new design both directions must cross the FortiGate, so I'd move the optimiser behind it or adjust the core routing, and if we truly need two firewalls sharing sessions we'd use FGSP. I'll add return-path tests to acceptance, and any exception gets the CISO's sign-off with an end date."
scenarios.best_way: Allowing asymmetry means accepting blind spots. Let's design them out instead of carrying them into the new firewall.

interview.question: How does FortiGate decide which route to use when several match?
interview.framework: Order of decisions with one example
interview.model_answer: "First the most specific prefix wins, regardless of source. For the same prefix, the lowest administrative distance goes into the routing table; on FortiOS static is 10, eBGP 20, OSPF 110. If distance ties, the route with the lower priority is preferred, and if that ties too, ECMP spreads traffic using the configured mode, source-IP-based by default. On top of that, policy routes, ISDB routes and SD-WAN rules are checked before the routing table, in that order."
could_have_added: The DHCP default route gets distance 5, a classic surprise
interview.best_way: Longest prefix, then distance, then priority, then ECMP. And policy routes go before all of it.

interview.question: What is reverse path forwarding and when have you seen it cause problems?
interview.model_answer: "RPF is an anti-spoofing check: when a packet arrives, the FortiGate checks it could route back to the source through that same interface. By default that's feasible mode, any active route back that way; strict mode requires the best route. The classic problem is a new VPN or second WAN where nobody added the route for the remote subnet, so replies get dropped. Debug flow shows the reverse-path drop, and the fix is adding the route, not disabling the check."
interview.best_way: RPF asks 'could I reach you back this way?'. When it says no, add the route; don't turn off the check.

interview.question: Why is asymmetric routing a problem for a firewall, and how do you fix it?
interview.framework: Mechanism → symptom → wrong fix → right fix
interview.model_answer: "A stateful firewall needs to see both directions. If the SYN goes through the FortiGate and the SYN/ACK goes around it, the ACK arrives with no established session and is dropped. You can enable asymroute, but then the FortiGate can't inspect all traffic, so it's a last resort. The right fix is routing: make both directions cross the same firewall, or use FGSP when two firewalls must share sessions."
interview.best_way: The firewall only sees half the conversation. Fix the path, not the firewall.

interview.question: Subnet 10.20.37.140/27 for me, out loud.
interview.model_answer: "A /27 is a block of 32 in the last octet: 0, 32, 64, 96, 128, 160. 140 sits in the 128 block, so the network is 10.20.37.128, the broadcast is .159, and usable hosts are .129 to .158, 30 hosts."
interview.best_way: Block of 32, so .128 to .159: thirty usable hosts.

interview.question: How would you give a branch dual-WAN failover without SD-WAN?
interview.model_answer: "Two default routes with different distances: the primary at 10 and the backup at, say, 20. The backup floats in the routing database and becomes active when the primary is withdrawn. Because an ISP can die while the interface stays up, I'd add a link monitor on the primary to withdraw its route when the gateway stops answering. Then I'd test failover and failback in a maintenance window."
could_have_added: Mention that SD-WAN gives SLA-based steering and is the better long-term answer
interview.best_way: A floating backup route plus a link monitor. Then prove it by pulling the cable in a window.

field_reports.title: Partners are half the breaches
field_reports.body: The 2026 DBIR found third-party involvement in **48 %** of breaches, up **60 %** in a year. Routing exceptions for partner links (disabled RPF checks, broad static routes, "temporary" policy routes) are exactly what an attacker coming through a partner rides on. In discovery, list every exception and give each an owner and an end date.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR, Key topics and findings

field_reports.title: Every hour of a breach costs money
field_reports.body: IBM's 2026 Cost of a Data Breach puts the global average at **USD 4.99 million** (+12 %), about USD 1,100 per hour, and **USD 11.5 million** in the US. Fast, correct routing changes during an incident aren't a nicety: they are cost control.
field_reports.source: IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026, Key findings

modules.title: FortiGate firewall policies, objects and NAT
objectives: Explain how FortiGate matches a new session to a policy, and what happens when nothing matches
Explain why VIP policies match differently, and when to use match-vip
Configure SNAT with the outgoing interface or an IP pool, and choose the right IP pool type
Configure DNAT with VIPs, including port forwarding and hairpin NAT
Explain central NAT, when to use it, and the planning a switch to it needs
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Policies (pp. 2094–2120), NGFW policy (p. 2121+), match-vip (pp. 2107–2108)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Source NAT, IP pools (pp. 2166–2176), Central SNAT (p. 2177+)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Destination NAT and static VIPs (pp. 2192–2200), Central DNAT (p. 2215), Hairpin NAT (pp. 2229–2231)

units.title: How a FortiGate matches a policy
units.body:
Every session through a FortiGate is tied to a policy. When the first packet arrives, FortiOS records the **incoming interface**, works out the **outgoing interface** from routing, and compares source, destination, **service** and **schedule** (time of day) with the policy table (Admin Guide, p. 2094).

## The rules of the match

- Policies are evaluated **in sequence, top to bottom**, and the **first match wins**. The GUI's *By Sequence* view shows the exact order they are checked.
- A policy matches only if **every** field matches: incoming and outgoing interface, source address (and user/group or device if set), destination address, service and schedule.
- **Accept** lets the session be created (with NAT, security profiles, logging and so on). **Deny** blocks it.
- If nothing matches, the **implicit deny** at the bottom drops the traffic. You add an explicit deny policy when you want to **log** those violations.

Because routing decides the outgoing interface **before** the policy lookup, a "policy problem" is often a routing problem: the packet is evaluated against the wrong interface pair.

## Objects

Policies reference objects, not raw IPs: address objects and groups (subnet, range, FQDN, geography, dynamic/fabric objects), **ISDB** (Internet Service Database) entries for cloud services, service objects and groups, schedules, users and groups. Good object hygiene (clear names, groups, comments) is half of a maintainable firewall, and the first thing a PS consultant cleans up in a migration.

:::recall
Q: Traffic matches no policy. What happens, and how do you get it logged?
A: The implicit deny drops it. Add an explicit deny policy with logging enabled to record the violations.
:::

:::why
Q: Why can a perfectly written policy never be hit?
A: Because a broader policy above it matches first, or because routing sends the traffic to a different outgoing interface than the policy expects.
:::

:::tip
On a call, read the policy table in *By Sequence* view, top to bottom, with the 5-tuple of the failing flow in front of you. Then confirm with debug flow, which names the policy ID that matched or says "policy 0" (implicit deny).
:::

units.title: VIPs, DNAT and the match-vip trap
units.body:
A **virtual IP (VIP)** is FortiOS's DNAT object: it maps an external IP (and optionally a port range) to an internal IP (Admin Guide, p. 2197).

- **Static NAT VIP:** the whole port range maps one-to-one.
- **Port forwarding VIP** (`set portforward enable`): only specific ports map, so one public IP can publish several servers on different ports.
- You use the VIP as the **destination** of an accept policy from the outside interface.

:::cli
config firewall vip
    edit "WebServer_VIP_Services"
        set service "TCP_8080-8082"
        set extip 10.1.100.199
        set extintf "any"
        set portforward enable
        set mappedip "172.16.200.55"
        set mappedport 80
    next
end
:::

## Why deny policies "don't work" against a published server

FortiGate matches policies with VIPs **differently**: policies with a VIP applied have **priority over typical policies** (Admin Guide, p. 2108). So a deny policy placed above the VIP policy, with destination "all", can be skipped and the blocked sources still reach the server.

The fix is **`set match-vip enable`** on the deny policy, so it also matches traffic headed to VIPs. New deny policies have match-vip **enabled by default**, and it can't be enabled on accept policies. Another option is a separate VIP with `src-filter` used in a deny policy above the accept one.

:::recall
Q: What does `match-vip` do on a deny policy?
A: It makes the deny policy match traffic destined to VIPs too, so it can block sources from reaching a published server.
:::

:::why
Q: Why would a customer's geo-block deny policy fail to stop attacks against their web server?
A: If match-vip is disabled on that deny policy, VIP traffic skips it because VIP policies have priority. Enable match-vip.
:::

:::threat ref=dbir-2026-vuln-exploitation-31pct
Published servers are where vulnerability exploitation (31 % of known initial access vectors in the 2026 DBIR) lands. Every VIP policy deserves IPS, a source restriction where possible, and a named owner for patching.
:::

units.title: SNAT and IP pools
units.body:
Outbound SNAT is enabled per policy (unless central NAT is on). The simplest form is **NAT with the outgoing interface address**. By default **source port translation** is *When port conflicts*: FortiGate keeps the original source port unless it collides (Admin Guide, p. 2167).

**IP pools** let sessions use addresses other than the interface IP. FortiOS has four IPv4 types (Admin Guide, pp. 2167–2170):

| Type | What it does | When to use |
|---|---|---|
| **Overload** | Many users share the pool IPs with PAT; about 60,416 ports per IP per destination service | Default choice for internet access |
| **One-to-one** | Each inside IP gets its own outside IP; no PAT | Few hosts that need a stable, unique public IP |
| **Fixed port range** | Defines internal *and* external ranges; each inside IP gets a predictable port range | When you must trace a public IP:port back to a user without per-session logs |
| **Port block allocation (PBA)** | Hands out blocks of ports per user (block size × blocks per user) | Carrier-grade and large guest networks; fewer NAT logs |

With an overload pool of several IPs, FortiOS picks the IP deterministically from the source IP (source IP as a number, modulo the pool size), so a given client keeps the same public IP.

:::cli
config firewall ippool
    edit "Overload-ippool"
        set type overload
        set startip 172.16.200.1
        set endip 172.16.200.2
    next
end
:::

Then, in the policy: `set nat enable` and `set ippool enable` with `set poolname "Overload-ippool"`.

:::recall
Q: Which IP pool type lets you know which internal IP used a public IP and port, without logging every session?
A: Fixed port range (each inside IP has a fixed port range). Port block allocation also reduces logging by logging blocks.
:::

:::why
Q: Why does a one-to-one pool with two public IPs only serve two users at a time?
A: One-to-one has no port translation; each inside IP needs its own outside IP.
:::

units.title: Central NAT, hairpin NAT and how to change NAT safely
units.body:
## Central NAT

By default NAT lives inside each policy. **Central NAT** moves it into its own ordered tables (Admin Guide, p. 2177):

- Enable with `config system settings` → `set central-nat enable`. **It isn't enabled by default.**
- Once enabled, the NAT option in IPv4 policies is **skipped**. SNAT must be done in the **central SNAT** table (`central-snat-map`), read **top-down** until a rule matches, and applied after the security policy.
- DNAT moves to the **DNAT & Virtual IPs** page (Central DNAT).
- In **policy-based NGFW mode**, central SNAT is assumed to be enabled implicitly.

Why customers choose it: large rule bases and migrations from vendors that already separate NAT from security rules, because translation can be reviewed in one place. Why it needs planning: switching it on or off changes how every policy behaves, so it is a **maintenance-window change** with a tested rollback (configuration backup) and an acceptance test for every published service.

## Hairpin NAT

Inside users reaching an inside server by its public name need hairpin NAT. FortiOS's example (Admin Guide, pp. 2229–2231) has four steps:

1. Create a VIP mapping the external IP to the internal server.
2. Create a DNAT policy using that VIP.
3. Create a SNAT policy so inside users reach the external address and the return traffic comes back through the FortiGate.
4. Verify from inside and outside.

Split DNS is the alternative when the customer controls internal DNS.

:::delta
FortiOS 7.6.5 and later: `allow-traffic-redirect` (global) is **disabled by default**, and it is disabled after upgrading even if it was enabled before. Traffic that must leave through the interface it arrived on then needs a matching IPv4 policy (Admin Guide, p. 2107). Check this on hairpin and one-arm designs after upgrades.
:::

:::ps
In a migration from another vendor, decide **policy NAT vs central NAT in discovery**, not during cutover. Write it in the low-level design, and list every VIP with its test case in the acceptance test plan.
:::

:::recall
Q: With central NAT enabled, where do you configure outbound SNAT?
A: In the central SNAT table (central-snat-map), not in the firewall policy.
:::

cards.front: In what order does FortiGate evaluate firewall policies?
cards.back: In sequence, top to bottom; the first full match wins.

cards.front: What happens to traffic that matches no policy?
cards.back: The implicit deny drops it.

cards.front: Why add an explicit deny policy at the bottom?
cards.back: To log the denied (violation) traffic; the implicit deny alone doesn't give you those logs.
Incoming and outgoing interface, source, destination, service, schedule (plus users/devices if set).

cards.front: Which GUI view shows policies in the exact order they are checked?
cards.back: By Sequence.

cards.front: Why is a 'policy problem' often a routing problem?
cards.back: Routing picks the outgoing interface before the policy lookup, so the wrong route makes FortiGate check the wrong interface pair.

cards.front: Static NAT VIP vs port forwarding VIP?
cards.back: Static: whole port range maps 1:1. Port forwarding: only specified ports map (set portforward enable).

cards.front: Do VIP policies match like normal policies?
cards.back: No: policies with a VIP applied have priority over typical policies.
Lets a deny policy also match traffic destined to VIPs.

cards.back: Enabled by default on deny; it can't be enabled on accept policies.

cards.front: Second way to block certain sources from a VIP?
cards.back: A VIP with `src-filter` used in a deny policy above the accept policy.

cards.back: Overload, one-to-one, fixed port range, port block allocation.

cards.back: When port conflicts: keep the original port unless it collides.

cards.back: One-to-one.

cards.back: Fixed port range (internal and external ranges); overload and one-to-one only need the external range.
Block size (ports per block) and blocks per user, plus the external IP range.

cards.back: It's skipped; SNAT must be done in central-snat-map.

cards.back: Policy & Objects > DNAT & Virtual IPs (Central DNAT).
