quiz.stem: Put the PS delivery phases in order.
quiz.explanation: Handoff, kickoff, discovery, design, build/test, implement, accept, hand over.

quiz.stem: During implementation the customer asks you to "also quickly set up SD-WAN for the two other branches", which isn't in the SOW. Best answer?

options.text: Welcome it and raise a change request so it's scoped, approved and scheduled
Do it tonight to keep the customer happy
options.why_wrong: Untracked work breaks timelines, testing and budgets.
Correct on scope, wrong on relationship; offer the proper path.
Own it: you can start the change request yourself.

quiz.explanation: Protect scope without saying no to the customer.

quiz.stem: Which document lists every interface, IP, policy and route needed to build the solution?

options.why_wrong: The HLD explains the architecture and reasoning, not every setting.
The SOW defines scope and responsibilities.

quiz.explanation: Low-level design = the build sheet.

quiz.stem: Which belong in the pre-checks of a FortiGate change window? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Backup, baseline, console. Then start.

quiz.stem: What makes a rollback plan usable at 2 a.m.?

options.text: A written trigger with a deadline, and exact steps back

options.why_wrong: Tired people need a script, not memory.

options.text: A vendor TAC case opened in advance
options.why_wrong: Useful backup, but not a rollback plan.
Too destructive; restore the backup or revision instead.

quiz.explanation: Decide when and how you roll back before you start.

quiz.stem: Which weekly status format do hiring managers usually want to hear?

options.text: A full log of every command

options.why_wrong: Silence breeds surprise; report every week.
Useful internally, not the status customers need.

quiz.explanation: Short, predictable, decision-oriented.

quiz.stem: Validation fails 20 minutes before the agreed go/no-go time. What do you do?

options.text: Try one targeted fix if time allows; at the go/no-go time, roll back as planned and communicate

options.why_wrong: That's how windows overrun into business hours.

options.text: Roll back immediately without telling anyone
options.why_wrong: Rollback is fine; skipping communication isn't.

options.text: Leave it half-done and fix it tomorrow
options.why_wrong: Never leave production in an untested state.

quiz.explanation: The go/no-go time is a commitment you made to the customer.

quiz.stem: Which ATP test is most likely to catch an MTU/MSS problem on new tunnels?

options.text: A large file transfer through each tunnel

options.why_wrong: Small pings pass even when large packets don't.
A tunnel can be up while large packets are dropped.

quiz.explanation: Small things pass; big things reveal MTU problems.

quiz.stem: A hiring manager asks: 'Have you led full Fortinet implementations end to end?' Best answer?

options.text: An honest 'not as the named delivery owner', then the concrete pieces you've done and how you'd close the gap

options.why_wrong: Untrue claims collapse under follow-up questions.
True but undersells real design, rollout and recovery work.

quiz.explanation: Honesty plus evidence plus a plan beats both bluffing and underselling.

quiz.stem: What's the strongest way to deliver bad news to a customer sponsor?

options.text: What we found, the impact, options, and my recommendation with reasons
Wait until you have a fix

options.why_wrong: Blame doesn't help the customer decide.

quiz.explanation: Bad news early, always with a plan.

quiz.stem: A partner did half of a customer's deployment and left. The customer is frustrated and the renewal is near. Based on your own experience, what's the best first move?

options.text: Audit what was delivered against what was promised, then propose a staged plan to complete it with quick wins first

options.why_wrong: Wastes what works and delays value.

options.text: Escalate to the partner's management only
options.why_wrong: The customer still has a half-done deployment.

quiz.explanation: That's exactly what you did at Netskope: gap analysis, then staged completion as QA on the partner's work.

quiz.stem: Mid-window, a routing change cuts off your SSH session to the FortiGate. The MOP was followed. What should have been in place?

options.text: Console or out-of-band access, checked in pre-checks, plus the rollback steps

options.why_wrong: It's cut off by the same routing change.
A reboot doesn't undo a saved bad config.

options.text: Nothing; wait for the route to recover

quiz.explanation: You've recovered FortiGates over console after bad routing; make console part of every pre-check.

quiz.stem: The customer's CISO wants SSL deep inspection on 3,000 endpoints in one go next week. Which plan shows PS maturity?

options.text: Pilot group, CA via GPO, exemptions for pinned and sensitive apps, waves with rollback, success criteria agreed
Enable it for everyone at once to meet the date
options.why_wrong: Breaks apps everywhere at once with no rollback path.

options.text: Refuse; deep inspection is too risky
options.why_wrong: It's valuable; the task is doing it safely.

options.text: Use certificate inspection only, without telling the CISO
options.why_wrong: Silently changing the requirement breaks trust.

quiz.explanation: Phased, reversible, agreed: your real rollout experience distributing the CA through Group Policy.

quiz.stem: Which handover item most reduces post-project support calls?

options.text: Hands-on knowledge transfer where the customer's team performs the key tasks

options.why_wrong: Doesn't scale or build their capability.

options.text: A list of FortiOS documentation links

quiz.explanation: Doing beats reading.

labs.title: Fill in a MOP skeleton
labs.goal: Complete the missing sections of a MOP for adding a VIP for a new web server.

worked.config:
CHANGE CHG-1042 · Window Sat 22:00–00:00 · Go/no-go 23:30
Contacts: PS consultant (you), customer network lead, approver: IT manager
PRE-CHECKS
  1. Backup config / FortiManager revision "pre-CHG-1042"
  2. Baseline: get system status, get system performance status,
     get router info routing-table all, get system session status
  3. Console access confirmed
STEPS
  1. Create VIP WEB-NEW (extip 203.0.113.20 → 10.0.20.20 tcp/443)
  2. Create policy wan1 → dmz, dst WEB-NEW, service HTTPS, IPS default, log all
  3. Install (FortiManager install preview reviewed first)
VALIDATION
  1. External HTTPS to 203.0.113.20 loads the site (customer confirms)
  2. Debug flow shows "Allowed by Policy-<id>"
  3. Logs reach FortiAnalyzer
ROLLBACK (trigger: validation fails at 23:30)
  1. Restore revision "pre-CHG-1042"; confirm baseline matches
COMMUNICATION
  Start / go-no-go / close messages to IT manager
notes: Every step has an expected result someone can check.
The rollback has a trigger time, not a feeling.

solo.prompt: Write the five headings of a MOP and, under ROLLBACK, a trigger and one restore step for a FortiManager-managed FortiGate.
solo.solution:
PRE-CHECKS / STEPS / VALIDATION / ROLLBACK / COMMUNICATION
ROLLBACK (trigger: any validation step fails at the 23:30 go/no-go)
  1. Revert the device to FortiManager revision "pre-CHG" and install
  2. Confirm baseline outputs match the pre-check capture

labs.title: Write the ATP for a branch cutover
labs.goal: List acceptance tests for moving a branch to a new FortiGate with an IPsec tunnel to HQ and one published service.

worked.config:
ATP-BR07
T1 Outbound web from staff VLAN → pass (FortiView shows sessions)
T2 Guest VLAN can't reach staff VLAN → blocked (log shows deny)
T3 Branch → HQ file share, 2 GB copy completes (MTU/MSS check)
T4 HQ → branch printer reachable (both directions of the tunnel)
T5 Published camera portal reachable from internet; blocked countries denied
T6 Logs visible in FortiAnalyzer within 5 minutes
T7 Admin access only from management subnet
Sign-off: customer IT lead ____  date ____
notes: Each test: action, expected result, evidence, signature.
T3 catches MTU problems that pings miss.

solo.prompt: Write three acceptance tests for an HA pair: one for failover, one for failback, one for sessions.
solo.solution:
T1 Failover: unplug the primary's monitored WAN → secondary becomes primary within the agreed time; users keep browsing
T2 Failback: restore the link → cluster returns to the expected primary (per override settings); no outage beyond the agreed time
T3 Sessions: long-running download / SSH survives failover (session pickup enabled)

scenarios.title: The half-finished partner deployment
scenarios.situation: You're assigned to a customer where a partner started a FortiGate + FortiManager deployment, configured half the branches, and stopped answering. The customer's IT director is angry and their renewal with Fortinet is in three months.
scenarios.ask: What are your first two weeks?
right_thinking: Listen first: the director's impact and expectations, without blaming the partner
Audit: what the SOW promised vs what exists (FortiManager ADOMs, policy packages, branch status)
Plan in stages: quick wins in week 1, risky items scheduled with MOPs
Weekly status with done/next/risks/decisions; one owner per action
Bring the account team in on the renewal risk with facts
scenarios.what: Gap audit plus staged completion plan, with visible quick wins.
scenarios.why: Trust returns when the customer sees progress and predictability; staged delivery limits risk.
pitfalls: Criticising the partner to the customer
Rebuilding everything from scratch
Promising dates before the audit
scenarios.model_answer: "I did almost exactly this at Netskope: I took over partner PS projects that were only partly delivered and finished them in stages. Week one I'd listen to the director, then audit what the SOW promised against what's really in FortiManager and on the branches. I'd come back with a staged plan: quick wins first so they see progress, riskier changes in proper windows with MOPs. From then on, a weekly status with done, next, risks and decisions, and I'd keep the account team informed because the renewal depends on it."
could_have_added: Name a measurable first-week win (e.g., three branches finished and validated)
scenarios.best_way: Listen, audit against the SOW, then finish it in stages the customer can see. I've done this before, at Netskope.

scenarios.title: Raid: 01:40, the cutover is failing
scenarios.situation: You're migrating a hospital's core firewall to a FortiGate HA pair. Window 00:00–03:00, go/no-go at 02:15. At 01:40 everything works except the radiology PACS system, which can't reach its cloud archive. The night IT supervisor is nervous; the morning shift starts at 06:00.
scenarios.ask: What do you do between 01:40 and 02:15?
right_thinking: Communicate: tell the supervisor what works, what doesn't, and that 02:15 is the decision point
Evidence: sniffer and debug flow for the PACS flow (policy? NAT? route? MTU on large images?)
One targeted change at a time, each tested by the PACS user
At 02:15 if not fixed: roll back as per the MOP, or (only if agreed) go live with a documented, approved workaround
Write up the open issue and next step before you leave
scenarios.what: Time-boxed evidence-based fix with a firm rollback decision at go/no-go.
scenarios.why: In healthcare, predictable rollback beats heroic overtime; the go/no-go time protects patient services.
pitfalls: Blowing through the go/no-go time
Several simultaneous changes
Leaving without a written status
scenarios.model_answer: "First I tell the supervisor: everything's up except PACS, I have 35 minutes to fix it, and at 02:15 we decide go or roll back. Then evidence: a filtered sniffer and debug flow on the PACS flow, because large medical images can also hit MTU limits. I make one targeted change at a time and have the PACS user test each. If it's not fixed at 02:15, we follow the MOP and roll back, unless the customer explicitly approves going live with a documented workaround. Either way, I leave a written status before the morning shift."
scenarios.best_way: One flow broken, 35 minutes, one change at a time, and at 02:15 we follow the plan, not our hopes.

scenarios.title: Scope creep from the sponsor
scenarios.situation: Two weeks before go-live, the customer's sponsor asks you to "also add ZTNA for the remote workers, since you're already here". It's not in the SOW and would affect the timeline.
scenarios.ask: How do you respond in the meeting?
right_thinking: Acknowledge the value of the idea
Explain the impact on timeline and testing honestly
Offer the path: a change request or a phase 2, scoped with pre-sales
Keep the current go-live safe
scenarios.what: A phase 2 / change request instead of silent scope creep.
scenarios.why: Untracked work threatens the agreed go-live and the quality of both deliveries.
scenarios.model_answer: "That's a great next step, and ZTNA fits well with what we're building. If we add it now, it puts the go-live and the testing at risk. Let me raise it as a change request, or a phase 2, with the account team this week, so it's scoped and tested properly, and we keep your go-live date safe."
scenarios.best_way: Great idea, wrong week. Let's make it phase 2 so both projects land well.

interview.question: Walk me through how you'd run a Fortinet implementation from kickoff to handover.
interview.testing: Whether you know the PS lifecycle and its documents
interview.framework: Phases with one key output each
interview.model_answer: "Before the kickoff I read the SOW and talk to pre-sales, so I know what was promised and why. At kickoff we agree on scope, roles, timeline and how we communicate. In discovery I collect the current configs and the requirements, then I write the HLD for the architecture and the LLD with every setting. We build and test, ideally staged in FortiManager or in a lab; at Fortinet I reproduced customer scenarios with Terraform templates before recommending changes. Production changes go in windows with a MOP: pre-checks, steps, validation, rollback with a trigger time. Then the acceptance test plan with the customer, the as-built, and hands-on knowledge transfer."
could_have_added: Weekly status: done, next, risks, decisions
interview.best_way: Know the promise, design it, prove it in a lab, change it safely, prove it again with the customer, and leave them self-sufficient.

interview.question: Tell me about a project someone else started that you had to finish.
interview.model_answer: "At Netskope, some partner professional-services projects were left half delivered. The customer had paid, adoption was stuck, and a renewal was coming. I audited what had actually been deployed against what was planned, then completed it in stages, quick wins first, effectively acting as the QA layer on the partner's work. The customer got to a working deployment, and I kept the partner relationship intact by focusing on the gaps, not on blame."
could_have_added: A number if you have it: adoption before and after, or time to complete
interview.best_way: I audited what was really there, finished it in stages, and kept the partner on side. In practice I was the QA on their PS work.
follow_ups: How did you handle the partner?

interview.question: Tell me about a time you turned a hostile customer situation around.
interview.model_answer: "At Netskope a named enterprise account escalated in a churn-shaped way; the relationship was hostile. Instead of treating it as a relationship problem, I went after the underlying technical issue, diagnosed and resolved it, and used that restored credibility to restructure the agreement as a license exchange rather than a cancellation. That kept more than 900 thousand dollars in total contract value. What I learned for PS: fix the real problem first and the relationship follows."
interview.best_way: I fixed the technical problem first; the trust came back with it, and we kept over 900k in contract value.

interview.question: Describe a rollout you planned that had to avoid disrupting users.
interview.model_answer: "At Netskope one account was using less than half of what they'd bought. I worked out what was blocking a secure rollout, planned a one-month rollout step by step, and brought in senior support and a dedicated manager. Utilisation went from below 50 % to 70 %. And at Fortinet I taught customers how to roll out SSL deep inspection estate-wide by distributing the CA certificate through Group Policy, so users didn't get certificate errors."
interview.best_way: Find the real blocker, plan it step by step with the right people, and measure it: below 50 % to 70 % utilisation.

interview.question: Have you led full Fortinet implementations end to end?
interview.testing: Honesty and self-awareness about the main gap
interview.framework: Honest answer → evidence of pieces → plan
interview.model_answer: "Not as the named delivery owner of a PS project. What I have done: at Fortinet I was a P3 escalation engineer, and many of my cases were implementations in progress: routing, failover, third-party switch integration, SD-WAN designs from requirements, HA in AWS and Azure, and recovering split-brain clusters. At Netskope I finished partners' half-delivered PS projects in stages. So I know the technology and the delivery steps; in my first 90 days I'd shadow your delivery process, use your templates and take ownership of smaller projects first."
could_have_added: Mention you're re-studying 7.6/8.0 right now with the official guides
interview.best_way: Not as the named owner, but I've done every piece of it, and here's how I'd close the gap in 90 days.

interview.question: Tell me about a time you worked with development or engineering to fix a product issue.
interview.model_answer: "At Fortinet a customer had packet duplication over SD-WAN across three ISPs over VPN. I reproduced it, traced it to specific SLA settings, and escalated to development with clear reproduction steps, then followed it to the fix. As one of the main escalation points for North American and Brazilian enterprise customers, that was my pattern: real defects went to development with evidence, not opinions."
interview.best_way: I reproduced it, narrowed it to specific SLA settings, and handed development a clean repro.

interview.question: How do you handle a customer who keeps adding scope?
interview.testing: Scope management without damaging the relationship
interview.model_answer: "I welcome the idea and make it visible: 'great idea, let's raise it as a change request so it's scoped and tested properly'. Then I bring in the account team so it can become a change order or a phase 2. That protects the go-live date and the quality, and the customer feels heard, not refused."
interview.best_way: Great idea, let's make it a change request so it gets done right.

interview.question: What does your weakness look like at work?
interview.framework: Real weakness → impact → what you changed → result
interview.model_answer: "Early in my customer-facing roles I let work fragment across email, chat and CRM, and it was hard to keep one source of truth per account. I fixed it by building my own tooling, Python scripts and AI workflows that consolidate account activity and turn notes into action items, so nothing slips. In PS I'd apply the same discipline from day one: one project tracker, weekly status, and a risk register."
could_have_added: Keep it short; end on the system you use now
interview.best_way: I used to let tasks scatter; now I build systems so nothing slips: one tracker, weekly status, a risk register.

interview.question: How do you mentor or bring others up to speed?
interview.model_answer: "At SYKES, on Cisco TAC, I mentored new engineers through structured training. At Netskope I led new Customer Success Manager hires through onboarding and ramp, without a formal reporting line. And I write things down: at Netskope I wrote customer-facing KB articles and how-to guides. In PS that becomes good as-builts and knowledge transfer sessions where the customer's team does the work themselves."
interview.best_way: I've onboarded engineers and CSMs, and I write the guides people actually use.

interview.question: A change you made caused an outage. What happened and what did you learn?
interview.testing: Accountability; works best with a real, small story
interview.model_answer: "Use a real, small story of your own here. If you don't have one from your own changes, use the closest true one: at Fortinet I recovered FortiGates that customers had cut off with bad routing changes, over console, sometimes with a TFTP restore or a live static-route fix. What it taught me, and what I put in every MOP now, is console access and a tested rollback before any routing change."
could_have_added: Own your part clearly if it was your change; interviewers respect it
interview.best_way: Routing changes can lock you out. That's why console access and a tested rollback are in every MOP I write.

interview.question: How would you handle a technical disagreement with the customer's architect?
interview.model_answer: "First I make sure I understand their reasoning; often they know a constraint I don't. Then I bring evidence: the documentation, a lab test, or numbers. I present options with trade-offs and let the customer decide, and I write the decision down in the design so it's clear later. If it's a security risk, I make the risk explicit and get sign-off on it rather than quietly going along."
interview.best_way: Understand, test, present options, and write the decision down. Risks get a signature, not silence.

interview.question: Why would you be good at professional services specifically?
interview.model_answer: "Because I've seen the product from both sides. At Fortinet TAC I learned how FortiOS behaves when it breaks: debug flow, NAT, SD-WAN, HA, VPN. At Netskope I learned to own customers: plans, QBRs with executives, and finishing partner PS work that stalled. PS needs both: the depth to design and change things safely, and the customer skills to keep everyone aligned. And I work in English, Spanish and Portuguese and can travel anywhere."
interview.best_way: I know how FortiOS breaks and how customers feel when it does. PS is where those two meet.

field_reports.title: Breaches take longer when nobody owns the plan

modules.title: Implementation craft and migrations: MOPs, cutovers and vendor conversions
objectives: Write a method of procedure (MOP) with pre-checks, steps, verification and rollback
Run a maintenance window calmly, with go/no-go points and clear communication
Plan a migration from Cisco ASA, Palo Alto or Check Point to FortiGate
Translate NAT correctly between vendors, the step where migrations break
Close with acceptance tests and a handover the customer can operate
sources: PS delivery practice (curriculum M11.2 Implementation craft and M11.3 Migrations, merged)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: NAT and VIPs (see M4.03), configuration backup and revisions
Your evidence: Terraform-based reproduction, console recoveries, guided HA upgrades (super-cv)

units.title: The MOP and the maintenance window
units.body:
A **method of procedure (MOP)** is the script for a change. A good one lets a colleague run it at 2 a.m. without you.

## MOP sections

1. **Purpose and scope:** what changes, which devices, which SOW item.
2. **Risk and impact:** what users will notice, expected downtime, who approved.
3. **Prerequisites:** backups taken, console access tested, firmware and licences checked, people on the call.
4. **Pre-checks with expected output:** `get system status`, `get system ha status`, `get router info routing-table all`, `get vpn ipsec tunnel summary`, a session count, a few application tests. Save the outputs: they're your baseline.
5. **Steps,** numbered, with the exact commands or GUI actions.
6. **Verification** after each block, against the baseline.
7. **Go/no-go points** and a time limit: "If X isn't working by 01:30, roll back."
8. **Rollback** steps, tested.
9. **Communication:** who's told at start, at each go/no-go, and at the end.

## In the window

- Start with a short call: scope, roles, go/no-go times.
- Take a fresh backup (`execute backup config` to a server, or a FortiManager revision).
- Change one block at a time; verify; tick the MOP.
- If something unexpected happens, **stop and assess** before trying fixes: a calm rollback beats a creative 3 a.m. fix.
- Close with a summary email: what was done, results, open items.

:::tip
Test the rollback, not just the change. At Fortinet you reproduced customer cases with shared Terraform templates before recommending a fix; a lab rehearsal of the MOP is the PS version of that habit.
:::

:::recall
Q: What turns pre-checks into evidence?
A: Saving their output as a baseline and comparing after the change.
:::

units.title: Migrations from other vendors
units.body:
## The phases

1. **Discover:** export the current configuration, hit counts and logs. Find what's actually used. Interview application owners.
2. **Convert:** Fortinet's **FortiConverter** (tool and service) translates configurations from vendors like Cisco, Palo Alto and Check Point; scripts help for special cases. Conversion is a draft, not a result.
3. **Clean up:** remove unused objects and zero-hit rules, merge duplicates, fix shadowed and overly broad rules (`any any`). Migration is the best chance the customer will get to tidy up.
4. **Rebuild what doesn't translate 1:1:** NAT, VPN parameters, routing, authentication, security profiles.
5. **Test** in a lab or with a parallel deployment; **cut over** in a window with a rollback (often: reconnect the old firewall).
6. **Hypercare:** a period of close monitoring and quick fixes after cutover.

## NAT: where migrations break

- **Cisco ASA:** object NAT (`nat (inside,outside) static 203.0.113.10` under an object) becomes a **VIP** plus a policy using the VIP; dynamic PAT (`dynamic interface`) becomes **`set nat enable`** on the outbound policy, or an IP pool. ASA access rules on the outside interface target the real (mapped) IP since 8.3; on FortiGate the inbound policy references the **VIP**.
- **Palo Alto:** security rules for destination NAT use the **pre-NAT destination IP** with the **post-NAT zone**. On FortiGate you use the VIP object and the real destination interface. Translating PAN rules literally creates rules that never match.
- **Check Point:** watch implied rules from global properties and automatic NAT on objects: they're not visible in the rule base but must be rebuilt as explicit policies or VIPs.

FortiGate reminders from M4.03: DNAT happens before routing and policy; VIP policies take priority; hairpin needs care.

:::pitfall
A converted rule base that "looks the same" can behave differently: implicit rules, NAT order and zone semantics change. Test real flows, not just syntax.
:::

units.title: Acceptance, handover and hypercare
units.body:
## Acceptance test plan (ATP)

Agreed **before** the change, signed **after** it. Each test: what's tested, how, expected result, actual result, pass/fail, who witnessed. Typical tests: each critical application from each site, internet access with security profiles working, VPNs up, HA failover, FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer connectivity, logging and reports.

## Handover pack

- As-built documentation: topology, addressing, policies, VPN and HA details.
- Admin access and credentials handled by the customer's process (never in email).
- Runbooks for common tasks and a short troubleshooting guide.
- Knowledge-transfer session, recorded if allowed.
- Open items with owners and dates.

## Hypercare

An agreed period after go-live (often one to two weeks) with faster response. Track issues, separate defects in your work from new requests (change requests), and close with a sign-off.

## Recoveries you can reference

At Fortinet you recovered FortiGates cut off by bad routing over the **console**, including TFTP restores and live static-route fixes, and guided HA firmware upgrades step by step, with a manual console upgrade when the online one failed. That's why your MOPs always list console access as a prerequisite.

:::ps
The customer remembers the handover more than the configuration. A clean ATP signature and a runbook they can use are what make them call you for the next project.
:::

labs.title: Translate ASA NAT to FortiGate
labs.goal: Rebuild an ASA static NAT for a web server and the outbound PAT on FortiGate (wan1 outside, dmz for the server, port2 inside).

worked.config:
# ASA (source)
# object network WEB
#  host 10.1.1.10
#  nat (dmz,outside) static 203.0.113.10
# object network INSIDE-NET
#  subnet 192.168.10.0 255.255.255.0
#  nat (inside,outside) dynamic interface
config firewall vip
    edit "WEB-VIP"
        set extintf "wan1"
        set extip 203.0.113.10
        set mappedip "10.1.1.10"
    next
end
config firewall policy
    edit 0
        set name "Internet-to-WEB"
        set srcintf "wan1"
        set dstintf "dmz"
        set srcaddr "all"
        set dstaddr "WEB-VIP"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
        set service "HTTPS"
    next
    edit 0
        set name "Inside-to-Internet"
        set srcintf "port2"
        set dstintf "wan1"
        set srcaddr "INSIDE-NET"
        set dstaddr "all"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
        set service "ALL"
        set nat enable
    next
end
notes: Static object NAT → VIP; the inbound policy uses the VIP, not the private IP.
dynamic interface → set nat enable (egress interface IP).
Restrict service to what the server really offers.

faded.template:
config firewall {{vip}}
    edit "WEB-VIP"
        set {{extintf}} "wan1"
        set extip 203.0.113.10
        set {{mappedip}} "10.1.1.10"
    next
end
config firewall policy
    edit 0
        set dstaddr "{{WEB-VIP}}"
    next
end

solo.prompt: An ASA publishes SSH on 203.0.113.20 port 2222 to 10.1.1.20 port 22. Write the FortiGate VIP with port forwarding (external interface wan1).
solo.solution:
config firewall vip
    edit "SSH-VIP"
        set extintf "wan1"
        set extip 203.0.113.20
        set mappedip "10.1.1.20"
        set portforward enable
        set extport 2222
        set mappedport 22
    next
end
solo.notes: Then an inbound policy with dstaddr SSH-VIP and service SSH (the mapped port).

scenarios.title: The 2 a.m. surprise
scenarios.situation: Mid-migration from an ASA, the new FortiGate is live. Email and web work, but the payroll app at a partner fails. Go/no-go is in 20 minutes. The customer's IT manager says, "Just make it work, we can't roll back, payroll runs tomorrow."
scenarios.ask: What do you do?
right_thinking: Stay calm and get evidence fast: sniffer and debug flow for the payroll flow
Likely a VPN or NAT translation difference
Be honest about the go/no-go; explain rollback is an option that protects payroll
Decide with the customer, document
scenarios.what: A fast, evidence-based decision with the customer.
scenarios.why: Pressure creates bad changes; the MOP exists for this moment.
how: Debug flow filtered on the partner IP
Check VPN selectors/NAT against the ASA config
Otherwise roll back that part or all, per MOP
scenarios.model_answer: I'd say: "Give me ten minutes of focused diagnosis." A filtered debug flow and the tunnel list for the partner usually show it fast: often the ASA did NAT inside the VPN, or the partner's selectors don't match ours. If the fix is clear and low-risk, I apply it and test payroll with them. If not, I'd remind the manager that rollback protects payroll tomorrow, and we can reconnect the old path for just that partner while we fix it properly. Either way the decision is theirs, made with facts, and I write it down.
scenarios.best_way: Ten minutes of focused evidence; fix if clear and safe, otherwise roll back that flow to protect payroll.

scenarios.title: "Just copy the old rules"
scenarios.situation: A customer migrating from Check Point says: "Don't clean anything up. Copy the rules exactly. We don't have time."
scenarios.ask: How do you handle it?
right_thinking: Respect the time constraint
Explain that a literal copy can still behave differently (implied rules, NAT)
Offer a minimal cleanup: only zero-hit and obviously broad rules, or a phase 2 cleanup
scenarios.what: A pragmatic agreement.
scenarios.why: You protect the customer from hidden behaviour changes without forcing a big project.
how: Flag implied rules and automatic NAT that must be explicit
Propose phase-2 cleanup with hit counts
scenarios.model_answer: Fine, we'll migrate like for like. One thing I can't skip: Check Point has implied rules and automatic NAT that aren't in the rule base, so I'll rebuild those explicitly, otherwise behaviour changes. After go-live, with a month of hit counts from FortiAnalyzer, I'd propose a short cleanup phase to remove unused rules. That keeps your timeline and gets you the cleanup later with data.
scenarios.best_way: Like for like now, but implied rules and NAT rebuilt explicitly; cleanup later with hit-count data.

interview.question: What goes into your method of procedure for a firewall change?
interview.model_answer: "Scope and approval, impact, prerequisites like a fresh backup and tested console access, pre-checks with saved outputs as a baseline, numbered steps, verification after each block, go/no-go times, a tested rollback, and who's informed when. A colleague should be able to run it without me."
interview.best_way: Prerequisites, baseline pre-checks, steps, verification, go/no-go, tested rollback, communication.

interview.question: Where do firewall migrations usually break?
interview.model_answer: "NAT semantics first: ASA object NAT, Palo Alto's pre-NAT IP with post-NAT zone, Check Point's automatic NAT and implied rules all translate differently into FortiGate VIPs and policies. Then VPN parameters with partners, and rules that were never used or are too broad. So I convert with FortiConverter, then review NAT line by line, clean up with hit counts and test real application flows."
interview.best_way: NAT semantics, partner VPNs and hidden rules. Convert, review NAT line by line, test real flows.

interview.question: Tell me about a change that went wrong and how you handled it.
interview.model_answer: "[Use a real case, e.g. a FortiGate cut off by bad routing that you recovered over the console with a TFTP restore or a live static-route fix.] Focus on: staying calm, restoring service first, telling the customer clearly what happened, and what you changed in your process afterwards, such as always testing console access before a change."
interview.best_way: Restore first, communicate clearly, then fix the process.

interview.question: How do you hand over a project so the customer can run it?
interview.model_answer: "A handover pack with as-built documentation and runbooks, a knowledge-transfer session, an agreed hypercare period, and the signed acceptance test plan. I also wrote KB articles and how-to guides at Netskope so customers could adopt features on their own, and I'd bring the same habit: leave them able to operate it without calling me."
interview.best_way: As-built docs, runbooks, knowledge transfer, hypercare and signed acceptance.

modules.title: Design documents and customer handling: HLD, LLD, status, scope and escalations
objectives: Write a high-level and a low-level design the customer can approve and an engineer can build from
Apply four design principles and name the failure modes in common Fortinet patterns
Run status reporting with a RAID log and RAG status that nobody is surprised by
Handle scope creep, difficult stakeholders and escalations without losing the relationship
sources: PS delivery practice (curriculum M11.4 Design patterns and M11.5 Customer handling, merged)
FortiTatake modules M4.09, M4.10, M8.03 and I3 for the technical patterns
Your evidence: escalation save, sponsor change, merger health checks, executive QBRs (super-cv)

units.title: HLD, LLD and four design principles
units.body:
## High-level design (HLD): for approval

Who reads it: the customer's architect, security lead and sponsor. Contents: **requirements and assumptions**, current state, the **target architecture diagram**, key decisions with **reasons and alternatives considered**, security zones, HA and resilience, management and logging, migration approach, risks.

## Low-level design (LLD): for building

Who reads it: the engineer who implements, maybe you at 2 a.m. Contents: **every interface, VLAN, IP, zone, route, VPN parameter, HA setting, SD-WAN member, health check and rule, policy matrix, NAT table, security profiles, admin access, logging**, naming conventions, and the acceptance tests.

If the LLD is good, the MOP almost writes itself.

## Four principles to justify any choice

1. **Segmentation and least privilege:** zones and policies that allow only what's needed; no `any any`.
2. **Resilience:** no single point of failure the customer can't accept (links, units, heartbeats, hubs).
3. **Manageability:** templates in FortiManager, naming standards, logs in FortiAnalyzer; the customer's team must be able to run it.
4. **Visibility and response:** logging, reports and alerts sized to what they must prove (compliance) and react to.

## Failure modes to design out (from the modules you've studied)

- SD-WAN: asymmetric routing, probes not reflecting the app path, leftover policy routes.
- HA: split brain from shared heartbeat paths; no session pickup for long sessions; override surprises.
- VPN: overlapping subnets, MTU, weak proposals, exposed gateways.
- Inspection: CA not distributed, pinned apps, proxy where flow would do.

:::recall
Q: Who is the HLD for, and who is the LLD for?
A: HLD for approval (architects, sponsor); LLD for building (the implementing engineer).
:::

units.title: Status, RAID and scope
units.body:
## Weekly status that prevents surprises

One page: **RAG status** (red/amber/green) for scope, schedule and budget; done this week; next week; **decisions needed** from the customer; risks and issues. Send it at the same time every week. Amber early is a gift; red at the end is a failure of communication.

## The RAID log

- **Risks:** might happen (a change freeze could delay cutover). Owner, likelihood, impact, mitigation.
- **Assumptions:** what you're relying on (the customer provides console access).
- **Issues:** happening now (ISP circuit not delivered). Owner and due date.
- **Dependencies:** what you need from others (partner VPN parameters by Friday).

## Scope creep

Requests will come: "while you're here, can you…". The pattern:

1. **Acknowledge** the request positively.
2. **Check the SOW.**
3. If out of scope: explain, estimate, and raise a **change request**, or park it for a follow-up project.
4. Never do unbilled work silently: it sets an expectation and hides the real cost.

At Netskope you kept reporting rhythms for a whole portfolio: weekly status on open issues, quarterly business reviews in three languages. PS status is the same discipline on a project scale.

:::pitfall
"Green, green, green, red" is the worst status pattern. If something might slip, show amber with the reason and what you need.
:::

units.title: Difficult moments and storytelling
units.body:
## Difficult stakeholders

- **The hostile sponsor:** treat it as a problem to solve, not a person to win. Find the technical cause behind the anger. Your evidence: a hostile escalation where you fixed the underlying technical issue first, and the customer exchanged licences instead of leaving: more than USD 900k in contract value kept.
- **The new team that inherits you:** start with something useful to them. After a whole security team was replaced, you opened with a health check; more than half the seats were in use within six weeks.
- **Two merged companies:** one shared view. After customer mergers you presented a health check and adoption dashboards so the combined team agreed on priorities.
- **The customer's architect who disagrees:** listen, compare options against their requirements, bring evidence (lab, docs), and if it's their risk to take, document the decision.

## Escalations

Escalate **early, factually, to the right level**, with options. Before a rollout at Netskope you escalated a support backlog to the director of support and set an AI agent to alert on every case update or idle case: the issue was visible and moving.

## Storytelling that lands

**Problem → impact → approach → proof.** "Branches lost voice quality at peak (problem); it cost them complaints from stores (impact); we moved voice to Best Quality on jitter with probes to the voice platform (approach); jitter fell and complaints stopped in the pilot stores (proof)." Use their words and their numbers.

:::ps
The relationship is built in the bad moments. Customers forgive problems; they don't forgive surprises.
:::

scenarios.title: Raid: the project is drifting
scenarios.situation: Week 5 of an 8-week SD-WAN rollout for 25 branches. Only 6 branches are done. The customer's network lead is on leave, two ISP circuits are late, and the sponsor has just asked for "a quick status" before tomorrow's board meeting.
scenarios.ask: What do you send the sponsor tonight, and what do you change in the plan?
right_thinking: Honest RAG: schedule red or amber with clear reasons
Separate causes: customer dependency (lead on leave), third party (ISPs), your own pace
Offer options to recover: parallel branches, temporary delegate, re-sequence by circuit availability
Ask for the decisions you need
scenarios.what: A one-page status with options and decisions requested.
scenarios.why: The board will ask; the sponsor needs facts and a plan, not reassurance.
pitfalls: Reporting green
Blaming the customer
No options
scenarios.model_answer: I'd send a one-page status tonight. Schedule: red, 6 of 25 branches done against a plan of 15. Causes, factually: two ISP circuits late (owner: ISP, escalated), and approvals slowed while the network lead is on leave. Recovery options: re-sequence so we do branches with circuits ready first, run two branches per window instead of one, and a temporary delegate for approvals. With those, the new forecast is week 10, or week 9 if we get a delegate by Monday. Decisions needed: approve the delegate and the double windows. That gives the sponsor a clear story for the board and a plan, not just bad news.
scenarios.best_way: Red, with causes, options and a new forecast, and the two decisions we need from you.

scenarios.title: The design review that turns hostile
scenarios.situation: In your HLD review, the customer's security lead says: "This design is too complex, our team can't run it. Why did Fortinet sell us this?"
scenarios.ask: How do you respond in the meeting?
right_thinking: Don't defend the sale; engage with the concern
Manageability is a design principle: it's a valid requirement
Simplify where possible; offer knowledge transfer and runbooks
scenarios.what: A respectful, constructive reply and a design adjustment.
scenarios.why: A design the team can't run will fail after handover.
scenarios.model_answer: "That's an important point: if your team can't run it, it's not the right design. Which parts worry you most?" Then I'd look for simplifications, like fewer SD-WAN rules, A-P instead of A-A, templates in FortiManager, and add knowledge transfer and runbooks to the plan. I'd update the HLD with those changes and the reasons, so the decision is clear for everyone.
scenarios.best_way: If your team can't run it, it's not right. Tell me which parts worry you, and we'll simplify and plan knowledge transfer.

interview.question: How do you keep a project's stakeholders informed?
interview.model_answer: "A one-page weekly status at the same time each week: RAG for scope, schedule and budget, done and next, decisions needed, and the RAID highlights. I show amber early with the reason, so nobody is surprised. At Netskope I kept that rhythm across a portfolio: weekly status on open issues and quarterly reviews with executives in three languages."
interview.best_way: Weekly one-pager with RAG, decisions and RAID. Amber early, no surprises.

interview.question: Tell me about a time you had to deliver bad news to a customer.
interview.model_answer: "[Use a real case: for example, telling an account that the support backlog was blocking their rollout, while escalating it to the director of support.] Show: you told them early, with facts and a plan, you followed up visibly, and the relationship held because there were no surprises."
interview.best_way: Early, factual, with a plan, and visible follow-up.

interview.question: How do you handle a customer who keeps changing requirements?
interview.model_answer: "I welcome the change and make its cost visible. Check it against the SOW, explain the impact on time and effort, and raise a change request, or park it for a later phase. And I write down each decision. Customers usually appreciate it, because they can prioritise with real information."
interview.best_way: Welcome it, show the impact, change request or later phase, and write it down.

interview.question: What's the difference between an HLD and an LLD?
interview.model_answer: "The HLD is for approval: requirements, target architecture, key decisions and why, risks. The LLD is for building: every interface, IP, route, VPN, HA, SD-WAN, policy and NAT detail, plus the acceptance tests. A good LLD makes the MOP straightforward."
interview.best_way: HLD for approval, LLD for building.

interview.question: Tell me about turning around an unhappy customer.
interview.model_answer: "A named enterprise account escalated and was ready to leave. I treated it as a technical problem first: diagnosed and fixed the underlying issue, and with that credibility we restructured the agreement as a licence exchange instead of a cancellation, keeping more than 900 thousand dollars in contract value. Learning: fix the real problem and the relationship follows."
interview.best_way: Fixed the technical cause first; the escalation became a licence exchange, more than USD 900k kept.

field_reports.title: Speed of response is money
field_reports.body: IBM's 2026 report found organizations using security AI and automation extensively saved **USD 1.93 million** and **65 days** per breach. Good designs include the logging, alerting and runbooks that make fast response possible.

modules.title: IPsec VPN on FortiGate: build, verify and troubleshoot
objectives: Explain phase 1 and phase 2 in plain words and say which settings must match on both sides
Build a route-based site-to-site tunnel with routes, blackhole route and policies in both directions
Choose modern proposals and DH groups, and justify IKEv2
Read diagnose vpn output and an IKE debug to find the failing step
Talk a customer through a tunnel that is up but passes no traffic
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: General IPsec VPN configuration, phase 1 (pp. 3128–3143), phase 2 (pp. 3168–3171)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: FortiGate-to-FortiGate site-to-site with the VPN Wizard (pp. 3247–3252)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: VPN IPsec troubleshooting, logs and diagnose commands (pp. 3754–3768)

units.title: Two phases, one tunnel
units.body:
An IPsec tunnel is built in two steps.

**Phase 1 (IKE SA)** is the two gateways agreeing to talk securely: who the peer is (`remote-gw`), how they authenticate (pre-shared key or certificates), which **IKE version**, and the **proposals** (encryption + hash) and **Diffie-Hellman groups** they accept (pp. 3129–3140). IKE uses **UDP 500**, and **UDP 4500** when NAT traversal is in use.

**Phase 2 (IPsec SA, "quick mode")** is the agreement for the actual traffic: the **selectors** (which local and remote networks), the phase 2 proposals, **PFS**, replay detection and key lifetime (pp. 3168–3170). In tunnel mode the original packet is encrypted inside ESP with a new IP header.

## Must match on both sides

- Phase 1: IKE version, at least **one proposal**, at least **one DH group**, the authentication method and key.
- Phase 2: at least one proposal and DH group (if PFS), and **mirror-image selectors** (my local = your remote).

## IKEv1 or IKEv2

Both are supported. IKEv1 uses XAuth for user authentication; IKEv2 uses EAP and can run over TCP. **New tunnels default to IKEv2** (p. 3142). Use IKEv2 unless the peer can't.

## Strong choices

The guide marks NULL, DES, 3DES, MD5 and SHA1 as **not recommended**; AES-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 are IKEv2-only; Fortinet recommends **DH groups 15–21 and 28–32** (pp. 3169–3170). By default the CLI only shows recommended IKE proposals (`ike-proposal-visibility`, p. 3139).

:::recall
Q: Phase 1 is up but phase 2 never comes up. What's the first thing to compare?
A: The phase 2 selectors (local/remote subnets must mirror each other) and the phase 2 proposals/PFS groups.
:::

units.title: Route-based site to site, the complete build
units.body:
On FortiGate the normal design is **route-based**: phase 1 is an interface (`phase1-interface`), and routing decides what enters the tunnel. The VPN Wizard's site-to-site template creates everything a working tunnel needs (pp. 3250–3251):

1. `config vpn ipsec phase1-interface`: interface, `ike-version 2`, `remote-gw`, `psksecret`, proposals.
2. `config vpn ipsec phase2-interface`: proposals and selectors.
3. **A static route** to the remote subnet with `device` = the tunnel interface.
4. **A blackhole route** to the same subnet with **distance 254**, so that when the tunnel is down the traffic is dropped instead of leaking out the default route in clear text.
5. **Two firewall policies**: LAN → tunnel and tunnel → LAN.

Forgetting steps 3–5 is the most common reason a tunnel is "up" but nothing works: IPsec builds the pipe, **routing and policy** decide whether anything uses it.

## Keeping it alive

- **DPD (dead peer detection):** `set dpd on-idle | on-demand`, with `dpd-retrycount` and `dpd-retryinterval` (p. 3140), so a dead peer is detected and the tunnel renegotiates.
- **add-route** (enabled by default) adds routes to the peer's selectors automatically, mainly useful for dial-up tunnels (p. 3141).
- `auto-negotiate` keeps phase 2 up without waiting for traffic.

:::cli
config router static
    edit 20
        set dst 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set device "to-branch"
    next
    edit 21
        set dst 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set blackhole enable
        set distance 254
    next
end
:::

:::pitfall
An MTU problem looks like a VPN problem: small pings work, file copies and web pages hang. ESP adds overhead, so clamp TCP MSS on the tunnel policy (`tcp-mss-sender` / `tcp-mss-receiver`), exactly as in the transport module.
:::

units.title: Reading what the FortiGate tells you
units.body:
Work bottom-up: is IKE reaching the peer, did phase 1 come up, did phase 2 come up, does traffic use it?

## Summary first

- `get vpn ipsec tunnel summary`: every tunnel, up/down, selectors up.
- `diagnose vpn ike gateway list`: **phase 1**: peer address and port (`:4500` means NAT-T), IKE version, negotiated **proposal**, `status: established`, DPD counters (pp. 3757–3758).
- `diagnose vpn tunnel list`: **phase 2**: `status=up`, the proxy ID **selectors** (`src:` / `dst:`), packet counters `rxp`/`txp`, DPD and NAT-T state (pp. 3758–3759).

If `txp` grows and `rxp` stays at zero, you're sending into the tunnel and nothing comes back: check the peer's routes and policies, not your phase 1.

## The IKE debug

:::cli
diagnose vpn ike log filter rem-addr4 203.0.113.10
diagnose debug application ike -1
diagnose debug enable
...bring the tunnel up...
diagnose debug disable
diagnose debug reset
:::

Always filter by the peer (p. 3761); on a busy hub an unfiltered IKE debug is unreadable. In the output, look for the **negotiation result** and **proposal** lines, `PSK authentication succeeded`, NAT detection, then the phase 2 **selectors** (p. 3762). A proposal mismatch typically shows as *no proposal chosen*; a wrong key fails at authentication.

## Logs

VPN event logs mirror the steps: *Progress IPsec phase 1* (negotiate → DONE), *IPsec connection status changed* (tunnel-up), *Progress IPsec phase 2*, *IPsec SA installed* with the SPIs, and tunnel-down or *phase 1 SA deleted* when it fails (pp. 3755–3756).

Sniff the control plane when nothing arrives: `diagnose sniffer packet any 'host 203.0.113.10 and (port 500 or port 4500)' 4`.

:::recall
Q: Which command shows the phase 2 selectors and packet counters?
A: diagnose vpn tunnel list.
:::

units.title: Remote access, and the consultant's view
units.body:
## Remote access in FortiOS 8.0

In 8.0 the browser-based SSL VPN portal is called **Agentless VPN**, and full-tunnel remote access is covered under **IPsec VPN** (dial-up, typically with FortiClient). Use IKEv2 for FortiClient 7.4.4 and later (p. 3142). Dial-up tunnels create a **dynamic instance per client** (`name_0`, `name_1` in `diagnose vpn ike gateway list`).

## Questions to ask before you build

- What's on each side: subnets, overlaps (overlapping subnets need NAT), and who manages the far end?
- Third-party peer? Agree a written parameter sheet: IKE version, proposals, DH groups, lifetimes, selectors, PSK delivery method.
- Redundancy: one tunnel per ISP? Then it belongs in **SD-WAN** (next module) with health checks.
- Security: which services cross the tunnel? A tunnel is a trust path; policies on it should be as tight as on the internet edge.

:::threat
Internet-facing VPN gateways are prime targets. In the 2026 DBIR, exploitation of vulnerabilities was the top initial access vector (31 %), and only 26 % of known-exploited vulnerabilities were fully remediated. Patch edge devices quickly, limit who can reach IKE with local-in policies (p. 3242), and keep strong proposals.
:::

:::ps
In a third-party tunnel the problem is usually a mismatch nobody wrote down. The parameter sheet is the deliverable that prevents the 2 a.m. call.
:::

labs.title: Build the HQ side of a route-based tunnel
labs.goal: HQ (LAN 10.10.0.0/24 on port2, WAN port1) connects to a branch at 203.0.113.10 protecting 10.20.0.0/24.

worked.config:
config vpn ipsec phase1-interface
    edit "to-branch"
        set interface "port1"
        set ike-version 2
        set peertype any
        set proposal aes256gcm-prfsha384 aes256-sha256
        set dhgrp 20 19
        set remote-gw 203.0.113.10
        set psksecret <strong-shared-key>
        set dpd on-idle
    next
end
config vpn ipsec phase2-interface
    edit "to-branch"
        set phase1name "to-branch"
        set proposal aes256gcm aes256-sha256
        set dhgrp 20 19
        set src-subnet 10.10.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set dst-subnet 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set auto-negotiate enable
    next
end
config router static
    edit 20
        set dst 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set device "to-branch"
    next
    edit 21
        set dst 10.20.0.0 255.255.255.0
        set blackhole enable
        set distance 254
    next
end
config firewall policy
    edit 0
        set name "HQ-to-branch"
        set srcintf "port2"
        set dstintf "to-branch"
        set srcaddr "HQ-LAN"
        set dstaddr "BRANCH-LAN"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
        set service "ALL"
    next
    edit 0
        set name "branch-to-HQ"
        set srcintf "to-branch"
        set dstintf "port2"
        set srcaddr "BRANCH-LAN"
        set dstaddr "HQ-LAN"
        set action accept
        set schedule "always"
        set service "ALL"
    next
end
notes: The branch mirrors it: its src-subnet is 10.20.0.0/24 and dst-subnet 10.10.0.0/24.
Tighten service ALL to what the business needs once it works.
No NAT on the tunnel policies: both sides route real addresses.

scenarios.title: The partner's tunnel: 'it's your side'
scenarios.situation: A customer's FortiGate must build a tunnel to a supplier's third-party firewall. Phase 1 is up. Phase 2 fails. The supplier's engineer says, "Our side is fine, it's your FortiGate."
scenarios.ask: How do you get it working without a blame game?
right_thinking: Phase 1 up means reachability, key and phase 1 proposals are fine
Phase 2 failures are selectors, proposals or PFS
Get evidence from your side (debug) and ask for theirs
Agree a written parameter sheet both sides sign off
scenarios.what: A matched phase 2 and a documented parameter sheet.
scenarios.why: Third-party tunnels fail on unwritten assumptions; evidence ends the argument.
how: Filtered IKE debug: read the phase 2 selectors and proposals we send and receive
Share the exact values; ask for their proposal and selector config
Fix the mismatch (commonly subnet mask or PFS group)
Document the final parameters for both teams
scenarios.model_answer: I'd keep it factual. Phase 1 is up, so reachability, the key and phase 1 are fine; the issue is phase 2. I'd run a filtered IKE debug and read the selectors and proposals we send and what they answer. Then I'd send the supplier a short table: our local and remote subnets, our proposals and PFS group, and ask for theirs. Usually it's a mask, like a /24 against a /23, or PFS on one side only. Once it's up, both teams sign off the same parameter sheet so the next change doesn't break it.
could_have_added: Offer a quick joint call with both screens on the debug
scenarios.best_way: Phase 1 is fine, so it's phase 2: here are our selectors and proposals from the debug, please share yours.

scenarios.title: Tunnel up, users still complaining
scenarios.situation: The tunnel shows up on both sides. Branch users can open the HQ intranet homepage, but uploading files to SharePoint on-prem hangs.
scenarios.ask: What do you suspect and how do you prove it?
right_thinking: Some traffic works, so routing, policies and selectors are fine
Large transfers failing = packet size
Prove with ping using DF and sizes, or a sniffer
Fix with MSS clamping on the tunnel policies
scenarios.what: An MTU/MSS diagnosis and fix.
scenarios.why: It's the classic "VPN works but doesn't" problem.
how: Ping with DF bit and decreasing size
Set tcp-mss on both tunnel policies
scenarios.model_answer: Since small requests work, the tunnel, routes and policies are fine. Big uploads hanging points at packet size: ESP adds overhead, so full-size packets don't fit, and if ICMP "fragmentation needed" is blocked somewhere, the hosts never learn it. I'd prove it with pings with the don't-fragment bit at decreasing sizes, then clamp the TCP MSS on both tunnel policies, for example around 1350, and retest the upload with the user.
scenarios.best_way: Small works, big hangs: packet size. Prove with DF pings, clamp MSS on the tunnel policies.

scenarios.title: What if the customer wants 3DES "for compatibility"?
scenarios.situation: An old partner device only supports 3DES-SHA1. The customer asks you to just enable it.
scenarios.ask: How do you respond?
right_thinking: Don't silently lower security; the guide marks 3DES and SHA1 not recommended
Offer options: upgrade or replace the partner device, limit the tunnel's scope, time-box the exception
Get the risk accepted in writing if they insist
scenarios.what: A risk-aware recommendation.
scenarios.why: A consultant protects the customer from quiet risk, even when it's what they asked for.
how: If accepted: narrow selectors, strict policies, review date, written acceptance
scenarios.model_answer: I'd explain that Fortinet's own guide marks 3DES and SHA1 as not recommended, so this weakens the tunnel. The best path is for the partner to upgrade their device. If that can't happen now, we can limit the risk: a separate tunnel just for that partner, narrow selectors, tight policies, and a review date. And I'd ask the customer to approve the exception in writing, so it's a decision, not an accident.
scenarios.best_way: It's not recommended. Best fix is the partner's upgrade; otherwise a narrow, time-boxed exception with written approval.

interview.question: Explain phase 1 and phase 2 to me as if I were a customer's manager.
interview.framework: Analogy → what must match → why it fails
interview.model_answer: "Phase 1 is the two firewalls proving who they are and agreeing how to talk privately, like two people agreeing a secure phone line. Phase 2 is agreeing what will travel on that line: which networks, and how it's encrypted. Both sides must agree on the details, and most tunnel failures are one detail that doesn't match, often in phase 2, like a subnet."
interview.best_way: Phase 1 is a secure line between the firewalls; phase 2 is what travels on it. Most failures are one detail that doesn't match.

interview.question: A tunnel is up but traffic doesn't pass. How do you troubleshoot?
interview.framework: Layers: routing → policy → selectors → counters → peer
interview.model_answer: "Up only means IPsec is built. I check that there's a route to the remote subnet via the tunnel, policies in both directions, and that the selectors include the hosts. Then diagnose vpn tunnel list: if txp increases and rxp is zero, I'm sending and the peer isn't answering, so I look at their route and policy back. A debug flow on our side confirms which policy and route the packet takes."
interview.best_way: Route, policies both ways, selectors, then counters. txp without rxp means look at the peer.

interview.question: Why does FortiGate add a blackhole route for VPN subnets?
interview.model_answer: "If the tunnel drops, the route via the tunnel disappears and traffic for the remote subnet would follow the default route to the internet, unencrypted. A blackhole route with distance 254 stays in the table and drops it instead. The VPN Wizard adds it automatically."
interview.best_way: So traffic is dropped, not leaked in clear text, when the tunnel is down.

interview.question: Which proposals and DH groups would you configure today, and why IKEv2?
interview.model_answer: "IKEv2 with AES-GCM, for example aes256gcm, and DH groups in Fortinet's recommended range, like 19, 20 or 21. IKEv2 is the default for new tunnels, it supports EAP and modern ciphers like GCM and ChaCha20, and it's what current FortiClient versions expect. I'd avoid 3DES, SHA1 and the old DH groups."
interview.best_way: IKEv2, AES-GCM, DH 19–21; no 3DES or SHA1.

interview.question: Tell me about a time you resolved a VPN problem for a customer.
interview.model_answer: "[Use a real Fortinet TAC case.] Structure it: situation (who, impact), the evidence you gathered (summary, gateway list, tunnel list, filtered IKE debug), the root cause in one sentence, the fix, and what you did so it wouldn't recur, such as documenting parameters or adding MSS clamping to the template."
could_have_added: Mention the customer outcome and CSAT if you have it
interview.best_way: Evidence first, one-line root cause, fix, prevention.

field_reports.title: VPN gateways are on the front line
field_reports.body: Exploitation of vulnerabilities was the **top initial access vector (31 %)** in the 2026 DBIR, and only **26 %** of known-exploited vulnerabilities were fully remediated in the period studied. Internet-facing VPN and firewall interfaces are exactly where those exploits land: patch fast and restrict who can reach IKE.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR

field_reports.title: Third parties extend your attack surface

modules.title: High availability: FGCP clusters, failover and upgrades
objectives: Explain FGCP, FGSP and VRRP and when each one fits
Predict which unit becomes primary, with and without override
Design heartbeat, monitored interfaces and session pickup for a customer's real failure modes
Upgrade a cluster with the right upgrade mode and verify it afterwards
Diagnose split brain and out-of-sync clusters calmly, from the console
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: High Availability overview and FGCP (pp. 4556–4559), primary selection and override (pp. 4561–4567), A-P / A-A setup (pp. 4567–4571)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: A-A load balancing (pp. 4583–4586), heartbeat (pp. 4586–4597), session failover (pp. 4598–4615)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: management interfaces (pp. 4620–4626), upgrades (pp. 4638–4640), troubleshooting (pp. 4701–4716)

units.title: Three ways to stay up
units.body:
A FortiGate carrying critical traffic is a single point of failure. The guide lists three HA answers (pp. 4556–4557):

- **FGCP (FortiGate Clustering Protocol):** the classic cluster. Two or more FortiGates of the **same model, firmware and hardware** negotiate a cluster and share one configuration; only the **hostname and the HA priority** differ. Modes: **active-passive (A-P)** and **active-active (A-A)**.
- **FGSP (Session Life Support Protocol):** for networks that already have **external load balancers or routers** spreading sessions; FGSP only synchronizes sessions (TCP, UDP, ICMP, NAT, expectation) between peers.
- **VRRP:** standard first-hop redundancy, versions 2 and 3, also with third-party routers.

## How FGCP keeps one brain

- Members talk over **heartbeat interfaces**. Fortinet recommends **two back-to-back heartbeat links** in a two-member cluster (p. 4557).
- All synchronization runs over the heartbeat link on **TCP/703 and UDP/703** (p. 4559).
- The primary owns the cluster's **virtual MAC addresses** and IPs. After a failover the new primary sends **gratuitous ARP** so switches learn the new path (p. 4564).
- All cluster members must be registered under the **same FortiCare account**, or you get licensing issues (p. 4557).

:::recall
Q: Which two settings may differ between FGCP members?
A: The hostname and the HA (device) priority. Everything else is synchronized.
:::

:::delta
Customers with an external load balancer in front of two FortiGates don't need FGCP: that is the FGSP use case.
:::

units.title: Who becomes primary
units.body:
Primary election is the most-tested HA topic and the first thing a customer asks after a failover. The order depends on **override** (pp. 4562–4563):

| override | Order (first difference wins) | Mnemonic |
|---|---|---|
| disabled (default) | Connected **M**onitored interfaces → HA **U**ptime → **P**riority → **S**erial number | MUPS |
| enabled | Connected **M**onitored interfaces → **P**riority → HA **U**ptime → **S**erial number | MPUS |

Details that matter in the field:

- **Priority:** 0–255, **default 128**, higher wins (pp. 4561, 4576).
- **Uptime tie:** uptimes within **300 seconds** count as a tie (`ha-uptime-diff-margin` changes it). A **monitored-interface failure or a reboot resets that unit's uptime to zero** (p. 4563).
- **Override:** make it the same on all members; mixing it causes unpredictable elections (p. 4561). With override enabled, the higher-priority unit takes over again as soon as it comes back, which means a **second failover**.
- **override-wait-time** (0–3600 s, default 0, not synchronized) delays that takeover after a reboot so the returning unit can sync first. From 8.0.1, during the wait the unit with the longest uptime stays primary (pp. 4563–4564).

:::cli
# get system ha status
...
Primary selected using:
<...> vcluster-1: FG101F...7 is selected as the primary because its override priority is larger than peer member FG101F...8.
:::

"Primary selected using" is the history that answers *why* (p. 4566). `diagnose sys ha dump-by group` shows the uptime difference between members (p. 4567).

:::pitfall
With override disabled, raising the priority on the unit you want as primary does nothing while the other unit has more than 5 minutes more uptime. Uptime beats priority.
:::

:::recall
Q: Override disabled, both units have all monitored ports up, A has 2 h more uptime, B has priority 200. Who is primary?
A: A. Uptime is checked before priority when override is disabled (and the difference is above 300 s).
:::

units.title: Heartbeat, monitoring and session pickup
units.body:
## Heartbeat timing

`hb-interval` (default 2, in units of `hb-interval-in-milliseconds`, default 100 ms) and `hb-lost-threshold` (typically 6 on hardware and 20 on VMs; check with `get system ha | grep hb-lost-threshold`). The guide's example: 2 × 100 ms × 20 = **4 seconds** to declare a peer dead (p. 4593). Lower values give faster failover but more false positives.

`backup-hbdev` is used only when the secondary stops hearing the primary on the normal heartbeat links, to prevent split brain; configuration isn't synchronized while it's in use (pp. 4589–4590).

## What triggers a failover

- **Device failure:** heartbeats stop.
- **Link failure:** `set monitor port1 port2`. A monitored port going down on the primary moves the role.
- **Remote link failure:** `pingserver-monitor-interface` checks reachability of a remote IP through an interface (p. 4576).

## Session pickup

**Session failover (`session-pickup`) is not enabled by default** (p. 4598). Without it, a failover keeps the cluster up but **drops existing sessions**; users reconnect.

- `session-pickup enable`: synchronizes the TCP session table.
- `session-pickup-connectionless enable`: adds UDP and ICMP (p. 4602).
- `session-pickup-delay enable`: only sessions older than **30 seconds** are synced, which cuts load with many short HTTP sessions (p. 4607).

## Active-active

In A-A, the primary receives all traffic on the virtual MACs and uses a **load-balancing schedule** to hand sessions to the others; `load-balance-all` extends this to all TCP sessions (pp. 4583–4584). A-A adds complexity; for most customers A-P plus right-sizing is easier to operate.

:::why
Q: Why is session pickup off by default?
A: Synchronizing every session costs CPU and heartbeat bandwidth. It's a design decision per customer: enable it when long-lived sessions (VoIP, database, VPN) must survive a failover.
:::

:::tip
In a change plan, write the expected failover time and whether sessions survive, so the customer approves a measured behaviour, not a hope.
:::

units.title: Upgrades, management and the bad days
units.body:
## Upgrade modes (pp. 4638–4640)

`set upgrade-mode {simultaneous | uninterruptible | local-only | secondary-only}`

- **uninterruptible:** the subordinates are upgraded first, a new primary is chosen from the upgraded units, then the former primary is upgraded. Traffic keeps flowing. Simultaneous (interrupted) upgrade is **disabled by default**.
- **simultaneous:** all members at once. Faster, but an outage.
- **local-only / secondary-only:** advanced, manual staged upgrades (multi-version cluster) for testing one member before the rest.

Always check the supported upgrade path and book a window first.

## Managing each unit

- `execute ha manage <id> <username>` jumps to the other member's CLI (p. 4597, p. 4707).
- **Reserved management interfaces** (`ha-mgmt-status enable`, `config ha-mgmt-interfaces`) give each unit its own management IP; `ha-direct` lets services such as SNMP, syslog and FortiAnalyzer logging leave from each unit's own interface (pp. 4622–4625).

## Split brain (pp. 4702–4703)

Both units think they're primary and use the **same IP and virtual MAC**: switches flap, admin access is intermittent, traffic drops. Cause: **all heartbeat links lost**, or congested links that exceed the lost threshold.

Fix: get to the **console** (on-site if possible), check the heartbeat ports are physically up and passing heartbeats, check **mode, group-name, group-id and password** match, then confirm with `get system ha status`.

Prevent: back-to-back heartbeat cables, **redundant heartbeat interfaces**, and for geo-separated members, thresholds longer than the link latency.

## Out of sync (pp. 4707–4709)

`get system ha status` → **Configuration Status** shows in-sync / out-of-sync per serial and the checksums. The GUI HA monitor highlights the member in red; **Force resync** pushes the primary's config. `diagnose sys ha checksum cluster` is the classic CLI comparison.

`execute ha failover set <cluster_id>` forces a failover for **testing in a maintenance window only** (p. 4703).

:::threat
Downtime is a big share of breach cost: in IBM's 2026 report, detection and escalation plus lost business are 63 % of the cost of a breach. A cluster that fails over cleanly during an incident protects revenue as well as security.
:::

labs.title: Build an active-passive cluster
labs.goal: Configure the first unit of an A-P cluster with two heartbeat links, session pickup and two monitored ports, preferring this unit.

worked.config:
config system global
    set hostname FGT-HQ-A
end
config system ha
    set mode a-p
    set group-id 10
    set group-name "HQ-CLUSTER"
    set password <shared-secret>
    set hbdev "ha1" 50 "ha2" 50
    set session-pickup enable
    set monitor "port1" "port2"
    set override disable
    set priority 200
end
notes: group-id, group-name, mode and password must match on both units.
Two heartbeat links, cabled back to back.
With override disabled, priority 200 only decides on a tie in uptime.

faded.template:
config system ha
    set mode {{a-p}}
    set group-name "HQ-CLUSTER"
    set {{hbdev}} "ha1" 50 "ha2" 50
    set {{session-pickup}} enable
    set {{monitor}} "port1" "port2"
    set priority {{200}}
end

solo.prompt: Configure the second unit: same cluster settings, hostname FGT-HQ-B, priority 100. Include mode, group-id 10, group-name, password, both heartbeats, session pickup and the monitored ports.

config system global
    set hostname FGT-HQ-B
end
config system ha
    set mode a-p
    set group-id 10
    set group-name "HQ-CLUSTER"
    set password <shared-secret>
    set hbdev "ha1" 50 "ha2" 50

    set monitor "port1" "port2"

end

labs.title: Verify the cluster and test failover safely
labs.goal: In the maintenance window, prove the cluster is healthy, then test a controlled failover and return.

worked.config:
# get system ha status
# diagnose sys ha dump-by group
# diagnose sys ha checksum cluster
# execute ha manage 1 admin
# execute ha failover set 1
# get system ha status
# execute ha failover unset 1
notes: Check Configuration Status is in-sync and HBDEV/MONDEV are up before touching anything.
dump-by group shows the uptime difference that drives elections.
Failover set/unset is for maintenance windows and testing only.

# get system ha {{status}}
# diagnose sys ha {{dump-by}} group

solo.prompt: Write the commands to confirm the cluster is in sync, force a test failover of cluster 1, check the new state, and undo the forced failover.
solo.solution:
# get system ha status
# execute ha failover set 1
# get system ha status
