modules.title: FortiManager Policy & Objects and the install process
objectives: Organise policy packages, installation targets, policy blocks and global policies
Use dynamic mapping and normalized interfaces so one package fits many FortiGates
Choose the right install operation and always read the preview
Explain the install sequence from ADOM database to device database to the FortiGate diff
Handle out-of-band changes, conflicts, imports, retrieves and reverts safely
sources: FortiManager 7.6.8 Admin Guide: Key concepts, operations and install sequence (pp. 55–63)
FortiManager 7.6.8 Admin Guide: Policy & Objects, policy packages and installs (pp. 382–400)
FortiManager 7.6.8 Admin Guide: Policy Blocks (pp. 491–504), dynamic objects (pp. 510–512)

units.title: Policy packages that scale
units.body:
Inside an ADOM you can have **many policy packages**. A package can target one device, many devices, a VDOM, or all devices; you can clone packages to provision new sites quickly (p. 382).

## Building blocks

- **Installation targets:** which devices or VDOMs a package installs to. Individual policies can also be limited to specific targets (p. 391).
- **Global policy packages:** header and footer policies from the global ADOM wrap local policies; each policy package can have **one** global package assigned (p. 383).
- **Policy Blocks:** a reusable set of policies appended to packages. Enable them in *Tools > Feature Visibility*. They simplify ADOM upgrades and are an alternative to global policy packages (pp. 384, 491–492).
- **Dynamic mapping and normalized interfaces:** one logical object (an address, or an interface name like `LAN`) maps to a different real value per device (p. 510). The same package then works at every branch.

## The rule that breaks installs

When a package installs, referenced objects go to the device, and **a default or per-device mapping must exist, or the installation fails** (p. 391). A new branch with no mapping for the `LAN` normalized interface is the classic first-install error.

## Policy theory still applies

Matching uses type, incoming interface, source, outgoing interface, destination, schedule and service; actions are ACCEPT, DENY or IPSEC; unmatched traffic is dropped, and an explicit DENY is only needed to **log** violations (pp. 382–383).

:::recall
Q: First install to a new branch fails on the 'LAN' interface. Likely cause?
A: No default or per-device mapping for the normalized interface on that device.
:::

units.title: Install operations and what really happens
units.body:
## The operations (pp. 55–57)

| Operation | What it does | Preview |
|---|---|---|
| Install Wizard: device settings only | Pushes the device database to the FortiGate | Yes, can cancel |
| Install Wizard: policy package and device settings | ADOM policies → device database → FortiGate; best for the first install | Yes |
| Re-install Policy | For packages already assigned; can do several packages in one workflow | Yes |
| Quick Install (Device DB) | Pushes the device database immediately | **No preview, can't cancel** |
| Scheduled install | Install at a set date and time | From the wizard |

## The sequence (pp. 59–61)

1. FortiManager copies the related ADOM objects (templates, policies) into the **device database**: the "VDOM copy". Order: system template → CLI template (pre) → threat weight → IPsec → static route → BGP → NSX-T → SD-WAN → AP profile → FortiSwitch → FortiExtender → **policy package** → CLI template (post).
2. It retrieves the real FortiGate configuration and **installs only the difference**. A CLI template's lines are not replayed one by one; FortiManager installs the diff.

## FGFM recovery (p. 56)

After each install the FortiGate restarts its FGFM tunnel. If `rollback-allow-reboot` is enabled (`config system dm`, **disabled by default**) and the reconnection fails, the FortiGate reboots to recover its previous configuration.

:::pitfall
Always read the install preview. It shows exactly what will change on the FortiGate, including deletions you didn't expect, like unused objects that FortiManager doesn't keep.
:::

units.title: When the FortiGate and FortiManager disagree
units.body:
## Auto-update and conflicts (p. 58)

**Auto-update is enabled by default**: a change made locally on a FortiGate is sent to FortiManager. A device-level change leaves the policy status alone; a **policy-level change can put the package into Conflict**. Fortinet's advice: make changes on FortiManager, not on the FortiGate.

## Import, retrieve, revert (pp. 57–59)

- **Import configuration:** copies policies and objects from the device into a new policy package in the ADOM; the FortiGate isn't changed. If an object with the same name exists, you choose: **update** it (all FortiGates using it go out of sync) or **keep** FortiManager's (the next install pushes FortiManager's version). After an import, the first install may delete **unused objects**.
- **Retrieve:** refreshes the device database from the FortiGate. The policy package isn't updated, so a policy-level local change will be overwritten at the next package install.
- **Revert:** loads an older revision into the device database only. Then **import** to realign the policy package and **re-install**.
- **Refresh:** checks the sync status.

## A safe routine for a change

1. Lock (workspace), edit in Policy & Objects.
2. Install Wizard → **preview** → download the preview for the change record.
3. Install; check the task log.
4. Verify on the FortiGate and with the user.
5. Revisions are kept in Device Manager: compare and revert if needed.

:::why
Q: Why might the first install after an import delete objects from the FortiGate?
A: They're unused by any policy, and FortiManager doesn't keep unused objects. They can be installed back by referencing them in a policy.
:::

scenarios.title: The install that deleted objects
scenarios.situation: After importing a FortiGate into FortiManager, the first install preview shows dozens of address objects being deleted. The customer is alarmed.
scenarios.ask: Explain and decide.
right_thinking: Expected behaviour: unused objects aren't kept by FortiManager
Check they're truly unused (no policy, route or other reference)
If needed, reference them or keep a record; then proceed
scenarios.what: A calm explanation and a verified decision.
scenarios.why: Previews are where you catch surprises before they hit production.
scenarios.model_answer: That's expected after an import: FortiManager doesn't keep objects that no policy uses, so the first install removes them from the FortiGate. Before installing, I'd confirm they're really unused, nothing in routes or other settings referencing them, and keep the preview as a record. If the customer wants to keep some for future rules, we can reference them or recreate them later. The preview did its job: no surprises in production.
scenarios.best_way: Expected: unused objects aren't kept. Confirm they're unused, keep the preview, then install.

scenarios.title: What if an install breaks management?
scenarios.situation: A colleague asks what happens if an install changes routing and the FortiGate can no longer reach FortiManager.
scenarios.ask: Explain the recovery behaviour and your precautions.
right_thinking: FGFM restarts after install; rollback-allow-reboot can reboot to recover (disabled by default)
Precautions: preview, console access, change window
scenarios.what: Accurate behaviour plus practical precautions.
scenarios.why: Management-plane changes are the riskiest installs.
scenarios.model_answer: After each install the FortiGate restarts its FGFM tunnel. If rollback-allow-reboot is enabled on FortiManager, which it isn't by default, and the reconnection fails, the FortiGate reboots to recover its previous configuration. Either way, for changes that touch routing or interfaces on the management path, I'd read the preview carefully, do it in a window, and have console or out-of-band access ready.
scenarios.best_way: FGFM recovery can roll back if enabled; I still preview, use a window and keep console access.

interview.question: Walk me through what happens when you install a policy package.
interview.model_answer: "FortiManager copies the relevant ADOM objects, templates and the policy package into the device database, in a fixed order, then retrieves the FortiGate's current configuration and installs only the difference. I always read the install preview, because it shows exactly what will change, including deletions."
interview.best_way: ADOM data into the device database, then only the diff to the FortiGate; read the preview.

interview.question: How do you make one policy package work for many branches?
interview.model_answer: "Normalized interfaces and dynamic objects with per-device mappings, so 'LAN' and 'BRANCH-USERS' resolve to each branch's real values, installation targets covering the branches, and policy blocks or global header and footer policies for rules everyone must have. The classic first-install failure is a missing mapping on a new branch."
interview.best_way: Per-device mappings, installation targets, and policy blocks for common rules.

interview.question: A FortiGate was changed locally. How do you reconcile it with FortiManager?
interview.model_answer: "Auto-update brings the change in; if it's policy-level the package may show Conflict. I decide with the customer whether to keep it: if yes, import or recreate it in the package; if not, the next install overwrites it. Then I fix the process so changes are made in FortiManager, with access for the local admin and workspace or workflow mode."
interview.best_way: Decide keep or overwrite, bring it into the package if kept, and fix the process.

modules.title: FortiManager SD-WAN and VPN Manager, FortiGuard, firmware and HA
objectives: Use the SD-WAN overlay orchestration wizard and know what it does and doesn't configure
Plan overlay addressing, loopbacks, BGP AS and branch IDs before running the wizard
Build IPsec VPN communities with VPN Manager and install them through policy packages
Run FortiManager as a local FDS and manage firmware with templates
Design FortiManager HA and explain how failover works
sources: FortiManager 7.6.8 Admin Guide: SD-WAN overlay orchestration (pp. 584–592)
FortiManager 7.6.8 Admin Guide: VPN Manager (pp. 708–712)
FortiManager 7.6.8 Admin Guide: FortiGuard local FDS (pp. 913–916), firmware templates (pp. 359–361), High Availability (pp. 1217–1222)

units.title: SD-WAN overlays at scale
units.body:
## Overlay orchestration (pp. 584–586)

The **SD-WAN overlay template** (SD-WAN Manager > Overlay Orchestration) is a wizard that builds hub-and-branch overlays with Fortinet's recommended **IPsec and BGP** design. It **generates IPsec, BGP and CLI provisioning templates** and assigns them to the hub and branch devices.

What it **doesn't** do:

- It **doesn't provide SD-WAN intelligence**. You still need an **SD-WAN template** (members, zones, health checks, rules).
- It assumes the hub and branches **can already reach each other** (static routes, BGP or DHCP-provided routes).

## Plan before you click (p. 586)

- Import the hub and branch FortiGates (or model devices) first.
- **Overlay address space:** default **10.10.0.0/16**.
- **Loopback address space:** default **172.16.0.0/16**.
- **BGP AS** for the region: default **65000**.
- **branch_id:** a metadata variable each branch needs, unique per branch; *Automatic Branch ID Assignment* can fill it for a branch device group (p. 585).

## Then the SD-WAN template

Members and zones (Underlay and Overlay), health checks to the hubs and to SaaS, and rules per application, exactly as in M8.03, defined once and assigned to device groups. Template order at install puts the SD-WAN template after IPsec, static route and BGP templates (p. 61).

:::pitfall
Overlapping the wizard's default 10.10.0.0/16 or 172.16.0.0/16 with the customer's existing networks breaks routing later. Check their IP plan first.
:::

:::recall
Q: The overlay wizard finished. Why does traffic still not prefer the overlay for the ERP?
A: The overlay template has no SD-WAN intelligence; you need an SD-WAN template with rules.
:::

units.title: VPN Manager
units.body:
## How central VPN works (pp. 708–709)

1. **Enable central VPN management** (VPN Manager > IPsec VPN, or when editing the ADOM).
2. Create an **IPsec VPN community** (a topology: for example a star of spokes to a hub, or a full mesh, or dial-up) and add the gateways.
3. Use the VPN objects in **policies** in the policy package.
4. Add the devices to the package's **installation targets** and **install the policy package**: that's what installs the VPN settings.

VPN Manager also shows an **IPsec VPN map** (topology or traffic view) and manages **Agentless VPN** settings, portals and monitoring.

Settings are **per ADOM**: after configuring VPN for FortiGates in an ADOM, don't move them to another ADOM (p. 708).

## VPN Manager or overlay templates?

For SD-WAN hub-and-spoke designs with BGP, the overlay orchestration wizard and provisioning templates are Fortinet's current path; VPN Manager communities suit classic site-to-site topologies and Agentless VPN management. Don't mix both on the same tunnels.

:::why
Q: Why does a VPN community need a policy package install?
A: VPN Manager settings are installed through the policy package; without policies using them and an install, nothing reaches the FortiGates.
:::

units.title: FortiGuard, firmware and FortiManager HA
units.body:
## Local FDS (pp. 913–916)

FortiManager can act as a **local FortiGuard Distribution Server**: it syncs updates (AV, IPS, web filter lookups, firmware) from the FDN and serves your FortiGates, which helps when they **can't reach the internet** and reduces internet load. Prerequisites: devices registered with valid FortiGuard licences, the built-in FDS enabled and configured, and each FortiGate pointed at it.

## Firmware templates (pp. 359–360)

Define the firmware version FortiGates, FortiAPs, FortiSwitches and FortiExtenders must run, assign them to devices, and track compliance in Device & Groups. Upgrade paths still matter: check the Fortinet upgrade path tool.

## FortiManager HA (pp. 1217–1219)

- Protects the **FortiManager database**; up to **five units**: one primary and up to four backups, **same series**.
- **FortiAnalyzer features must be disabled** before forming a cluster.
- Units can be in **different locations** (geographic redundancy).
- Admins and managed devices work with the **primary**; FortiGuard updates can come from primary or secondaries.
- Heartbeat and sync use **TCP port 5199** between the configured peer IPs.
- Failover: **manual** (you promote a secondary) or **automatic with VRRP**.

:::tip
In a design document, state which failover mode you chose and why: manual is simpler and avoids unwanted role changes; VRRP gives automatic recovery.
:::

cards.front: What does the SD-WAN overlay template generate?
cards.back: IPsec, BGP and CLI provisioning templates for hub and branches.

cards.back: No SD-WAN intelligence; needs an SD-WAN template. Also assumes hub-branch reachability.
A metadata variable, unique per branch; can be auto-assigned for a branch device group.

cards.back: Enable central VPN, create community, use in policies, add targets and install the policy package.

Five: one primary, up to four backups, same series.

cards.back: FortiAnalyzer features.
Manual or automatic (VRRP).

scenarios.title: The overlay that routes nowhere
scenarios.situation: After the overlay wizard and install, tunnels are up but some branches can't reach a data-centre subnet 172.16.40.0/24.
scenarios.ask: What's your hypothesis and fix?
right_thinking: Default loopback space 172.16.0.0/16 overlaps the DC subnet
BGP advertises loopbacks; routing conflict
Re-plan loopback space and reinstall in a window
scenarios.what: Root cause and a planned correction.
scenarios.why: Defaults that overlap real networks are a classic rollout trap.
how: Check routing table at a branch for 172.16.40.0
scenarios.model_answer: My first suspect is the default loopback range: the overlay template uses 172.16.0.0/16, which overlaps the customer's 172.16.40.0/24. The branches may be routing it towards a loopback instead of the DC. I'd confirm with the routing table at a branch, then change the template's loopback space to an unused range and reinstall in a window. And I'd add "check every default against the IP plan" to our checklist.
scenarios.best_way: The default 172.16.0.0/16 loopbacks overlap the DC subnet; re-plan and reinstall.

interview.question: How would you roll out SD-WAN to many branches with FortiManager?
interview.model_answer: "Plan the overlay and loopback ranges, BGP AS and branch IDs against the customer's IP plan. Run the overlay orchestration wizard, which generates the IPsec, BGP and CLI templates for hubs and branches. Then an SD-WAN template with zones, health checks and rules, because the overlay itself has no SD-WAN intelligence. Assign everything to device groups, pre-install to model devices, then zero-touch the branches."
interview.best_way: Plan addressing, overlay wizard for tunnels and BGP, SD-WAN template for intelligence, then ZTP.

interview.question: How does FortiManager HA work?
interview.model_answer: "Up to five units of the same series, one primary and up to four backups, possibly in different locations. The primary's database is synchronised to the backups over TCP 5199. Admins and FortiGates use the primary. Failover is manual or automatic with VRRP. FortiAnalyzer features must be off to form the cluster."
interview.best_way: Primary plus up to four backups, sync on 5199, manual or VRRP failover.

interview.question: When would you use FortiManager as a local FortiGuard server?
interview.model_answer: "When FortiGates can't reach the internet, like OT or air-gapped sites, or to cut internet load. FortiManager syncs updates from FortiGuard and serves them. The devices still need valid licences, the built-in FDS must be enabled, and each FortiGate pointed at it."
interview.best_way: Isolated networks or lower internet load; licences, FDS enabled and devices pointed at it.

field_reports.title: Isolated networks still need fresh signatures
field_reports.body: With exploitation the top initial access vector (**31 %**, 2026 DBIR), OT and isolated sites can't wait for manual updates. A local FDS keeps IPS and AV current without opening them to the internet.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR

sources: FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Key concepts: modes, ADOMs, logs, log storage (pp. 45–52)
FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Device Manager and ADOMs (pp. 95–99), log forwarding and fetching (pp. 573–586)
FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: High Availability (pp. 667–668), Collectors and Analyzers (pp. 678–680)

units.title: Modes, ADOMs and getting logs in
units.body:
## Two operation modes (pp. 45–47)

- **Analyzer (default):** all features: FortiView, Log View, Incidents & Alerts, reports.
- **Collector:** receives logs, keeps them in **original binary format** and forwards them to an Analyzer; most features are off (Log View shows raw archive logs only), and the SQL database is disabled by default.

**Analyzer–Collector collaboration:** collectors at the edge take the log-receiving load (or buffer logs at remote sites); the Analyzer focuses on analysis and reports. For very large estates, a **FortiAnalyzer Fabric** has members syncing incidents, events and logs to a **supervisor**.

## ADOMs (pp. 47, 97)

ADOMs restrict which devices' data an admin sees, down to VDOMs. Organise by firmware version, region, administrators, customer or Security Fabric. Each ADOM can have its **own data policy** (retention).

## Getting logs in (p. 48)

- The sending device must be **registered and authorised**: add it by serial number, or point the FortiGate at FortiAnalyzer and authorise it from **Unauthorized Devices**.
- Logs from Fortinet devices travel over **OFTP** and **must be encrypted**. FortiAnalyzer's level must be **equal to or lower than** the device's:

:::cli
# FortiAnalyzer
config system global
    set enc-algorithm {high | medium | low}
end
# FortiGate
config log fortianalyzer setting
    set enc-algorithm {high-medium | high | low}
end
:::

:::recall
Q: Logs arrive at a FortiAnalyzer in Collector mode. Can you run a report on them there?
A: No. Collector mode disables reporting; forward them to an Analyzer.
:::

units.title: The life of a log and storage sizing
units.body:
## Three phases (pp. 48, 50–51)

1. **Real-time:** just arrived, stored uncompressed in Archive, not yet in the SQL database.
2. **Archive (offline):** the log file is **rolled and compressed**. You can't see it in FortiView, Log View (except Log Browse), Incidents or Reports. Archive logs can be uploaded to a server and are used to **rebuild the database**.
3. **Analytics (online, historical):** indexed into the **SQL database**; the only logs used for FortiView, Log View, Incidents & Events and Reports.

## Data policy (p. 51)

Per ADOM: **how long to keep Analytics** (then purged from SQL, still in Archive) and **how long to keep Archive** (then deleted). Most administrators keep **30–60 days in Analytics**; compliance usually drives Archive retention (months or years).

## Disk sizing (p. 52)

An average **Analytic log is ~600 bytes**, an **Archive log ~80 bytes**; after seven days analytic logs compress to ~150 bytes. Set the Analytics/Archive ratio with that in mind.

## Rolling and deletion (p. 49)

- Log files roll at **200 MB by default** or on a schedule. **Roll daily** so a file never spans more than 24 hours.
- FortiAnalyzer deletes **files, not individual logs**: a file spanning months can't be deleted until all its logs are out of retention, which is why Archive can show "100/90 days".
- **RAID is not a backup.** Upload archives, or snapshot the VM data disk.

Need to analyse dates older than Analytics retention? **Rebuild the database** for that date range from Archive, then rebuild again for current logs (p. 51).

:::pitfall
Customers often size by "days of retention" and forget that indexed logs take about 7× the space of archived ones. Ask for the log rate first, then size.
:::

units.title: Forwarding, fetching and HA
units.body:
## Log forwarding (pp. 573–575)

- **Forwarding (default):** real-time or near real-time to another FortiAnalyzer, a **syslog** server or a **CEF** server, with device and log filters. The client keeps its own copy.
- **Aggregation:** stores logs and forwards them at a scheduled time, **only between two FortiAnalyzers**, configured in the CLI.
- The forwarding buffer cache is sized from the log rate: the guide's examples give about **2 GB for 100 logs/s, 20 GB for 1,000 logs/s, 200 GB for 10,000 logs/s** (`set log-forward-cache-size`, p. 585).
- A **SIEM Collector** option also exists for forwarding to SIEM platforms (pp. 534–542).

## Log fetching (p. 585)

Pulls **archived logs** for a device and time range from one FortiAnalyzer to another, then indexes them for queries and reports: ideal for **forensics** on old data. Both units must run the **same firmware**; one fetch session at a time between two units.

## FortiAnalyzer HA (pp. 667–668)

- Up to **four units**: one primary and up to three secondaries, **same series**, same operation mode, same platform for VMs.
- Logs and data are **synchronised**; secondaries can take load such as **running reports**.
- **Active-Passive** or **Active-Active** (A-A enables geo-redundant designs).
- Same **group name, group ID and password**; peers listed by IP and serial on every unit.
- Mixed licences: the cluster uses the one with the **smallest** number of managed devices.

:::tip
Compare with FortiManager HA (up to five units, TCP 5199, manual or VRRP failover). Panels like asking for the difference.
:::

worked.config:
logs/day      = 1,000 × 86,400 = 86.4 million

scenarios.title: "Our FortiAnalyzer only shows 3 weeks"
scenarios.situation: A customer bought a FortiAnalyzer for 90-day investigations. FortiView only goes back three weeks, and the disk is full.
scenarios.ask: Explain and propose a fix.
right_thinking: Analytics vs Archive: FortiView needs indexed logs
Disk ratio and data policy likely not sized for the log rate
Options: adjust ratio and policy, reduce noisy logs, add storage or a Collector/Analyzer design
scenarios.what: A sizing-based explanation and options.
scenarios.why: Retention problems are usually sizing problems.
how: Check log rate and data policy
scenarios.model_answer: FortiView only uses Analytics logs, the indexed ones, which take about seven times the space of archived logs. With their log rate, the disk can't hold 90 days indexed, so old logs are purged from Analytics. I'd check the data policy and the Analytics/Archive ratio, then look at reducing noise, like traffic logs on low-value policies. If they truly need 90 days indexed, it's a capacity decision: more storage, or a Collector plus Analyzer design. Meanwhile, older data is still in Archive and can be rebuilt for a specific investigation.
scenarios.best_way: FortiView needs indexed logs, which are big; resize the data policy and ratio, cut noise, or add capacity.

interview.question: Explain how FortiAnalyzer stores logs.
interview.model_answer: "Logs arrive as real-time, go into Archive, compressed files on disk, and are indexed into the SQL database as Analytics logs, which is what FortiView, Log View, incidents and reports use. A data policy per ADOM sets how long to keep each. Analytics logs are much bigger, about 600 bytes against 80 archived, so most customers keep 30 to 60 days indexed and longer in Archive for compliance."
interview.best_way: Archive for retention, Analytics for analysis; size from the log rate.

interview.question: When would you use Collector mode?
interview.model_answer: "When log volume or geography makes one box impractical: Collectors at regions or remote sites receive and archive logs in raw format and forward them to a central Analyzer, which does the analysis and reporting. It also buffers logs if the WAN to the Analyzer drops."
interview.best_way: Collectors receive and forward; the Analyzer analyses and reports.

interview.question: How would you get FortiGate logs into a customer's SIEM?
interview.model_answer: "Through FortiAnalyzer log forwarding in syslog or CEF format, with device and log filters so the SIEM only gets what it needs, which keeps SIEM licensing costs down. At Netskope I set up log streaming into customers' SIEMs, so I'd agree the format, fields and volume with the SOC first."
interview.best_way: FortiAnalyzer forwarding in syslog or CEF, filtered; agree format and volume with the SOC.

field_reports.title: Detection time is the expensive part
field_reports.body: Detection and escalation plus lost business make up **63 %** of breach costs (IBM 2026). Logs that are kept, indexed and searchable for the right period are what make fast investigation possible.
field_reports.source: IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report 2026

Filter and read logs in Log View, and know when to use Log Browse
Group devices with log groups and import old logs for analysis

sources: FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: FortiView and Monitors (pp. 112–160)
FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Log View, log types, log groups, Log Browse, importing (pp. 158–180)
FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Fabric View and Asset Identity Center (pp. 191–193), Security Fabric correlation (pp. 214–217)

units.title: FortiView and Monitors
units.body:
**FortiView** combines real-time and historical data in one place: top threats, sources, destinations, applications, cloud apps and users, websites, VPN and more, each with **drill-down** to the detail (pp. 112–115). **Monitors** are dashboards designed for NOC and SOC screens.

Key facts:

- FortiView uses **Analytics logs only**, not Archive (p. 113). If it looks empty for older dates, check the data policy.
- With ADOMs enabled, each ADOM has its own FortiView; a **Fabric ADOM** shows all eligible devices in the Security Fabric.
- **Top Threats** includes things like malicious websites caught by web filtering, IPS attacks and malware; the **Threat Map** shows destinations by country with threat scores.
- In very high-capacity environments FortiView can be **disabled** to save CPU and memory (pp. 112, 157).

## Drill-down method

Start broad, then narrow: time range → device → top threat or source → the user or IP → the sessions → the raw logs. Every click is a filter; keep the filter chips visible in your screenshots so the customer can repeat it.

:::recall
Q: FortiView shows nothing for last quarter. First thing to check?
A: Analytics retention in the data policy: FortiView only uses indexed (Analytics) logs.
:::

units.title: Log View, log groups and old logs
units.body:
## Log View (p. 158)

- **Logs > All / Fortinet Logs:** real-time or historical (Analytics) logs, with filters and columns.
- **Log Browse:** the actual log files, current and **compressed (archived)**; useful in Collector mode or for old data. Files are named `xlog.N.log` where x is the log type and N relates to the first log's time (p. 179).
- Log View isn't available while the **SQL database is rebuilding**.

## What a FortiGate sends (p. 158)

**Traffic**, **Security** (antivirus, IPS, application control, web filter, file filter, DNS, DLP, email filter, WAF, vulnerability scan, VoIP, FortiClient) and **Event** logs (endpoint, HA, compliance, system, router, VPN, user, WAN opt, WiFi, FortiSASE). FortiAnalyzer also takes logs from FortiMail, FortiWeb, FortiSandbox, FortiEDR, FortiNAC, FortiClient and others, and from **syslog** sources.

## Log groups (p. 179)

Virtual groups of up to **100 devices** for FortiView, logs, reports and alert handlers, with **no extra SQL database or disk**. Adding a device with VDOMs adds all its VDOMs.

## Importing old logs (p. 180)

You can import log files (for example, old files from a device) to analyse them or report on them. Add the devices first, and set `config system sql` → `start-time` and `rebuild-event-start-time` earlier than the logs, with Analytics retention long enough, so they're inserted into SQL.

:::tip
Save useful filters as custom views. Your handover pack can include the three or four views the customer's team should check every morning.
:::

units.title: Fabric View and the investigation routine
units.body:
## Asset Identity Center (p. 191)

The central place to see **endpoints and users**: who used which device, interfaces and IPs, and OT/IoT vulnerabilities detected on assets. It helps with **incident response** (which assets are infected or vulnerable) and **compliance** (unknown or non-compliant users and endpoints). Mapping users to endpoints makes logs, events and reports far easier to read.

## Security Fabric correlation (pp. 214–217)

Add the FortiGates of a Security Fabric as a **Security Fabric group** to see the topology and correlate **traffic logs with UTM logs** across the Fabric, so one session can be followed through several devices.

## A 10-minute investigation routine

1. **Scope:** what triggered it (alert, user report), which device and time window.
2. **FortiView:** Top Threats or Compromised Hosts for that window; identify the host.
3. **Asset Identity Center:** who the user is, which endpoint, other IPs.
4. **Log View:** filter by that IP/user; read the traffic and security logs around the event.
5. **Correlate:** DNS, web filter, IPS and AV logs tell the story (lookup → connection → download → callback).
6. **Decide and document:** contain (quarantine, block), raise an incident, attach the logs.

:::ps
Customers buy FortiAnalyzer and then don't use it. Leaving them with a written routine and saved views is what turns it into a security tool.
:::

cards.back: Analytics (indexed) logs only.

To save CPU and memory in high-capacity environments.

scenarios.title: "Show me it's worth the money"
scenarios.situation: A CIO says the FortiAnalyzer "just sits there". The team never opens it.
scenarios.ask: How do you turn it into something they use?
right_thinking: Find what they need to know daily and weekly
Saved views and monitors for the NOC; a morning routine
Scheduled reports for management; alerts for critical events
Short training with their own data
scenarios.what: A usage plan built on their questions.
scenarios.why: Unused tools are cut at renewal; value comes from routine.
how: Ask the top 3 questions they need answered
scenarios.model_answer: I'd ask the team and the CIO what three questions they need answered, like "is anyone infected", "what's using our bandwidth", "are we compliant". Then I'd build saved views and a monitor for the NOC screen, a ten-minute morning routine, two scheduled reports for management, and alert handlers for critical events. A 30-minute session with their own data closes it. At Netskope I turned unused capabilities into routines with health checks and dashboards, and that's what moves an account from red to green.
scenarios.best_way: Start from their three questions; give them views, a routine, scheduled reports and alerts, with training on their own data.

interview.question: Walk me through investigating a malware alert in FortiAnalyzer.
interview.model_answer: "Scope the alert and time window. In FortiView, find the host in Top Threats or compromised hosts. Use the Asset Identity Center to get the user and endpoint. Then Log View filtered on that IP: DNS and web filter logs for what was looked up and visited, antivirus for the file, traffic logs for any callbacks. Raise an incident with the logs attached and recommend containment."
interview.best_way: Scope, FortiView, Asset Identity Center, filtered Log View, correlate, raise an incident.

interview.question: Why might FortiView look empty when logs are clearly arriving?
interview.model_answer: "FortiView uses Analytics logs, so if the time range is older than Analytics retention it's empty. Other causes: the wrong ADOM, the SQL database rebuilding, FortiView disabled for performance, or the device not authorised so logs aren't inserted."
interview.best_way: Analytics retention, wrong ADOM, SQL rebuilding, FortiView disabled, or device not authorised.

field_reports.title: Ransomware leaves a trail first
field_reports.body: Ransomware featured in **48 %** of breaches in the 2026 DBIR. The DNS lookups, web connections and callbacks that come before encryption are in the logs; a team that looks every morning can catch them early.
field_reports.source: Verizon 2026 DBIR

objectives: Explain basic and correlation alert handlers, data selectors and notification profiles
Raise incidents manually and automatically, and map them to MITRE ATT&CK
Describe playbooks and connectors for automated response

sources: FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Incidents (pp. 222–226), Alerts and alert handlers (pp. 235–256)
FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Automation, playbooks and connectors (pp. 399–402)
FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Reports, how reports are populated, datasets (pp. 465–470, 505–507)

units.title: Alert handlers and incidents
units.body:
## Alert handlers (pp. 254–256)

Alert handlers decide which **alerts** are generated from logs:

- **Basic:** an alert fires when **any** of its rules is met (rules are ORed).
- **Correlation:** an alert fires when a **sequence** of rules is met, with operators such as AND, AND_NOT, OR and FOLLOWED_BY.
- **Predefined** handlers exist for FortiGate, FortiSandbox, FortiMail and FortiWeb (some disabled by default); the easy way to build your own is to **clone** a predefined one.
- **Data selectors** (which devices and logs) and **notification profiles** (who's told, how) are configured separately and reused across handlers.
- Handlers only use **Analytics logs**. In an Analyzer–Collector design, the **Analyzer** evaluates them. Each ADOM has its own handlers; you can export and import them.

## Incidents (pp. 222–224)

Incidents track an investigation: category, **MITRE ATT&CK technique IDs**, severity, status, affected endpoint, assignee, attachments, audit history. You can raise one from an alert (only from alerts for **one endpoint**) or create it manually.

Automatic creation happens when:

- a handler has **Automatically Create Incident** enabled (it has the highest priority; later alerts with the same subject attach to the same incident until it's closed);
- **alert grouping** raises an incident for alerts at or above a severity with the same target: on by default at **critical** (`config system log alert` → `set min-severity-to-raise-incident-by-grouping {critical | high | none}`);
- the **Automated Correlation Threat Hunting** playbook runs after the Malicious IP Intrusion Detection handler fires.

:::recall
Q: Basic vs correlation alert handler?
A: Basic fires when any rule matches (OR). Correlation fires on a sequence or combination of rules (AND, AND_NOT, OR, FOLLOWED_BY).
:::

units.title: Automation with playbooks and connectors
units.body:
**Incidents & Alerts > Automation** (pp. 399–401) holds **playbooks** (sequences of tasks) and **connectors** (what the tasks can act on). Full capacity needs a **Security Automation subscription**.

- Default connectors: **Local**, **FortiGuard** and **VirusTotal**, used by default playbooks.
- Fabric connectors: **FortiOS** (for example, quarantine or block on FortiGates), **FortiManager**, **EMS**.
- Others appear once created: **ServiceNow**, **Slack**, **MS Teams**.

## A sensible first automation

1. Trigger: a critical alert from a compromised-host handler.
2. Enrich: look up the IP and hash with FortiGuard or VirusTotal.
3. Create or update the incident with the enrichment attached.
4. Notify the on-call channel (Teams or Slack).
5. Containment (quarantine via FortiOS or EMS) only after the customer approves automatic actions; start with a manual approval step.

The summary dashboard shows how many playbooks and tasks ran, useful evidence for the customer's management.

:::pitfall
Automatic quarantine on a noisy handler can take down production users. Tune the handler, run it in notify-only mode first, then automate containment.
:::

units.title: Reports that answer real questions
units.body:
## How a report is built (pp. 465–466)

- **Datasets:** SQL queries that pick the log type and data (for example, FortiGate botnet events).
- **Charts:** visualise a dataset (table, bar, pie, line…).
- **Macros:** put a single value from a dataset into text (a count, bandwidth, duration, percentage).
- **Reports / templates / layouts:** charts and macros plus cover page, text and images.

Reports use **Analytics logs**. Many predefined reports, templates, charts, datasets and macros exist; **clone and customise** them rather than starting from zero.

## When a report shows "No Data"

- Use **Report Guidance** to check the required logs exist (p. 466).
- Wrong ADOM (each ADOM has its own reports and libraries); a FortiGate report only imports into a FortiGate or Fabric ADOM.
- The time range is beyond Analytics retention.
- The FortiGate isn't sending that log type (for example, a policy without logging or without the profile).
- The SQL database is rebuilding (reports wait until it's done).

## Performance

Large reports can take a long time to assemble. **Auto-cache** builds an **hcache** in advance so scheduled reports run much faster (p. 466). Schedule heavy reports at night and send them through output profiles (email, file server).

## Which reports to set up first

Executive security summary (weekly), threat and compromised-host report (daily for the SOC), bandwidth and application usage (monthly), and compliance-oriented reports matching the customer's frameworks. You've done this before: turning log data into SOC 2, ISO 27001 and PCI-DSS evidence a board could read.

:::why
Q: Why clone a predefined report instead of building from scratch?
A: The datasets and charts are already tested against the log schema; you change scope, layout and wording, not SQL.
:::

units.title: Who is the user? Types, groups and identity policies
units.body:
FortiOS controls access **by user group**: users go into groups, and policies, VPN portals, SSIDs, ZTNA and remote
admin accounts reference the groups (p. 3909).

| User type | Who checks the password | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| Local | The FortiGate's own database | Small sites, break-glass and vendor accounts |
| Remote | LDAP, RADIUS, TACACS+ or FortiNAC | Corporate users from AD or a NAC |
| FSSO | Nobody at the FortiGate: Windows logon events | Transparent identity on AD networks |
| PKI / peer | Client certificate | Machines, VPN with certificates |
| SAML | An IdP (Entra ID, FortiAuthenticator, Okta…) | Cloud identity, MFA at the IdP |

User types and their authentication methods are on p. 3906.

## Identity-based policies

Add `set groups` (or `users`) to a firewall policy and it only matches traffic from a source IP that has an
**authenticated user in those groups**. With the default `auth-on-demand implicitly`, unauthenticated traffic
that doesn't match keeps going down the policy list; `always` forces the login whenever an identity policy could
match (p. 3920).

Users authenticate through the **captive portal**: an HTTP or HTTPS request that hits an identity policy is
redirected to the FortiGate's authentication page (port 1003 for HTTPS by default, p. 4001). SSH, RDP or a
database connection can't show a login page, so the user logs in once over the web first.

## How long does the login last?

`config user setting` → `auth-timeout` (minutes, **default 5**) and `auth-timeout-type`: `idle-timeout`,
`hard-timeout` or `new-session` (p. 3917).

:::cli
config user setting
    set auth-timeout-type idle-timeout
    set auth-timeout 480
end
:::

:::recall
Q: An identity policy for Finance sits above a general Internet policy. A Staff user who never logged in browses. What happens with the default auth-on-demand?
A: The Finance policy doesn't match an unauthenticated IP, so the traffic falls through to the general policy and works.
:::

:::pitfall
Identity is tied to the **source IP**. Anything that hides the user's real IP (a proxy, a Citrix server, NAT in
front of the FortiGate) breaks per-user policies, unless you use the matching agent (TS agent for Citrix) or
explicit proxy authentication.
:::

units.title: LDAP to Active Directory
units.body:
## The settings that matter (p. 3931)

| Setting | What it does | AD value |
|---|---|---|
| `server` | DC address or FQDN | Use the FQDN when using LDAPS |
| `cnid` | Attribute the username is matched against (case sensitive) | `sAMAccountName` (users type `jperez`) |
| `dn` | Where the search starts | `DC=andes,DC=local` for the whole domain |
| `type` | Bind type | `regular` |
| `username` / `password` | The service account for a regular bind | Full DN of a read-only account |
| `secure` | `disable`, `starttls` or `ldaps` | `ldaps` (port 636) or `starttls` (389) |

## Bind types (p. 3931)

- **Simple:** binds as `cnid=user,dn` with the typed password. It **doesn't search** the subtree, so it only works
  when users sit directly in that one container and are named by that attribute.
- **Anonymous:** binds without credentials and searches from the DN down. Many directories (AD included) refuse
  it.
- **Regular:** binds as a service account, searches for the user, then binds as the user with the typed password.
  This is the AD choice.

Fortinet's own guidance: secure the connection with **LDAPS**, and give the bind account **least privilege**,
never a domain admin (p. 3905).

## Groups

The search returns the user's `memberOf` DNs. In a user group, `config match` / `set group-name` compares them
**as full DNs**. Nested groups need `set search-type recursive`: without it only direct memberships come back
(pp. 3934–3935).

## Prove it before you build on it

:::cli
diagnose test authserver ldap DC-LDAP jperez Andes.Fin26
authenticate 'jperez' against 'DC-LDAP' succeeded!
Group membership(s) - CN=Finance,OU=Groups,DC=andes,DC=local
                      CN=Staff,OU=Groups,DC=andes,DC=local
:::

:::why
Q: Why does a regular bind need a service account at all, if the user types a password?
A: The FortiGate must first find the user's DN by searching for sAMAccountName=jperez, and AD doesn't allow anonymous searches. The service account does the search; the user's own bind then checks the password.
:::

:::pitfall
Domain-controller hardening that requires LDAP signing or channel binding breaks plain LDAP binds overnight.
Move to LDAPS or STARTTLS, and point `server` at the name on the DC's certificate instead of turning off
`server-identity-check`.
:::

units.title: RADIUS, VSAs and FSSO
units.body:
## RADIUS

Typical in front of NPS, FortiAuthenticator or a NAC. The FortiGate sends an Access-Request; the server answers
Accept or Reject. Two things identify the FortiGate to the server: its **source IP** (a RADIUS client entry) and
the **shared secret**.

- NPS **silently drops** requests from an IP that isn't a client: you see a timeout.
- A wrong secret makes the server decrypt a garbage password: you see a **reject**.

To place users in groups, the server returns the **Fortinet-Group-Name** vendor-specific attribute (Fortinet
vendor ID 12356, attribute 1, a string), and the user group's `match` entry compares it (pp. 3956, 3959).
RADIUS returns plain names (`Contractors`), not DNs.

Fortinet suggests **RADSEC** (RADIUS over TLS) to secure RADIUS connections (pp. 3905, 3987).

:::cli
diagnose test authserver radius NPS pap lgomez Contr4t1sta!
:::

## FSSO

Single sign-on for AD: users never see a login page. The components (p. 4094):

- **DC agent** on each domain controller, in DC agent mode: watches logon events and sends them to the collector.
- **Collector agent (CA):** gathers logons, can also **poll the DCs** so DC agents aren't needed, does DNS
  lookups, group checks and workstation checks, and updates the FortiGates (p. 4095).
- **TS agent** for Citrix/terminal servers (many users behind one IP), and an eDirectory agent for Novell.
- FortiAuthenticator can also collect logon events.

On the FortiGate: `config user fsso` (server, port 8000 by default, password), then an `fsso-service` user group
whose members are the AD groups the agent monitors. `logon-timeout` keeps known logons for a while (default
5 minutes) if the agent goes down (p. 4102).

:::recall
Q: Contractors get "timeout" from RADIUS, not "rejected". What do you check first?
A: That the server has a RADIUS client entry for the IP the FortiGate actually sources from (egress interface or source-ip).
:::

units.title: Troubleshooting authentication like a PS engineer
units.body:
Split every problem into **authentication** (is the password accepted?) and **authorization** (does the user land
in the group the policy wants?).

| Step | Command | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `diagnose test authserver ldap|radius …` | Server reachable, bind OK, password OK, which groups come back |
| 2 | `diagnose debug application fnbamd -1` + `diagnose debug enable` | Live trace of the auth daemon: search filter, bind result, group matching |
| 3 | `diagnose firewall auth list` | Which IPs have an authenticated user, in which group, for how long |
| 4 | `diagnose debug authd fsso server-status` / `… fsso list` | Is the collector agent connected, which logons it sent |
| 5 | `diagnose debug flow` | Which policy the traffic actually matched |

## Patterns

- **Everyone fails at once:** something shared broke: the bind account's password, the DC, TLS requirements.
- **One user fails:** their password, account state, or group.
- **Login succeeds, access still fails:** authorization: a group DN mismatch, a missing match entry, or the
  traffic matching another policy.
- **Timeouts:** routing or source IP to the server, or a RADIUS client entry.

:::ps
In a cutover, test with `diagnose test authserver` and two real accounts (one that should get in, one that
shouldn't) before the users arrive. Put the service account in the customer's password-rotation runbook, so the
next rotation doesn't take the firewall login down with it.
:::

cards.front: What does FortiOS use to grant access to users: users or user groups?

5 minutes (`config user setting` → `auth-timeout`).
idle-timeout, hard-timeout, new-session.

options.text: The search for cn=jperez finds nothing, so login fails
It works, because cn and sAMAccountName are the same in AD

Encryption doesn't change which attribute is searched.

quiz.stem: diagnose test authserver radius NPS pap lgomez ... → 'failed(no response)'. NPS is running. Most likely cause?

scenarios.title: "Just disable the certificate check, it works"
scenarios.situation:
During go-live, LDAPS fails with a certificate error because the LDAP server is set to the DC's IP. The customer's
admin says: "Disable server-identity-check, we're inside our own network."
scenarios.ask: What do you do and say?
right_thinking: Explain the risk: without the check, any host with a certificate can impersonate the DC and harvest passwords
Offer the fix that keeps the check: use the FQDN on the certificate and import the AD CA
If they still choose to disable it, record the risk acceptance in the change
scenarios.what: A secure fix proposed in minutes, and the decision documented.
scenarios.why: PS engineers own the quality of what they leave behind.
scenarios.model_answer:
"We can make it work without lowering security. The certificate is issued to dc01.andes.local, and we're
connecting by IP, so the name check fails. If I point the FortiGate at the FQDN and import your AD CA, LDAPS works
with the check on. Turning it off means any machine with a certificate could pretend to be your DC and see every
password. If you still prefer to disable it today, I'll note it in the change record as an accepted risk."
scenarios.best_way: Keep the control, fix the name.
rubric: explains the risk in business terms

scenarios.title: Monday morning, nobody can log in
scenarios.situation:
100 users fail firewall authentication since 7:00. The FortiGate config hasn't changed in a month. AD admins
rotated service-account passwords on Sunday.
scenarios.ask: Your first three moves?
right_thinking: Everyone at once points to something shared: the bind account or the DC
diagnose test authserver with a known-good account; fnbamd debug for the bind result
Update the bind password; add the account to the rotation runbook
scenarios.what: Root cause in minutes, not a password reset storm.
scenarios.why: Pattern recognition saves hours.
scenarios.model_answer:
"If everyone fails at once, it isn't their passwords. I'd run diagnose test authserver with a test account and
the fnbamd debug: if the bind as svc-fortigate fails with invalid credentials, the rotation changed it. Update
the password on the FortiGate, retest, and ask the AD team to add this account to their rotation checklist."
scenarios.best_way: Shared failure → shared component.

interview.question: How would you integrate a FortiGate with Active Directory for user-based policies?
interview.testing: LDAP vs FSSO judgement and correct settings
interview.model_answer:
"If users must log in explicitly, LDAP: regular bind with a least-privilege service account, cnid
sAMAccountName, the domain as the base DN, LDAPS. Then a user group matched on the AD group DN and identity
policies. If they want transparency, FSSO with the collector agent, ideally polling or DC agents on every DC,
and fsso-service groups. Either way I prove it with diagnose test authserver and two test users before go-live."
interview.best_way: Two options, the trade-off, and how you'd test.

interview.question: Users authenticate fine but still can't reach the application. How do you troubleshoot?
interview.model_answer:
"If the password is accepted, I look at authorization. diagnose firewall auth list shows which group the user
landed in; the fnbamd debug shows whether group matching passed; diagnose test authserver lists the real group
DNs to compare with the match entry. Then debug flow shows which policy the traffic hits, in case another
policy matches first."
interview.best_way: Name the split, then the tools in order.

interview.question: RADIUS authentication times out. What could it be?
interview.model_answer:
"A timeout means no answer, so: is there a route from the FortiGate to the server on UDP 1812, and is the
FortiGate's source IP, the egress interface or source-ip, configured as a RADIUS client? NPS drops unknown
clients silently. A wrong secret or password usually gives a reject instead."
interview.best_way: Timeout vs reject is the key.

field_reports.title: Credentials are the front door
field_reports.body:
Stolen or guessed credentials are one of the most common ways attackers get in. A firewall that can tie every
session to a named user turns "an IP on the LAN" into "Juan from Finance", in policies and in the logs your SOC
reads. That's the business case for identity-based policies, and MFA on remote access is the second half of it.
field_reports.source: General industry knowledge; see the DBIR for current figures

units.title: AAA and the three classic protocols
units.body:
**Authentication** proves who you are. **Authorization** decides what you may do. **Accounting** records what you
did. Every access design answers all three.

| Protocol | Transport | Strengths | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LDAP** | TCP 389, LDAPS 636 | A directory: users, groups, attributes | Look up users and group membership in AD |
| **RADIUS** | UDP 1812 auth, 1813 accounting | AAA for network access, vendor attributes (VSAs) | VPN, Wi-Fi, 802.1X, firewall auth via NPS or a NAC |
| **TACACS+** | TCP 49 | Separates authn, authz and accounting; per-command authorization | Network device administration |

## Details that come up in interviews

- RADIUS only obscures the **password** with the shared secret; the rest of the packet is in clear. That's why
  Fortinet recommends **RADSEC** (RADIUS over TLS) for untrusted paths (pp. 3905, 3987).
- TACACS+ encrypts the whole payload and can authorize **each command** an admin types: the usual choice for
  managing switches, routers and firewalls.
- LDAP is a **directory protocol**, not an AAA protocol: the firewall uses it to check a password with a bind
  and read groups, but the policy decision stays on the firewall.

:::recall
Q: Which protocol would you choose to control which commands each network admin may run?
A: TACACS+, because it authorizes per command and encrypts the whole session.
:::

units.title: Federation with SAML and OIDC
units.body:
Federation lets one **identity provider (IdP)** (Entra ID, Okta, FortiAuthenticator) vouch for users to many
**service providers (SPs)**. The SP never sees the password; it trusts a **signed assertion** from the IdP.

## SAML 2.0, SP-initiated (as FortiOS uses it, pp. 3994–4008)

1. The user opens a resource on the SP (for example, browses through an identity-based firewall policy).
2. The SP redirects the browser to the IdP with an authentication request. On FortiGate the captive portal port
   (1003 by default) does this redirect.
3. The user authenticates at the IdP, MFA included.
4. The IdP returns a **signed XML assertion** with the username and group attributes, through the browser.
5. The SP checks the signature with the IdP's certificate, reads the group, and applies the policy.

Configuration is an exchange of **metadata**: entity IDs, URLs and the IdP signing certificate.

## OIDC

**OpenID Connect** is an identity layer on **OAuth 2.0**: JSON tokens instead of XML, the **ID token** (a signed
JWT) carries who the user is, and an access token is for APIs. It's the modern default for web and mobile apps;
SAML still dominates enterprise SSO for older apps and network devices.

:::why
Q: Why is MFA usually configured at the IdP rather than on each firewall or app?
A: Federation centralizes authentication. One strong policy at the IdP (MFA, conditional access) then protects every SP that trusts it.
:::

:::pitfall
SAML depends on **clocks** (assertions have validity windows) and on the **certificate** the SP trusts. An IdP
certificate rollover that nobody copied to the SP breaks every login at once.
:::

units.title: 802.1X, EAP and network access control
units.body:
**802.1X** controls access at the **switch port or SSID** before the device gets a network:

| Role | Who | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Supplicant | The laptop or phone | Sends credentials |
| Authenticator | Switch or AP (or FortiGate/FortiSwitch/FortiAP) | Relays EAP inside RADIUS; opens the port |
| Authentication server | RADIUS (NPS, FortiAuthenticator, a NAC) | Decides, can return a VLAN |

**EAP** carries the actual method:

- **EAP-TLS:** certificates on both sides. The strongest common choice, no passwords to phish.
- **PEAP-MSCHAPv2:** a TLS tunnel protecting a username and password. Common, weaker if clients don't validate
  the server certificate.
- **MAB** (MAC authentication bypass) for printers and cameras that can't do 802.1X; a MAC is easy to spoof, so
  pair it with a restricted VLAN.

On FortiOS, `diagnose sys 802-1x status` shows the 802.1X state of switch members (p. 3986).

:::recall
Q: In 802.1X, which device talks RADIUS to the server?
A: The authenticator (the switch or AP), not the laptop.
:::

units.title: MFA, phishing resistance and provisioning
units.body:
## Factors

Something you **know** (password), **have** (token, phone, key), **are** (biometric). MFA combines two different
kinds.

| Factor | Phishing-resistant? | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| SMS or email code | No | Can be intercepted or relayed |
| TOTP app (FortiToken Mobile) | No | A fake page can relay the code in real time |
| Push approval | No | Push fatigue: attackers spam prompts until one is approved |
| FIDO2 / passkeys, certificates | **Yes** | Bound to the real site's origin or to a private key |

FortiOS supports FortiToken hardware and mobile tokens and FortiIdentity Cloud for MFA on local and remote users
(pp. 3907, 4054).

## Provisioning with SCIM

SAML answers "who is logging in now". **SCIM** answers "which users and groups exist": the IdP pushes users and
group changes to the SP over a REST API, so a user disabled in the IdP disappears from the app too. FortiOS can act
as a SCIM server for this (p. 4043).

:::ps
In an access project, always ask about the **joiner-mover-leaver** process: how a leaver's access is removed
everywhere. SCIM, FSSO with AD, or RADIUS to a central directory all solve it; local accounts on every firewall
don't.
:::

cards.back: Who you are · what you may do · what you did.
UDP 1812 (authentication), 1813 (accounting).

cards.back: TCP 49. Encrypts the whole payload and authorizes per command.

cards.back: Only the password attribute. Use RADSEC (TLS) for the rest.

cards.front: SAML: who signs the assertion, who verifies it?
cards.back: The IdP signs; the SP verifies with the IdP's certificate.
An identity layer on OAuth 2.0: a signed JWT ID token says who the user is.

Attackers send repeated push prompts until a tired user approves one.

scenarios.title: "We have MFA, we're safe"
scenarios.situation:
A customer's CISO says remote access is solved: "Everyone has push MFA." Last month a contractor approved a push
at 2 a.m. after twenty prompts.
scenarios.ask: How do you respond in the design review?
right_thinking: Acknowledge MFA is a big improvement
Explain push fatigue and that push/TOTP aren't phishing-resistant
Propose number matching as a quick win and FIDO2/certificates for admins and high-risk users
scenarios.what: A respectful upgrade path, not a lecture.
scenarios.why: Credibility comes from specific, proportionate advice.
scenarios.model_answer:
"MFA was the right move, and it stops most password attacks. The 2 a.m. approval shows its limit: push and codes
can be fatigued or relayed. Quick win: number matching and alerts on repeated prompts. Target state: FIDO2 keys
or certificates for admins and contractors, enforced at the IdP so the VPN and every app inherit it."
scenarios.best_way: Credit, gap, quick win, target.

interview.question: RADIUS or TACACS+ for administering 200 FortiGates and switches?
interview.model_answer:
"For admin access I prefer TACACS+: it encrypts the whole session, separates authentication from authorization,
and can authorize and account per command. RADIUS works too, especially with MFA through FortiAuthenticator, but
it only protects the password and has no per-command control. Either way, local break-glass accounts stay, vaulted."
interview.best_way: Pick one, give the reason, mention break-glass.

interview.question: Explain SAML to a customer who only knows usernames and passwords.
interview.model_answer:
"Think of a passport. Your company's identity system, the IdP, checks who you are once, with MFA, and gives the
app a signed pass saying 'this is Juan from Finance'. The app trusts the signature and never sees your password.
You get one strong login for everything, and when HR disables you, every app stops trusting you."
interview.best_way: One analogy, then the benefit.

objectives: Walk through the OSPF neighbor states and name what each mismatch breaks

sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Dynamic routing overview and OSPF (pp. 675–716), basic OSPF example and outputs (pp. 699–707)
Protocol knowledge: OSPFv2 (RFC 2328), NSSA (RFC 3101)

units.title: How two routers become neighbors
units.body:
OSPF is a **link-state** IGP: every router floods descriptions of its links (LSAs), builds the same map (the
LSDB), and runs Dijkstra's **SPF** algorithm to find shortest paths. Metric = **cost**, summed along the path.

## Neighbor states

| State | What happened |
|---|---|
| Down | No hellos heard |
| Init | I hear your hellos, but I'm not in yours yet |
| 2-Way | We see each other. On broadcast segments, DROthers stop here with each other |
| ExStart / Exchange | Master/slave chosen, database description (DBD) packets exchanged |
| Loading | Requesting the LSAs I'm missing |
| **Full** | Databases synchronized |

## What must match in the hello

Area ID, subnet and mask, **hello and dead intervals**, authentication, the stub/NSSA flags, and the router IDs
must differ. A mismatch here means **no neighbor at all**.

**MTU** is checked later, in the DBD exchange: a mismatch leaves the pair stuck in **ExStart/Exchange**. That's
why someone can "see the neighbor" and still have no routes.

:::recall
Q: One side says hello 10/dead 40, the other 2/8. Which state do they reach?
A: None: the hellos are discarded, so the neighbor never appears.
:::

:::pitfall
Duplicate router IDs (often from cloned VM configs) cause flapping and odd SPF results. Set router IDs
explicitly, usually from a loopback.
:::

units.title: DR/BDR and network types
units.body:
On a **broadcast** segment with many routers, full adjacency between every pair would flood the same LSA many
times. So routers elect a **Designated Router** and a **Backup DR**; everyone forms Full adjacencies only with them
and stays **2-Way** with the other DROthers.

Election: highest **priority** (default 1; 0 means "never DR"), then highest router ID. It's **not preemptive**: a
better router joining later doesn't take over until the DR fails.

**Point-to-point** network type skips the election: faster, and the right choice on /30 or /31 transit links,
tunnels and most WAN links. Both sides must agree: one side broadcast and the other point-to-point usually
breaks the adjacency or the routes.

In FortiOS output, `Full/DR`, `Full/Backup` or `Full/DROther` is the **neighbor's** role (p. 705).

:::why
Q: Why set the network type to point-to-point on a FortiGate-to-core transit /29 with only two routers?
A: There's nothing to gain from a DR with two routers, and skipping the election and wait timer speeds up adjacency and failover.
:::

units.title: LSAs, areas and route types
units.body:
| LSA | Name | Generated by | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Router | Every router | Its area |
| 2 | Network | The DR | Its area |
| 3 | Summary | ABR | Other areas |
| 4 | ASBR summary | ABR | How to reach an ASBR in another area |
| 5 | AS external | ASBR | Whole domain (not stub areas) |
| 7 | NSSA external | ASBR inside an NSSA | Its NSSA; the ABR translates it to type 5 |

- **Area 0** is the backbone; every other area attaches to it through an **ABR**.
- An **ASBR** redistributes routes from outside OSPF (static, connected, BGP).

## Route types in a routing table

- **O** intra-area: from type 1/2 in your area.
- **O IA** inter-area: from type 3.
- **O E2** external type 2 (the default): the metric is the external metric only and doesn't grow inside OSPF.
- **O E1** external type 1: external metric **plus** the internal cost.

Preference: intra-area > inter-area > E1 > E2, regardless of metric.

:::recall
Q: A redistributed default route shows as O*E2 0.0.0.0/0 [110/10] on every router, whatever the distance from the ASBR. Why the same metric everywhere?
A: E2 routes carry only the external metric; internal cost isn't added.
:::

units.title: Stub areas and branch designs
units.body:
| Area type | Blocks | Branch gets |
|---|---|---|
| Stub | Type 5 externals | Inter-area routes + a default from the ABR |
| Totally stubby | Type 3 and 5 | Only a default route |
| NSSA | Type 5, but allows local redistribution (type 7) | Inter-area routes, its own externals |

Smaller areas mean smaller LSDBs and less SPF churn, useful for many small branches. On the other hand, a
branch that only sees a default can't pick the best exit per prefix.

## Summarization

Only at the edges: ABRs (`area range`) and ASBRs (summary addresses). One summary hides the flapping of every
subnet behind it.

:::ps
Most FortiGate designs today use OSPF inside the campus or data center and BGP over the WAN or SD-WAN overlays.
When a customer asks for OSPF across 200 branches, ask what problem it solves first: BGP with ADVPN or SD-WAN
usually scales better.
:::

cards.back: Down, Init, 2-Way, ExStart, Exchange, Loading, Full.
Area, subnet/mask, hello and dead intervals, authentication, stub/NSSA flags (router IDs must differ).

cards.front: Neighbor stuck in ExStart/Exchange: classic cause
cards.back: MTU mismatch.
Cost, summed along the path.
Highest priority (0 = never), then highest router ID. Not preemptive.

cards.front: Why DROthers stay in 2-Way with each other
cards.back: They only need Full adjacencies with the DR/BDR, which reduces flooding.

cards.front: Network type for a two-router transit link
cards.back: Point-to-point: no DR election, faster adjacency.
Summary LSA, generated by an ABR for other areas.
5: AS external from an ASBR, domain-wide. 7: NSSA external, translated to 5 by the ABR.
E1 adds internal cost; E2 (default) keeps only the external metric.
Intra-area > inter-area > E1 > E2.
Stub blocks type 5; totally stubby also blocks type 3. Both get a default from the ABR.
Only at ABRs (area ranges) and ASBRs (external summaries).

scenarios.title: "OSPF is up, so it's not the network"
scenarios.situation:
After a core switch swap, an integrator says OSPF is fine because "the FortiGate is in the neighbor list". The
warehouse has no routes. The neighbor state is EXSTART.
scenarios.ask: Explain to the integrator and the customer.
right_thinking: Neighbor listed ≠ adjacency Full
ExStart points at MTU (jumbo on the new switch)
Short-term mtu-ignore or match MTU; long-term consistent MTU
scenarios.what: A clear explanation and a fix plan.
scenarios.why: Precise language avoids blame games.
scenarios.model_answer:
"The FortiGate hears the switch's hellos, so it's listed, but they're stuck in ExStart, which means they never
exchanged databases, so no routes. That state points at an MTU mismatch: the new switch uses jumbo frames on the
uplink. We can set mtu-ignore now to restore service and align MTUs in the next window."
scenarios.best_way: State, cause, now, later.

interview.question: An OSPF neighbor is stuck in ExStart. What do you check?
interview.model_answer:
"ExStart means hellos match but the database description exchange fails, and the classic cause is an MTU
mismatch between the two interfaces. I'd compare MTUs, run the OSPF debug, and either align the MTU or set
mtu-ignore as a temporary fix."
interview.best_way: Name the state's meaning first.

interview.question: Explain E1 vs E2 routes.
interview.model_answer:
"Both are external routes from an ASBR. E2, the default, keeps only the external metric, so every router sees
the same cost. E1 adds the internal cost to reach the ASBR, so with two ASBRs advertising the same prefix, E1
lets each router pick the closest exit."
interview.best_way: Definition plus the two-ASBR case.

sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: BGP (pp. 716–805): basic example (p. 718), neighbor password (p. 727), network prefixes (p. 749), conditional advertisement (p. 751)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: BFD (p. 806), routing objects: prefix lists, route maps (p. 817)

units.title: Sessions and the finite-state machine
units.body:
BGP is a **path-vector** protocol between configured neighbors over **TCP 179**. Neighbors in different ASes are
**eBGP**; in the same AS, **iBGP**.

| State | Meaning | Usual cause when stuck |
|---|---|---|
| Idle | Not trying, or reset after an error | Admin shutdown, NOTIFICATION (e.g., Bad Peer AS) |
| Connect / Active | Trying to open TCP | No route, wrong IP, wrong update-source, TCP 179 blocked, MD5 mismatch |
| OpenSent / OpenConfirm | OPEN messages exchanged | AS or router-ID problems |
| **Established** | Exchanging routes | — |

In `get router info bgp summary` the last column shows the **state**, or the **number of prefixes received** once
Established.

## eBGP vs iBGP rules

- eBGP peers are expected to be **directly connected** (TTL 1). Loopback peering needs multihop
  (`ebgp-enforce-multihop` on FortiOS).
- iBGP usually peers between **loopbacks** with `update-source`, reached through the IGP.
- Both sides need a neighbor statement for the other's **exact source IP** and the right remote AS.

:::recall
Q: The session is Idle and the neighbor log says "Bad Peer AS". Where's the error?
A: A remote-as value on one side doesn't match the other side's local AS.
:::

units.title: What gets advertised, and to whom
units.body:
## Origination

- `network` statements: on FortiOS, with **network-import-check** (enabled by default) the exact prefix must be
  in the routing table, or nothing is advertised (p. 749).
- Redistribution: connected, static, OSPF into BGP (origin incomplete, `?`).
- Aggregates: summaries, often anchored by a blackhole static route.

## The rules of propagation

- eBGP: prepend your AS, set the **next hop to yourself**.
- iBGP: **don't** change the AS path, **don't** change the next hop (by default), and **never pass an iBGP-learned
  route to another iBGP peer** (split horizon). Hence full mesh, or **route reflectors**: a RR may reflect routes
  between clients and non-clients.
- Loop prevention: a router drops a route whose AS path contains its own AS.

## The next-hop trap

An HQ router learns an Internet prefix from its ISP via eBGP and passes it by iBGP to a second router. The next
hop is still the ISP's IP. If the second router has no route to it, the BGP route is **invalid**: present in the
table, not installed. Fix: `next-hop-self` on the iBGP neighbor, or advertise the link into the IGP.

:::why
Q: Why doesn't iBGP just forward iBGP-learned routes like eBGP does?
A: iBGP doesn't modify the AS path, so the AS path can't detect loops inside the AS. Split horizon prevents them instead.
:::

units.title: Best-path selection
units.body:
When several paths exist for the same prefix, the first difference decides:

1. Highest **weight** (local to the router; FortiOS gives locally originated routes 32768)
2. Highest **local preference** (default 100, shared across the AS)
3. Locally originated
4. Shortest **AS path**
5. Lowest **origin** (IGP < EGP < incomplete)
6. Lowest **MED** (compared only between paths from the same neighbor AS by default)
7. **eBGP over iBGP**
8. Lowest IGP metric to the next hop
9. Oldest path / lowest router ID / lowest neighbor IP

## Influencing traffic

| You want to control | Attribute | Where |
|---|---|---|
| How **you** leave (outbound) | Local preference (AS-wide) or weight (one router) | Inbound route map on your routers |
| How **others** come in (inbound) | AS-path prepend, MED | Outbound route map toward the provider |

:::recall
Q: Two ISPs. You want all outbound traffic through ISP-A, and inbound to prefer ISP-A too. What do you set?
A: Higher local preference on routes from ISP-A (inbound route map), and prepend your AS a few times toward ISP-B (outbound route map).
:::

units.title: Filtering with prefix lists and route maps
units.body:
## Prefix lists

Ordered rules: `permit`/`deny` a prefix with optional `ge`/`le`. Without ge/le a rule matches **only that exact
prefix**; `10.20.0.0/16 le 24` matches the /16 and anything more specific down to /24. The end has an **implicit
deny**.

## Route maps

Ordered rules that **match** (a prefix list, AS path, community…) and **set** (local preference, weight, MED,
AS-path prepend, community). A route map with no matching rule denies the route.

:::cli
config router route-map
    edit "FROM-ISP-A"
        config rule
            edit 1
                set set-local-preference 200
            next
        end
    next
end
config router bgp
    config neighbor
        edit "203.0.113.1"
            set route-map-in "FROM-ISP-A"
        next
    end
end
:::

Apply filter changes without dropping the session: `execute router clear bgp ip <peer> soft in|out`.

:::pitfall
Always filter what you accept from a provider and what you announce to it. A FortiGate announcing a full
table it learned from ISP-A to ISP-B makes your company a transit AS, and a route leak with your name on it.
:::

cards.back: TCP 179.
