interview.question: Walk me through BGP best-path selection.
interview.framework: List the order, then one example
interview.model_answer:
"Highest weight, which is local; highest local preference, AS-wide; locally originated; shortest AS path;
lowest origin; lowest MED from the same neighbor AS; eBGP over iBGP; lowest IGP cost to the next hop; then
tie-breakers like router ID. In practice I use local preference to control how we leave and AS-path
prepending to influence how traffic comes in."
interview.best_way: Order, then how you use it.

interview.question: An iBGP route is in the BGP table but not in the routing table. Why?
interview.model_answer:
"Most likely the next hop isn't reachable: iBGP keeps the eBGP next hop, the ISP's IP, and this router has no
route to it. next-hop-self on the edge router, or advertising the link into the IGP, fixes it. I'd confirm with
the BGP table output, which shows the path isn't marked valid."
interview.best_way: Name the next-hop rule.

modules.title: Routing on FortiGate: static, policy routes, ECMP and the routing database
objectives: Read the routing table and the routing database and explain why a route is or isn't active
Use distance and priority for primary/backup and ECMP designs
Configure policy routes and know where they sit in the lookup order
Build dual-Internet failover with a link health monitor
Use blackhole routes and understand reverse path checks and asymmetric routing
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Routing concepts, default route, distance and priority (pp. 644–651)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Route look-up, blackhole routes, reverse path, asymmetric routing, routing changes (pp. 652–658)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Policy routes (pp. 659–664), ECMP (pp. 665–668), dual Internet connections and link health monitor (pp. 669–674)

units.title: Table vs database, distance vs priority
units.body:
- `get router info routing-table all` shows the **active** routes, the ones used for forwarding.
- `get router info routing-table database` shows **every** candidate, including those that lost (pp. 649–650).

## Which route wins

1. **Longest prefix match**: a /24 beats a /16 regardless of protocol.
2. For the same prefix: lowest **administrative distance** (connected 0, static 10 by default, eBGP 20, OSPF
   110, iBGP 200). The losers stay in the database only.
3. Same prefix and distance: static routes stay **all** in the table, and the lowest **priority** (default 1)
   is preferred; equal priority means **ECMP** (pp. 646–648, 665).

:::cli
get router info routing-table details 10.20.70.10
:::

## Floating static routes

A static route with a higher distance (say 20) sits in the database and becomes active only when the better
route disappears: the classic backup for an OSPF or BGP route.

:::recall
Q: OSPF learns 10.20.70.0/24 but an old static route to it still exists. Which one forwards traffic?
A: The static route (distance 10 beats OSPF's 110). The OSPF route is only in the database.
:::

units.title: Policy routes and the lookup order
units.body:
**Policy routes** (PBR) match on incoming interface, source, destination, protocol and ports, and send traffic to a
specific gateway. The FortiGate walks the policy-route list first; if nothing matches it does a normal route
lookup (p. 660). SD-WAN rules are implemented as policy routes too, which is why they're checked before the
routing table.

| Order | What |
|---|---|
| 1 | Policy routes (including SD-WAN rules and ISDB routes) |
| 2 | Routing table (longest match, distance, priority) |

A policy route with action **Stop Policy Routing** sends matching traffic straight to the routing table: useful
to exempt internal destinations from a broad PBR rule.

:::pitfall
A policy route only forwards if its gateway is reachable through an active route on that interface. And the
firewall policy still has to allow the traffic: PBR chooses the path, it doesn't permit anything.
:::

units.title: Dual Internet, ECMP and link health
units.body:
## Failover (pp. 669–674)

Two default routes with **different distances** (or the same distance and different priorities), plus a **link
health monitor** on the primary. The monitor probes a server through the link; when it fails, the FortiGate
removes that route and the backup takes over.

:::cli
config system link-monitor
    edit "ISP1"
        set srcintf "wan1"
        set server "8.8.8.8"
        set gateway-ip 190.14.8.1
    next
end
:::

## ECMP (pp. 665–668)

Routes with the same destination and the same cost (for static routes: distance **and** priority) load-balance.
The algorithm is `v4-ecmp-mode` under `config system settings`: source-ip-based (default), weight-based,
usage-based or source-dest-ip-based. With SD-WAN enabled it moves to the SD-WAN `load-balance-mode`.

:::why
Q: Why doesn't a plain physical-link-down check catch most ISP failures?
A: The usual failure is upstream: the port stays up while the ISP's network is broken. Only probing through the link (link monitor or SD-WAN health checks) detects it.
:::

units.title: Blackholes, RPF and asymmetric routing
units.body:
- **Blackhole routes** drop traffic for a prefix (p. 652). Typical uses: stop private ranges from leaking to the
  Internet's default route when a VPN is down, and anchor BGP aggregates.
- **Reverse path forwarding (RPF)** check: when a session starts, the FortiGate checks it has a route back to the
  source through the incoming interface (loose by default: any route back; strict with `src-check` strict mode).
  A failed check drops the packet ("reverse path check fail") (p. 653).
- **Asymmetric routing**: request and reply cross different firewalls or interfaces. A stateful firewall that sees
  only one direction drops the rest. Fix the routing, don't just enable `asymroute` (p. 654).
- **Routing changes and sessions**: existing sessions keep their route until a routing change marks them dirty;
  with SNAT, `snat-route-change` forces a new lookup (p. 656).

:::ps
In migrations, list every static route on the old firewall and decide for each: keep, replace by dynamic
routing, or delete. A forgotten static with distance 10 beats OSPF and BGP for years.
:::

scenarios.situation:

interview.model_answer:

distance between protocols, then for static routes the lowest priority, and equal ones are ECMP. I check
with get router info routing-table details for one destination, and the database view to see what lost."

modules.title: Advanced routing on FortiGate: OSPF and BGP configuration, debugging, BFD
objectives: Configure OSPF on FortiOS with areas, network statements, passive interfaces, authentication and default origination
Configure eBGP and iBGP on FortiOS with update-source, multihop, next-hop-self, filters and route maps
Redistribute between protocols safely
Troubleshoot with get router info, the routing database and the protocol debugs
Use BFD for fast failure detection
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: OSPF (pp. 698–716) with the basic example and outputs (pp. 699–707)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: BGP (pp. 716–805): basic example (p. 718), neighbor password (p. 727), network prefixes (p. 749)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: BFD (pp. 806–816), routing objects (p. 817)

units.title: OSPF on FortiOS
units.body:
:::cli
config router ospf
    set router-id 10.20.255.1
    set default-information-originate enable
    set passive-interface "port2"
    config area
        edit 0.0.0.0
        next
    end
    config network
        edit 1
            set prefix 10.20.50.0 255.255.255.248
            set area 0.0.0.0
        next
        edit 2
            set prefix 10.20.10.0 255.255.255.0
            set area 0.0.0.0
        next
    end
    config ospf-interface
        edit "CORE"
            set interface "port5"
            set network-type point-to-point
            set authentication message-digest
            config md5-keys
                edit 1
                    set key-string <key>
                next
            end
        next
    end
end
:::

- **network** statements enable OSPF on every interface whose IP falls inside the prefix and put it in that area.
- **passive-interface**: advertise the subnet, send no hellos (user LANs).
- **ospf-interface**: per-interface cost, network type, timers, authentication, MTU handling.
- **default-information-originate**: `enable` advertises a default (external) only while the FortiGate has one;
  `always` advertises it regardless.
- **redistribute** connected/static/bgp with a metric and metric type; `default-metric` applies when you set
  none.

:::recall
Q: Why put the user LAN in a network statement and also make it passive?
A: The network statement advertises the subnet; passive stops hellos to PCs, so nobody on the LAN can form an adjacency and inject routes.
:::

units.title: BGP on FortiOS
units.body:
:::cli
config router bgp
    set as 65010
    set router-id 10.20.255.1
    config neighbor
        edit "10.255.0.1"
            set remote-as 64600
            set password <md5>
            set prefix-list-in "ANDES-ONLY"
            set bfd enable
        next
        edit "10.20.255.2"
            set remote-as 65010
            set update-source "loopback0"
            set next-hop-self enable
        next
    end
    config network
        edit 1
            set prefix 10.20.10.0 255.255.255.0
        next
    end
end
:::

| Setting | Why |
|---|---|
| `update-source` | iBGP between loopbacks: the session survives a link failure if the IGP reroutes |
| `ebgp-enforce-multihop` | eBGP to a non-connected address (loopback peering) |
| `next-hop-self` | iBGP peers can't reach the eBGP next hop |
| `route-reflector-client` | Avoid an iBGP full mesh |
| `password` | TCP MD5 on the session (p. 727) |
| `network-import-check` | Default enable: advertise a network only if it exists in the RIB (p. 749) |

Distances: eBGP 20, iBGP 200 (`distance-external`, `distance-internal`).

units.title: Troubleshooting dynamic routing
units.body:
| Question | Command |
|---|---|
| Is the adjacency Full / session Established? | `get router info ospf neighbor` · `get router info bgp summary` |
| Why not? | `get router info ospf interface <port>` · `get router info bgp neighbors <ip>` · `diagnose ip router ospf all enable` / `diagnose ip router bgp all enable` + `diagnose debug enable` |
| What did I learn / send? | `get router info ospf database` · `get router info bgp network` · `get router info bgp neighbors <ip> received-routes|advertised-routes` |
| Which route is used? | `get router info routing-table all` · `… details <ip>` · `… database` |
| Apply a filter change | `execute router clear bgp ip <peer> soft in|out` |

## Symptom → cause cheat sheet

- OSPF neighbor missing: timers, area, mask, authentication, passive, or no network statement covering the port.
- OSPF ExStart: MTU.
- BGP Active: no route to the peer, wrong neighbor IP or update-source, MD5 mismatch, TCP 179 blocked.
- BGP Idle with Bad Peer AS: wrong remote-as.
- Prefix in BGP table but not installed: next hop unreachable, or a better distance from another protocol.
- Advertised nothing: network-import-check, outbound filters.

:::pitfall
Redistributing BGP into OSPF and OSPF back into BGP at two points creates feedback loops. Tag routes when you
redistribute and filter the tag on the way back, or redistribute in one direction only.
:::

units.title: BFD and convergence
units.body:
Protocol timers are slow: OSPF's default dead interval is 40 s; BGP's hold timer is 180 s by default. **BFD**
sends lightweight packets at a negotiated rate and tells the routing protocol the moment the neighbor stops
answering (p. 806).

FortiOS: enable BFD globally, per VDOM or per interface (`config system settings` / `set bfd enable` with
`bfd-desired-min-tx`, `bfd-required-min-rx`, `bfd-detect-mult`), then on the protocol (`set bfd enable` on a BGP
neighbor or in OSPF). Echo mode and authentication aren't supported for BFD on FortiGate (p. 806).

:::why
Q: Why use BFD instead of setting OSPF hello to 1 s?
A: BFD is light and hardware-friendly, works for several protocols at once, and doesn't require both sides to agree on aggressive OSPF timers (a mismatch kills the adjacency).
:::

:::ps
In a change window, capture `get router info routing-table all` and the neighbor summaries **before** you start.
The comparison after the change is your acceptance test.
:::

scenarios.situation:

scenarios.model_answer:
"First, advertised-routes on the site's FortiGate toward the PE: if it's empty, the network statement doesn't
match a route in its table, the classic network-import-check issue. Fix the prefix, check HQ receives it, test
from a user PC. If I can't prove it works by 23:55, I re-enable the old static routes as the MOP says, and we
schedule the BGP part again."
scenarios.best_way: Evidence, fix, test, or roll back on time.

interview.question: BGP is Established but the remote prefix isn't in the routing table. Walk me through it.
interview.model_answer:
"I follow the route: on the remote side, is it advertised (advertised-routes; if not, network-import-check or an
outbound filter)? On my side, is it received and accepted (received-routes, inbound filters)? Is it valid
(next hop reachable)? Is it best and installed, or does another protocol win on distance? Each step has its
command, so it's quick."
interview.best_way: Four stages, one command each.

modules.title: Switching on FortiSwitch: VLANs, LAG, MCLAG and STP protection
objectives: Explain native, allowed and untagged VLANs on a switch port and predict frame handling
Build LAGs and explain what MCLAG adds
Protect a topology with STP edge ports, BPDU guard, root guard, loop guard and flap guard
sources: FortiSwitchOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide (Standalone): Link aggregation and MCLAG (pp. 170–181), loop guard (p. 183), LLDP-MED (p. 184)
FortiSwitchOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide (Standalone): STP, root guard and BPDU guard (pp. 263–284), flap guard (p. 285)
FortiSwitchOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide (Standalone): VLANs: native, allowed, untagged (pp. 370–373)

units.title: VLANs on a port
units.body:
Every FortiSwitch port has three VLAN settings (pp. 370–371):

| Setting | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Native VLAN** | The VLAN untagged incoming frames belong to (the port's "default" VLAN) |
| **Allowed VLANs** | Tagged VLANs the port accepts and sends |
| **Untagged VLANs** | Allowed VLANs whose frames leave the port **without** a tag |

- A PC or printer: native VLAN only (an **access** port).
- An AP or a hypervisor: native VLAN for management plus allowed (tagged) VLANs for SSIDs or VMs (a **trunk**).
- A frame tagged with a VLAN that isn't native or allowed is dropped.

:::recall
Q: An IP phone sends tagged VLAN 20 frames and the PC behind it sends untagged frames. What do you configure on the switch port?
A: Native VLAN = the data VLAN (for the PC), allowed VLANs includes 20 (for the phone's tagged voice).
:::

:::pitfall
Leaving every unused port in the default/native management VLAN gives anyone who plugs in a laptop a foothold
on the management network. Shut unused ports or put them in a dead VLAN.
:::

units.title: LAG and MCLAG
units.body:
A **LAG** (trunk of several ports, usually with **LACP**) gives link-level redundancy and more bandwidth between two
devices. Traffic is spread per flow by a hash, so one flow never exceeds one member's speed (pp. 170–174).

An **MCLAG** pairs two FortiSwitches so they look like **one** switch to the device below: a server or an access
switch connects one LAG with members on both. If either switch fails, the LAG keeps working, with no STP
reconvergence (p. 174). The two peers are joined by an **ICL** (inter-chassis link), and the guide covers how to
detect a split-brain state when the ICL fails (p. 177).

:::why
Q: Why is MCLAG preferred over two separate uplinks protected by STP?
A: Both links forward at the same time and failover doesn't wait for STP; with STP one uplink is blocked and convergence takes time.
:::

units.title: Keeping loops and rogue switches out
units.body:
| Feature | Protects against | Action |
|---|---|---|
| **STP edge port** | Delays on host ports | Port forwards immediately |
| **BPDU guard** | A switch plugged into an edge port | Any BPDU received shuts the port for a set time (p. 276) |
| **Root guard** | A downstream switch becoming STP root | Port blocked while it receives superior BPDUs |
| **Loop guard** (FortiSwitch feature) | Downstream loops, even without STP | Port detects its own loop-detection frames and shuts (p. 183) |
| **Flap guard** | A port going up/down rapidly (bad cable, attack) | Shuts the port after N changes in a time window (p. 285) |

:::ps
A standard access-port profile for a customer: edge port, BPDU guard, loop guard, a data VLAN as native, and
port security (next module). Apply it everywhere users plug in; keep uplinks without those protections.
:::

cards.back: The VLAN untagged incoming frames belong to on a port.
Tagged VLANs a port accepts and sends.
Allowed VLANs whose frames leave the port without a tag.

cards.front: Does a LAG make one flow faster?
cards.back: No: flows are hashed onto members; one flow uses one member.
Two FortiSwitches act as one LAG peer; node-level redundancy without STP blocking.
Inter-chassis link between MCLAG peers.
Shuts an edge port that receives a BPDU, for a set time.
Blocks a port receiving superior BPDUs, so no downstream switch becomes root.
Detects downstream loops with its own frames and shuts the port; works with or without STP.
Shuts a port that changes state too many times within a time window.

scenarios.title: The Monday-morning broadcast storm
scenarios.situation:
A warehouse network melts down every Monday. A cleaner reconnects a loose cable between two wall ports on the
same switch.
scenarios.ask: What do you propose?
right_thinking: Loop guard on access ports (and BPDU guard where STP is used)
Storm control to cap broadcast while it happens
Shut unused ports
scenarios.what: Protection that works without depending on the cleaner.
scenarios.why: Layer-2 loops are a design problem, not a people problem.
scenarios.model_answer:
"That's a loop through two access ports. I'd enable loop guard on all access ports so the second port shuts the
moment it sees its own loop-detection frames, add storm control to cap broadcast if anything slips through, and
shut unused wall ports. Then we alert on port shutdowns so the IT team finds the cable on Monday morning."
scenarios.best_way: Prevent, contain, detect.

interview.question: What's the difference between native, allowed and untagged VLANs on a FortiSwitch port?
interview.model_answer:
"Native is the VLAN untagged incoming frames go into. Allowed are the tagged VLANs the port carries. Untagged
VLANs are allowed VLANs sent out without a tag. A PC port only needs native; an AP port has its management
VLAN as native and the SSID VLANs as allowed."
interview.best_way: Three definitions, one example.

modules.title: FortiSwitch access security: 802.1X, MAB, DHCP snooping and friends
objectives: Configure port security with 802.1X and MAB and choose VLAN outcomes
Explain DHCP snooping, IP source guard and dynamic ARP inspection and how they build on each other
Use storm control, sticky MAC and LLDP-MED in access designs
sources: FortiSwitchOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide (Standalone): Port security / 802.1X (pp. 201–259), MAC security (p. 260)
FortiSwitchOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide (Standalone): DHCP snooping (p. 288), IP source guard, dynamic ARP inspection (pp. 288–340)
FortiSwitchOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide (Standalone): Storm control (p. 388), sticky MAC, LLDP-MED (p. 184), deployment scenario (p. 555)

units.title: Who may plug in? 802.1X and MAB
units.body:
FortiSwitch supports **IEEE 802.1X** port security (p. 201): the port lets nothing but EAP through until a RADIUS
server accepts the device.

- **Port-based** mode authenticates the first device and opens the port; **MAC-based** mode authenticates every
  MAC on the port separately (phone + PC on one port).
- **MAB** (MAC authentication bypass) sends the device's MAC to RADIUS as its identity, for printers, cameras and
  phones that have no supplicant.
- The RADIUS server can return a **VLAN** (dynamic VLAN assignment); a **guest VLAN** catches devices that don't
  do 802.1X, and an **auth-fail VLAN** catches failed attempts.

The guide's deployment scenario authenticates a phone with MAB and the PC behind it with EAP on the same port
(p. 555).

:::recall
Q: A port has an IP phone with no supplicant and a PC with 802.1X behind it. Which mode and methods?
A: MAC-based 802.1X: MAB for the phone, EAP for the PC.
:::

units.title: DHCP snooping, IP source guard, DAI
units.body:
These three build on one another:

1. **DHCP snooping** (p. 288): only **trusted** ports (uplinks to the real DHCP server) may send DHCP offers;
   offers from untrusted ports (a rogue router a user brought in) are dropped. The switch records a **binding
   table**: MAC, IP, VLAN, port.
2. **IP source guard**: on untrusted ports, only traffic whose source IP/MAC match a binding passes. A user can't
   just set a static IP.
3. **Dynamic ARP inspection (DAI)**: ARP replies must match a binding, which stops ARP spoofing and
   man-in-the-middle attacks on the LAN.

:::pitfall
Forget to trust the uplink toward the DHCP server, and every client loses its address the moment snooping is
enabled.
:::

units.title: Storms, MACs and phones
units.body:
- **Storm control** (p. 388): limits broadcast, unknown unicast and multicast per second, so a loop or a flood
  degrades instead of melting the network. Disabled by default.
- **Sticky MAC**: learned MACs on a port become permanent, so a port can be locked to the device that was there
  when you secured it. **Learning limits** cap how many MACs a port may learn.
- **LLDP-MED** (p. 184): the switch advertises the voice VLAN and QoS to IP phones, so phones tag voice traffic
  without manual configuration.

:::ps
Turning on 802.1X across a site is a project, not a setting: inventory devices, start in monitor mode, build MAB
lists for headless devices, then enforce, one floor at a time.
:::

cards.back: Port-based: first device opens the port. MAC-based: each MAC authenticates separately.
MAC authentication bypass: the MAC is sent to RADIUS as the identity for devices without a supplicant.
Guest: device doesn't do 802.1X. Auth-fail: device tried and failed.
The only ports allowed to send DHCP server messages (uplinks to the real server).
On untrusted ports, only traffic matching a DHCP-snooping binding (IP/MAC) passes.
Drops ARP packets that don't match the binding table: stops ARP spoofing.
Disabled.
Learned MACs on a port are kept permanently, locking the port to them.
Advertises the voice VLAN and QoS so phones tag voice automatically.

without supplicants go offline. I'd run monitor mode this week to find every device that would fail, build
the MAB list, and enforce floor by floor starting next Monday, finishing in three weeks, with a rollback per

interview.question: How would you stop a rogue DHCP server and ARP spoofing on an access network?
interview.model_answer:
"DHCP snooping with only the uplinks trusted, so offers from user ports are dropped and the switch builds a
binding table. Then dynamic ARP inspection checks ARP against those bindings, which stops spoofing, and IP
source guard stops users from setting static IPs. I'd enable them in that order and test DHCP right after
the first step."
interview.best_way: Three features in dependency order.

modules.title: FortiLink: managing FortiSwitch from the FortiGate
objectives: Set up a FortiLink interface and authorize FortiSwitch units
Create FortiLink VLANs and assign switch ports from the FortiGate
Troubleshoot discovery, authorization and VLAN placement
Handle switch replacement and scale with FortiManager
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Switch Controller (p. 4120) and the FortiLink Guide it references
FortiManager 7.6.8 Admin Guide: FortiSwitch Manager (pp. 970–1024)
FortiSwitchOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: QoS (p. 394), PoE (p. 355)

units.title: What FortiLink is
units.body:
**FortiLink** (the Switch Controller) lets a FortiGate discover, authorize and manage FortiSwitch units. VLANs are
created on the FortiGate as interfaces on the FortiLink interface, and the FortiGate's security (firewall
policies, 802.1X, NAC) extends to every switch port (p. 4120).

- Typical layer-2 design: the FortiGate connects to distribution switches, which connect down to access
  switches.
- A **third-party switch between** the FortiGate and the FortiSwitch isn't supported in layer-2 FortiLink mode;
  FortiLink over a **layer-3** network is (p. 4120).
- The FortiGate is the gateway, DHCP server and firewall for every FortiLink VLAN: traffic between VLANs always
  crosses a policy.

:::recall
Q: Where do you change the native VLAN of port 12 on a FortiLink-managed switch?
A: On the FortiGate: config switch-controller managed-switch → the switch's serial → config ports → port12 → set vlan.
:::

units.title: From cable to working port
units.body:
1. **FortiLink interface**: a physical port or an aggregate (`set fortilink enable`), with an IP (often
   10.255.1.1/24) and a DHCP scope for the switches' management.
2. **Discovery**: the switch appears under `config switch-controller managed-switch`, keyed by **serial**, with
   `fsw-wan1-admin discovered`.
3. **Authorization**: `set fsw-wan1-admin enable`. Until then, the switch passes no user traffic.
4. **VLANs**: `config system interface` → `edit SCANNERS` → `set interface fortilink` → `set vlanid 60` → IP,
   DHCP server.
5. **Ports**: `config ports` → `edit port1` → `set vlan SCANNERS` (native), `set allowed-vlans` for trunks,
   `set status down` for unused ports, PoE and security policies per port.
6. **Policies**: between VLANs and to the Internet, like any other interface.

:::cli
execute switch-controller get-conn-status
:::

:::pitfall
A port with no VLAN set stays in the FortiLink native VLAN, usually the switch management network. "It gets an
IP but nothing works" often means "it got an address on the wrong network".
:::

units.title: Operations at scale
units.body:
- **Replacement (RMA)**: managed switches are keyed by serial. A new unit appears as a new, unauthorized switch;
  its port settings must move from the old serial (the FortiLink Guide documents a replace-device command for
  this).
- **Firmware**: the FortiGate can stage and push FortiSwitch firmware.
- **FortiManager FortiSwitch Manager** manages switch templates, VLANs and port profiles centrally for many
  FortiGates (pp. 970–1024), in the same ADOM workflow as policies.
- **QoS and PoE**: per-port PoE status and power, and QoS policies so voice keeps priority on uplinks
  (FortiSwitchOS pp. 355, 394).

:::ps
In a FortiLink rollout, label every switch with its serial and location before it leaves the box, and keep a
port map per switch. Authorization, RMA and troubleshooting all start from the serial.
:::

cards.back: The FortiGate discovers, authorizes and manages FortiSwitches; VLANs are FortiGate interfaces.

cards.front: Third-party switch between FortiGate and FortiSwitch in L2 FortiLink?
cards.back: Not supported. FortiLink over a layer-3 network is.

cards.front: How is a managed switch identified on the FortiGate?
cards.back: By serial number (config switch-controller managed-switch → edit <serial>).
set fsw-wan1-admin enable
config system interface → edit <name> → set interface fortilink → set vlanid <id> → IP.

cards.back: managed-switch → config ports → edit portN → set vlan <VLAN interface>.

shows up by serial as discovered, and I authorize it. Then I create VLANs as interfaces on the FortiLink

VLANs. Finally I test from a device on each VLAN."

modules.title: VDOMs and advanced HA

objectives.Design multi-VDOM deployments: global vs per-VDOM, management VDOM, VDOM types and resources

objectives: Connect VDOMs with inter-VDOM links and route/NAT between them
Delegate administration with VDOM-scoped admins
Combine HA with VDOMs (virtual clustering) and explain what fails over
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: VDOMs: multi-VDOM mode, global and per-VDOM resources, management VDOM, VDOM types, administrator roles (pp. 4284–4325)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: HA (pp. 4556–4813)

units.title: What a VDOM is
units.body:
In **multi-VDOM mode** a FortiGate runs several VDOMs that act as independent firewalls, each with its own routing
table, policies, objects, VPNs and logs. When you first enable it, the existing configuration moves into the
**root** VDOM, which can't be deleted (p. 4285).

| Global (outside any VDOM) | Per VDOM |
|---|---|
| Interfaces and their VDOM assignment, firmware, DNS, HA, admins, some logging | Policies, routes, addresses, VPNs, security profiles, SD-WAN |

- The **management VDOM** (root by default) sources management traffic: FortiGuard updates, logs to remote
  servers (p. 4285).
- VDOM **types**: Traffic (normal), Admin (management only, no transit traffic, at most one), LAN extension
  (p. 4286).
- **Resources**: by default no per-VDOM limits, so one tenant can starve the others; set maximums for sessions,
  policies and so on (p. 4285).

:::cli
config system global
    set vdom-mode multi-vdom
end
config vdom
    edit CUST-A
end
config global
    config system interface
        edit "port2"
            set vdom "CUST-A"
        next
    end
end
:::

:::recall
Q: Two tenants both use 192.168.10.0/24. Can one FortiGate serve both?
A: Yes, in separate VDOMs: each has its own routing table.
:::

units.title: Inter-VDOM links and delegated admins
units.body:
An **inter-VDOM link** (`config system vdom-link`) creates a pair of virtual interfaces, `<name>0` and
`<name>1`, that you assign to two VDOMs and address like a point-to-point link. Traffic crossing it is
inspected by **both** VDOMs' policies.

Common patterns:

- **Shared Internet**: root owns the WAN; tenant VDOMs route to root over links; tenants NAT to their link
  address, root NATs to the public IP (this is what makes overlapping tenant subnets work).
- **Segmentation**: separate VDOMs for OT and IT, joined by a link with tight policies.

## Administrators

- A **global** admin with the `super_admin` profile sees and changes everything (p. 4286).
- A **VDOM admin** is created in `config global` → `config system admin` with `set vdom <name>` and a profile
  such as prof_admin: full control inside that VDOM, nothing global.

:::pitfall
Debugging in multi-VDOM mode means choosing the context first: `get router info routing-table all` shows a
different table in each VDOM. Half of "it's not in the routing table" cases are the wrong VDOM.
:::

units.title: HA with VDOMs
units.body:
FGCP works the same with VDOMs: the cluster synchronizes global and every VDOM's configuration.

**Virtual clustering** splits the VDOMs into two **virtual clusters** (vcluster1, vcluster2) with different
primary units: VDOM A active on unit 1, VDOM B active on unit 2. Both units carry traffic, and each takes over the
other's VDOMs on failure. It's active-passive per VDOM, active-active per device.

Points to check in a design:

- Interface monitoring is per virtual cluster: a failed monitored port moves only that vcluster's VDOMs.
- Session pickup, heartbeat links and management access (an HA reserved management interface) apply as in a
  single-VDOM cluster.
- Firmware upgrades still upgrade the whole device.

:::ps
VDOMs are a tenancy and segmentation tool, not a licence to put everything on one box. Ask about failure domains:
one firmware bug or one bad global change affects every tenant on that device.
:::

scenarios.title: "Can we put the OT network in a VDOM on the office firewall?"
scenarios.situation: A manufacturer wants to save a firewall by putting the plant (OT) network in a VDOM on the office FortiGate.
scenarios.ask: What do you advise?
right_thinking: VDOMs give separate policies and routing
But a shared failure domain: firmware, global config, resource exhaustion, HA
Decide by risk: separate device for critical OT, or VDOM with resource limits and strict link policies
scenarios.what: A risk-based recommendation, not a yes/no.
scenarios.why: Senior PS engineers talk about failure domains.
scenarios.model_answer:
"A VDOM gives OT its own policies, routing and admins, and an inter-VDOM link with tight rules. But it shares the
box: a firmware issue, a global change or the office exhausting sessions affects the plant. If downtime in the
plant is expensive, I'd recommend a separate FortiGate for OT. If budget wins, a VDOM with resource limits,
separate admins and a change process that treats global changes as plant-impacting."
scenarios.best_way: Benefit, risk, mitigations, recommendation.

interview.question: How do you give two tenants Internet access from one FortiGate when their subnets overlap?
interview.model_answer:
"A VDOM per tenant and root for the Internet edge. Each tenant connects to root with an inter-VDOM link. The
tenant VDOM NATs its LAN to its link address, and root NATs the links to the public IP. Root never sees the
overlapping subnets, each tenant has its own policies and logs, and I give each tenant a VDOM-scoped admin."
interview.best_way: Pattern, NAT, admin.

modules.title: FortiOS administration: access, admins, firmware, backups and FortiGuard
objectives: Harden administrative access (allowaccess, trusted hosts, admin profiles, MFA)
Navigate the CLI config tree confidently (show, get, full-configuration, diff habits)
Back up, restore and upgrade firmware safely
Explain FortiGuard services and API access at a high level
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Getting started (pp. 32–146)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: System settings, administrators, profiles (pp. 4139–4330), configuration backups (p. 4530)

units.title: Who can manage the FortiGate, from where
units.body:
Administrative access has three layers, and all three must say yes:

1. **Interface `allowaccess`**: which management protocols the interface answers (ping, https, ssh, snmp,
   fgfm, fabric…). Remove HTTPS/SSH from Internet-facing interfaces unless you have a strong reason.
2. **Trusted hosts** on each admin account (`trusthost1`…): the source addresses that admin may log in from.
   FortiOS checks them before the password.
3. **Admin profile** (`accprofile`): what the admin may read or write. `super_admin` is everything;
   `prof_admin` is full access within its VDOM.

Add **MFA** (FortiToken) to admin accounts, and use remote authentication (RADIUS/TACACS+/SAML) with a vaulted
local break-glass account.

:::recall
Q: HTTPS is allowed on port1, but an admin from 200.1.1.1 can't even get the login page. What's the likely cause?
A: Trusted hosts: if no admin account trusts that source, FortiOS refuses the connection before showing the login.
:::

:::pitfall
Exposed management interfaces are a recurring entry point in exploited vulnerabilities. A firewall whose admin
GUI answers from the Internet is a finding in every audit.
:::

units.title: Reading and changing configuration safely
units.body:
| Command | Shows |
|---|---|
| `show <path>` | Only what differs from defaults |
| `show full-configuration <path>` | Everything, defaults included |
| `get <path>` | Current values in key: value form |
| `get system status` | Model, serial, firmware, VDOM mode, HA mode |

Editing habits that save outages:

- `config` / `edit` / `set` / `next` / `end`. Nothing is saved until `end` (or `next` for that entry).
- `append` adds to a list without retyping it; `set` replaces the whole list; `unset` returns to the default.
- `abort` leaves a config block without saving.
- Take a backup before the change: `execute backup config tftp|ftp|usb …` or from the GUI.

:::why
Q: Why use `append member DNS` instead of `set member HTTP HTTPS DNS` on a production service group?
A: set replaces the list: one typo and you remove services in use. append only adds.
:::

units.title: Firmware, backups and FortiGuard
units.body:
## Firmware

- Follow the **upgrade path** (Fortinet's upgrade tool lists the intermediate versions).
- Back up the configuration (and keep the old firmware image) first.
- In an HA cluster, the upgrade is staged (secondaries first) to keep traffic flowing.
- After: check `get system status`, logs, HA sync, VPNs and a few user flows.

## Backups and restore

A restore replaces the whole configuration and reboots. Encrypted backups need their password. Restoring a
backup from another model or firmware may need adjustments.

## FortiGuard

FortiGuard delivers the security intelligence behind the profiles: antivirus and IPS signatures, web and DNS
filter categories, application signatures, the Internet Service Database, and more. A FortiGate with expired
or unreachable FortiGuard keeps running but with stale protection.

## API

FortiOS has a REST API with token-based **API admins** (restricted by trusted hosts and profile), used by
automation tools and orchestration.

:::ps
Every PS change starts with "backup taken, version recorded" in the change record. It costs a minute and turns a
bad night into a 5-minute rollback.
:::

cards.back: Interface allowaccess, admin trusted hosts, admin profile.
Before the password: an untrusted source never gets the login.
super_admin: everything (global). prof_admin: full access within its VDOM.
show: only non-default settings. full-configuration: everything.

cards.front: set vs append on a list attribute
cards.back: set replaces the list; append adds to it.

cards.front: Leave a config block without saving
cards.back: abort

cards.front: First command on an unknown FortiGate
cards.back: get system status
Check the upgrade path, back up config, keep the old image, plan tests.
Signatures and ratings: AV, IPS, web/DNS categories, application control, ISDB…

scenarios.title: The GUI on the Internet
scenarios.situation:
During a health check you find HTTPS management open on a customer's WAN interface, with the default admin
account and no trusted hosts.
scenarios.ask: What do you tell the customer, and what do you change?
right_thinking: Flag it as critical, calmly
Remove HTTPS/SSH from WAN, add trusted hosts, MFA, rename/disable default admin
Check logs for logins from unknown sources
scenarios.what: Immediate risk reduction and a check for compromise.
scenarios.why: Exposed management is a top entry point.
scenarios.model_answer:
"The firewall's management page is reachable from the Internet with the default account, which is one of the
most common ways attackers get in. I'd remove HTTPS and SSH from the WAN today, restrict admins to the
management subnet with trusted hosts, add MFA, and check the event logs for logins from unknown addresses, so
we know it wasn't already used."
scenarios.best_way: Risk, fix, verify.

interview.question: How do you harden administrative access on a FortiGate?
interview.model_answer:
"Expose management only on internal or dedicated interfaces with allowaccess, restrict each admin with trusted
hosts, use named accounts with least-privilege profiles and MFA, ideally through RADIUS or SAML with a vaulted
local break-glass account, and send admin login events to FortiAnalyzer or the SIEM with alerts."
interview.best_way: Four layers, in order.

modules.title: Interfaces and network services: VLANs, aggregates, zones, DHCP and DNS
objectives: Choose between physical, VLAN, aggregate, redundant, loopback and zone interfaces
Configure DHCP servers (ranges, options, reservations) and relay
Configure the FortiGate's own DNS and DNS service on interfaces
Troubleshoot addressing problems from the client side
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Network: interfaces, VLANs, aggregates, zones (pp. 236–404)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: DNS (p. 405+), DHCP (p. 607+)

units.title: Interface types
units.body:
| Type | Use |
|---|---|
| Physical | A port |
| **VLAN** | 802.1Q sub-interface on a physical or aggregate interface (`set interface port2`, `set vlanid 20`) |
| **Aggregate** | LACP bundle of ports to a switch: more bandwidth, link redundancy |
| **Redundant** | Active/standby ports without LACP |
| **Loopback** | Always up: router IDs, BGP peering, management IPs |
| **Zone** | Groups interfaces so one policy covers them all |
| Tunnel | Created by IPsec phase1-interface |

## Zones

Policies can reference a zone instead of each interface. Traffic **between** interfaces in the same zone is
blocked by default (`intrazone deny`); set `intrazone allow` or write intra-zone policies.

:::recall
Q: VLAN 10 and VLAN 20 are in the same zone LAN-ZONE. A PC in VLAN 10 can't reach VLAN 20. Why?
A: Intra-zone traffic is denied by default: set intrazone allow on the zone or add a policy.
:::

units.title: DHCP
units.body:
DHCP is DORA: **D**iscover (broadcast), **O**ffer, **R**equest, **A**ck. A FortiGate interface can be a DHCP server
(per interface) or a **relay** to a central server (`set dhcp-relay-service enable` and the server IP on the
interface).

:::cli
config system dhcp server
    edit 2
        set interface "SCANNERS"
        set default-gateway 10.20.60.1
        set netmask 255.255.255.0
        set dns-service specify
        set dns-server1 8.8.8.8
        config ip-range
            edit 1
                set start-ip 10.20.60.100
                set end-ip 10.20.60.199
            next
        end
    next
end
:::

- `dns-service`: `default` (the FortiGate's system DNS), `local` (the interface IP: the FortiGate as DNS
  server), `specify` (explicit servers).
- Reservations (`config reserved-address`) pin an IP to a MAC.
- Options (e.g. 66/67 for PXE, 150 for phones) go under `config options`.

:::pitfall
A Windows PC with 169.254.x.x got no DHCP answer at all: no server on that VLAN, a wrong VLAN on the switch port,
or a full scope. A PC with an address in the **wrong** subnet is in the wrong VLAN.
:::

units.title: DNS on and through the FortiGate
units.body:
- **System DNS** (`config system dns`): what the FortiGate itself uses for FortiGuard, FQDN addresses, updates.
- **DNS service on an interface** (`config system dns-server`): the FortiGate answers DNS for clients, either
  forwarding (recursive) or from its own DNS database (split DNS for internal names).
- FQDN addresses in policies depend on the FortiGate resolving the same answers the clients get. A mismatch
  (different DNS servers, CDN answers) makes FQDN policies miss.

:::ps
In a cutover, write down for each VLAN: gateway, DHCP range, DNS servers handed out, and reservations. Most
Monday-morning tickets after a firewall migration are DHCP or DNS details.
:::

cards.back: set interface <parent>, set vlanid <id>, IP.
Aggregate: LACP, all members active. Redundant: one active member, no LACP.
Always up: router IDs, BGP peering, management.
Denied (intrazone deny).
Discover, Offer, Request, Ack.

cards.front: dns-service options in a DHCP server
cards.back: default (system DNS), local (interface IP), specify (explicit).
No DHCP answer (APIPA).
System DNS: what the FortiGate uses. dns-server: the FortiGate answering clients on an interface.

quiz.explanation: DORA.

scenarios.title: "Half the floor has no network after the migration"
scenarios.situation:
After migrating to a new FortiGate, PCs on floor 3 show 169.254.x.x. Floor 2 is fine. Both floors are VLANs on
the same aggregate.
scenarios.ask: How do you narrow it down?
right_thinking: APIPA = no DHCP answer
Check the VLAN interface exists with the right VLAN ID, and a DHCP server on it
Check the switch tags that VLAN on the aggregate
scenarios.what: A quick split between FortiGate config and switch config.
scenarios.why: Migrations often miss one VLAN or one tag.
scenarios.model_answer:
"169.254 means no DHCP answer, so the broadcast isn't reaching a DHCP server. I'd check that floor 3's VLAN
interface exists with the right ID and has a DHCP server, then that the switch tags that VLAN on the aggregate
to the new FortiGate. A sniffer on the VLAN interface for UDP 67 tells me in seconds which side it is."
scenarios.best_way: Symptom, both sides, one test.

interview.question: When would you use a zone on a FortiGate?
interview.model_answer:
"To group interfaces that share policies, like several user VLANs or two ISP links in older designs, so one
policy covers them. The caveat is that traffic between members of the same zone is denied by default, so I
either allow intra-zone traffic deliberately or write policies for it."
interview.best_way: Use, then the intra-zone default.

modules.title: WAN, overlays and SD-WAN concepts
objectives: Compare MPLS, Internet and LTE/5G transports for branch connectivity
Explain overlays (IPsec, GRE, VXLAN) and why SD-WAN runs on top of them
Explain SLA probes, steering modes and ADVPN shortcuts
Design a hub-and-spoke overlay with dynamic routing
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: SD-WAN overview and SD-WAN chapter (pp. 1155–1833), ADVPN (p. 3626), Overlay Orchestrator (p. 3669)
Protocol knowledge: IPsec (RFC 4301), GRE (RFC 2784), VXLAN (RFC 7348)

units.title: Transports and overlays
units.body:
| Transport | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| **MPLS** L3VPN | Carrier SLA, low jitter, private | Cost, slow to provision, one carrier |
| **Broadband / fiber Internet** | Cheap, fast, everywhere | Best effort, shared |
| **LTE / 5G** | Quick to deploy, diverse path | Data caps, variable latency |

An **overlay** is a logical network built over the transport:

- **IPsec**: encryption and authentication; the default for SD-WAN over the Internet.
- **GRE**: simple encapsulation, no encryption (often inside IPsec for multicast or routing protocols).
- **VXLAN**: layer-2 over layer-3 (stretches a LAN segment), can run inside IPsec.

The overlay gives every site a consistent private network regardless of which ISP carries it, and lets routing
protocols (BGP) run between sites.

:::recall
Q: Why run BGP over IPsec tunnels instead of over the raw Internet?
A: The tunnels make a private, encrypted network between sites; BGP inside them advertises private subnets that the Internet can't carry.
:::

units.title: How SD-WAN decides
units.body:
SD-WAN treats several links (physical or overlay tunnels) as one logical WAN and picks a link **per session**:

1. **Health checks** (SLA probes) measure latency, jitter and packet loss to a target through each member.
2. **Rules** (services) match traffic (destination, application, user…) and choose a member by a strategy:
   manual order, best quality (lowest latency/jitter/loss), lowest cost that meets an SLA, or load balancing.
3. When a member breaks its SLA, **new sessions** move; existing sessions usually stay unless configured to
   move.

On FortiOS, SD-WAN rules sit before the routing table (they're policy routes), and dead members are removed from
routing (p. 1155+).

:::why
Q: Why probe a server at HQ through each tunnel rather than 8.8.8.8 through each ISP?
A: It measures the path the application really uses, tunnel and far-end included.
:::

units.title: Hub-and-spoke and ADVPN
units.body:
With many branches, a full mesh of static tunnels doesn't scale. The usual design:

- **Hub-and-spoke**: each spoke has one tunnel per transport to each hub; hubs use dial-up (dynamic) phase 1 so
  spokes can be added without hub changes.
- **BGP over the overlay**: spokes peer with the hubs (often iBGP with the hub as route reflector, using
  neighbor ranges), advertise their LANs and learn everything else.
- **ADVPN** (Auto-Discovery VPN): when spoke A sends traffic to spoke B through the hub, the hub tells both
  spokes about each other and they build a **shortcut** tunnel directly. Traffic then goes spoke to spoke, and
  the shortcut is torn down when idle (p. 3626).
- FortiOS 8.0's **Fabric Overlay Orchestrator** automates building such overlays from the Security Fabric
  (p. 3669); FortiManager's SD-WAN overlay templates do it from central management.

:::ps
In design workshops, ask about traffic patterns first: if 90 % goes to the data center and SaaS, ADVPN shortcuts
matter less than good hub capacity and local breakout. Voice and video between branches is where shortcuts pay.
:::

cards.back: MPLS: SLA, low jitter, private. Internet: cheap, fast, everywhere.
GRE: encapsulation, no encryption (carries multicast). IPsec: encryption and authentication.
Layer-2 over layer-3 encapsulation (UDP), stretches LAN segments.
Latency, jitter and packet loss through each member.

cards.front: When a member breaks SLA, what moves?
cards.back: New sessions; existing ones usually stay.
Rules are checked first (policy routes).
Spoke-to-spoke shortcut tunnels built on demand after traffic flows through the hub.
New spokes can join without changing the hub.

quiz.stem: Which overlay encrypts traffic by default?
quiz.explanation: IPsec provides confidentiality and integrity.

quiz.stem: With ADVPN, how does spoke A first reach spoke B?

options.text: Through the hub, then a shortcut is built
Directly from the start, through a static tunnel

quiz.explanation: First packets via hub, then shortcut.

quiz.stem: What does an SD-WAN SLA usually include? Select all that apply.
quiz.explanation: Link quality metrics.

quiz.stem: Protocol most often run inside the overlay to exchange branch routes (three letters)?
quiz.explanation: iBGP with route reflection on the hubs is the common design.

labs.title: Sketch a 40-branch overlay
labs.goal: Write the design decisions for 40 branches with fiber + LTE and two data centers.

worked.config:
# Transports: fiber (primary), LTE (backup) at each branch
# Overlay: per branch, 2 tunnels per DC (fiber, LTE) = 4 tunnels; DCs use dial-up phase1
# Routing: iBGP over tunnels, DC hubs as route reflectors, neighbor-range for spokes
# SD-WAN: zone overlay with all tunnels; health check to a DC server per tunnel
# Rules: voice → lowest latency meeting SLA; ERP → DC1 preferred; SaaS → local breakout
# ADVPN: enabled for branch-to-branch voice/video
# Management: FortiManager SD-WAN and overlay templates; FortiAnalyzer SD-WAN monitoring
notes: Plan IP addressing for tunnel interfaces and loopbacks up front.
Document how a new branch is added in under an hour.

solo.prompt: Write the three measurements an SD-WAN SLA uses, one per line.
solo.solution:
latency
jitter
packet loss
solo.notes: Per member, per health check.

scenarios.title: "Do we still need MPLS?"
scenarios.situation: A logistics customer with 25 branches pays for MPLS and wants to know if SD-WAN over Internet can replace it.
scenarios.ask: How do you answer?
right_thinking: Ask about applications and their sensitivity (voice, ERP, video)
Dual Internet links with SD-WAN often match MPLS for most sites
Propose a pilot with measurements; keep MPLS where SLAs are critical during transition
scenarios.what: A data-driven recommendation.
scenarios.why: Customers trust measured pilots over vendor claims.
scenarios.model_answer:
"Often yes, but it depends on your applications. Two diverse Internet links per branch under SD-WAN, with
health checks steering voice and ERP to the best link, usually matches MPLS for most sites at lower cost. I'd
pilot five branches for a month, measure latency, jitter and loss per application, and decide site by site,
keeping MPLS where the numbers say so."
scenarios.best_way: Depends, pilot, measure, decide.

interview.question: Explain ADVPN to a customer.
interview.model_answer:
"In hub-and-spoke, branch-to-branch traffic goes through the hub, adding latency. With ADVPN, the first packets
still go through the hub, but the hub tells the two branches about each other and they build a direct tunnel on
demand. Voice between two branches then takes the short path, without configuring a full mesh."
interview.best_way: Problem first.

modules.title: FortiSIEM architecture, licensing and the CMDB
objectives: Describe Supervisor, Worker, Collector and Manager roles and when you add each
Explain how FortiSIEM is licensed (devices, agents, EPS) and what "Unmanaged" means
Explain multi-tenancy with Organizations
Get devices into the CMDB through discovery and log reception
sources: FortiSIEM 7.6.1 User Guide: Key concepts: clustering, licensing, multi-tenancy, discovery and CMDB (pp. 365–384)
FortiSIEM 7.6.1 User Guide: Setup (pp. 409–487), CMDB (pp. 857–898)

units.title: Nodes and scale
units.body:
FortiSIEM runs as one all-in-one **Supervisor** in small deployments, or as a cluster (pp. 365–366):

| Node | Role |
|---|---|
| **Supervisor** | GUI, application server, configuration database; master of the analysis tasks |
| **Worker** | Heavy lifting: indexing, searching, rule correlation, baselines |
| **Collector** | Near the devices (remote sites, other networks): collects, parses, compresses, sends to Workers over HTTPS |
| **Manager** | Separately licensed: monitors several FortiSIEM instances and their incidents |

Event storage options: local disk (appliances, all-in-one), FortiSIEM's NoSQL database on NFS, or Elasticsearch
(p. 366). The guide also lists the five analysis tasks the cluster splits up: indexing, searching, streaming
correlation, the identity and location database, and baselines.

:::recall
Q: A customer has 12 branches behind firewalls and one data center. Where do Collectors go?
A: At the branches (or per network segment) so devices send to a local Collector, which forwards compressed, parsed data to the Workers over HTTPS.
:::

units.title: Licensing and tenants
units.body:
FortiSIEM is licensed by (p. 367):

- **number of devices** it monitors or receives logs from,
- **number of Windows and Linux agents** (collectors),
- aggregate **events per second (EPS)**.

Not by storage. The CMDB can hold unlimited devices, but only the licensed number are **Managed**; the rest are
tagged **Unmanaged**. EPS is measured over 3-minute intervals; unused EPS accumulates and can be used for bursts
during attacks (p. 367).

**Multi-tenancy** (Service Provider install): **Organizations** separate devices, users and logs at the
application layer. A device belongs to an Organization through its Collector, or by IP ranges assigned to the
Organization (p. 368).

:::pitfall
Sizing on "how many firewalls" alone misses EPS: one busy FortiGate with traffic logging on every policy can
produce more EPS than 200 servers. Estimate EPS per source type before quoting.
:::

units.title: Getting data in and the CMDB
units.body:
Devices enter the CMDB two ways:

1. **Discovery**: FortiSIEM logs in with credentials (SNMP, WMI/WinRM, SSH, APIs) and builds device records:
   hardware, software, interfaces, running services, relationships.
2. **Log reception**: a device that starts sending syslog (a FortiGate, a switch) is recognized from its log
   format and added.

Windows and Linux servers usually use **agents** (host collectors), which ship event logs reliably and add file
integrity and process data.

The CMDB gives incidents context: which business service a host belongs to, who owns it, whether it's a domain
controller. Rules and reports can use CMDB groups ("all domain controllers").

:::cli
config log syslogd setting
    set status enable
    set server 10.20.40.50
end
:::

:::ps
In a SIEM project, onboarding is 70 % of the work: list every source, its method (syslog, agent, API), the
expected EPS and an owner, and track it like a migration. Rules are useless on data that never arrived.
:::

cards.back: Supervisor, Worker, Collector (and the separately licensed Manager).
Collects from nearby devices, parses, compresses, sends to Workers over HTTPS.
Local disk, FortiSIEM NoSQL on NFS, Elasticsearch.
Devices, Windows/Linux agents, EPS. Not storage.
In the CMDB but beyond the device licence: not monitored/collected.
Multi-tenancy: logical separation of devices, users and logs; assigned via Collector or IP range.

cards.front: Two ways devices enter the CMDB
cards.back: Discovery with credentials; recognition from received logs.
Reliable event shipping plus host data (FIM, processes) without remote pulling.

interview.question: Explain FortiSIEM's architecture to a customer's IT manager.
interview.model_answer:

volume grows. Collectors sit close to devices, in branches or other networks, and send parsed, compressed data
securely to the Workers. You pay for devices, agents and events per second, not for storage."

modules.title: FortiSIEM ingestion: event types, attributes and parsers
objectives: Explain how raw logs become events with an event type and normalized attributes
Choose push (syslog) or pull (API, WMI, agents) per source
Diagnose why a source shows "unknown" events or isn't parsed
sources: FortiSIEM 7.6.1 User Guide: Device Support and event pulling (pp. 489–583)
FortiSIEM 7.6.1 User Guide: Key concepts: parsers and monitors (pp. 365–384)

units.title: From raw log to event
units.body:
Every received log goes through a **parser** chosen by its format and source. The parser produces an **event**:

- an **event type**, for example `Win-Security-4625` (failed logon) or a FortiGate IPS event type,
- **normalized attributes** with the same names across vendors: `srcIpAddr`, `destIpAddr`, `user`,
  `reptDevName` (the reporting device), `hostName`, and so on,
- the raw log, kept for evidence.

Because attributes are normalized, one rule ("N failed logons from one source") works for Windows, Linux and
VPN logins alike.

:::recall
Q: Why do correlation rules use srcIpAddr instead of each vendor's own field name?
A: Parsers normalize vendor fields into common attributes, so a single rule covers every source.
:::

units.title: Push and pull
units.body:
| Method | Examples | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Push** (device sends) | Syslog from FortiGate, switches, Linux | Simple; UDP can drop under load; check the device's source IP |
| **Pull** (FortiSIEM fetches) | Cloud APIs (Microsoft 365, AWS), WMI/WinRM, databases | Needs credentials and polling intervals |
| **Agent** | Windows and Linux agents | Reliable, adds host telemetry |

The Device Support section of the guide lists, per product, which method and which events are supported
(pp. 489–583).

:::pitfall
A FortiGate behind NAT or with a different egress IP than expected shows up as a new, unknown device, or its
logs land in the wrong Organization. Fix the source IP (`source-ip` in the syslog setting) rather than the SIEM.
:::

units.title: When parsing goes wrong
units.body:
Symptoms and causes:

- **Events arrive as "unknown"**: no parser recognized the format (custom app, changed log format). Write or adapt
  a parser, or switch the device to a supported format.
- **Attributes missing** (no `user` in VPN events): the parser version doesn't cover that message; update the
  parser or extend it.
- **Nothing arrives**: network path (firewall, route), wrong port/protocol, or the device sends to another IP.
- **Time is wrong**: device clock or time zone; correlation windows then miss events.

For custom sources, FortiSIEM parsers are written in its XML parser language and tested against sample logs
before deployment.

:::ps
Before writing a single rule, verify each source with a search: "show me the last 10 events from this device,
with srcIpAddr and user". If an attribute is empty there, every rule using it is blind.
:::

scenarios.title: The rule that never fires
scenarios.situation: A "VPN brute force" rule never fires, though the FortiGate logs hundreds of failed SSL VPN logins.
scenarios.ask: How do you troubleshoot?
right_thinking: Search the raw events: are they arriving?
Is the event type specific and is the user/srcIpAddr attribute populated?
Does the rule's filter match that event type and attributes?
scenarios.what: Find where the chain breaks.
scenarios.why: Rules depend on parsing.
scenarios.model_answer:
"I'd follow the data: search for events from the FortiGate in that time window. If they're there, check the event
type and whether srcIpAddr and user are filled. If the rule filters on an event type the parser doesn't produce, or
groups by an empty attribute, it never fires. Fix the parser or the rule, then replay a test."
scenarios.best_way: Data first, then rule.

interview.question: Logs from a new device arrive in FortiSIEM as unknown events. What do you do?
interview.model_answer:
"Unknown means no parser recognized them. First I check whether the device can send in a format FortiSIEM supports,
for example the vendor's standard syslog or CEF. If not, I write or adapt a parser and test it against sample
logs, then verify the attributes the rules need are populated."
interview.best_way: Format first, parser second.

modules.title: FortiSIEM rules, incidents and cases
objectives: Tune with exceptions instead of disabling rules
Move from incident to case and to response (remediation, ticketing, SOAR)
sources: FortiSIEM 7.6.1 User Guide: Rules (pp. 925–942), Incidents (pp. 1256–1311), Cases (pp. 1229–1255)
FortiSIEM 7.6.1 User Guide: Key concepts: rules and incidents, incident automation policy, remediation library (pp. 365–384)

units.title: Anatomy of a correlation rule
units.body:
A FortiSIEM rule watches the event stream and raises an **incident** when a pattern appears in a time window:

- **Sub-patterns**: filters on event type and attributes (e.g. `eventType = Win-Security-4625`).
- **Group by**: the entity the count is per (e.g. `srcIpAddr`, `user`, destination host).
- **Aggregate condition**: `COUNT(Matched Events) >= 5`.
- **Time window**: e.g. 600 seconds.
- **Relationships between sub-patterns**: "A followed by B" with the same user and source (failures then a
  success).
- **Incident attributes and severity**, which carry into the incident.

FortiSIEM ships hundreds of rules, mapped to MITRE ATT&CK techniques, and can import community **Sigma** rules
(pp. 925–942).

:::recall
Q: "Successful Logon After Multiple Failures" uses two sub-patterns. What links them?
A: The same user and source IP, with the success following the failures inside the time window.
:::

units.title: Triage
units.body:
For each incident, answer in order:

1. **What fired, how bad?** Rule, severity, count, first/last seen.
2. **Who and what?** Entities: source IP, user, host, destination; look them up in the CMDB (is it a domain
   controller? a scanner?).
3. **What happened around it?** Search all events for the entity in a window before and after: the incident is
   a pointer, the timeline is the story.
4. **Decision**: false positive (tune), benign true positive (document), or true positive (escalate, contain).

Incident views in FortiSIEM include risk-based views, MITRE ATT&CK mapping and UEBA anomalies (pp. 1256–1311).
Use **cases** to group related incidents, assign owners and keep the investigation record (pp. 1229–1255).

:::why
Q: Why search events around an incident instead of only reading its triggering events?
A: The rule only shows the pattern it matched; what the attacker did before and after (a service install, a new admin) is in other events.
:::

units.title: Tuning and response
units.body:
## Tuning

- Prefer **exceptions** (this source, this user, this host) over disabling a rule.
- Adjust **thresholds** with data: look at how often the pattern occurs normally.
- Record why, who asked, and a review date for every exception.

## Response

- **Incident automation policies** notify or act when incidents match conditions.
- The **remediation library** runs actions on devices (block an IP on a firewall, disable an account).
- External **ticketing** integrations open tickets; **FortiSOAR playbooks** orchestrate multi-step response
  (pp. 1005–1052).

:::ps
In the first month of a SIEM, plan weekly tuning sessions with the customer: list the top 10 noisiest rules,
decide exception, threshold or keep, and document it. That rhythm is what turns a SIEM into a SOC tool.
:::

scenarios.title: Alert fatigue
scenarios.situation: Three months after go-live, the SOC ignores FortiSIEM: 900 incidents a day, mostly the same five rules.
scenarios.ask: What's your plan?
right_thinking: Measure: top rules by volume and their true-positive rate
Tune with exceptions/thresholds; fix parsing gaps
Weekly tuning ritual with owners; measure again
scenarios.what: A data-driven tuning plan.
scenarios.why: A SIEM nobody reads is a compliance checkbox.
scenarios.model_answer:
"I'd start with data: incidents per rule over 30 days and how many were real. The top five noisy rules get
exceptions for known sources or better thresholds, and any that depend on bad parsing get fixed. Then a weekly
30-minute tuning session with the SOC lead. The target is fewer than 50 incidents a day, most of them worth
opening."
scenarios.best_way: Measure, tune, repeat.

interview.question: How do you reduce false positives in a SIEM without missing real attacks?
interview.model_answer:
"I measure which rules create the noise, then narrow them with exceptions for specific known sources or adjust
thresholds based on real baselines, never by disabling the rule. Every exception has an owner, a reason and a
review date, and I review true-positive rates monthly."
interview.best_way: Narrow, not silence.

modules.title: FortiSIEM analytics, ML, dashboards and automation
objectives: Build searches with filters, grouping and display columns to answer investigation questions
Explain baselines and machine-learning anomaly detection
Build dashboards and scheduled reports for operations and compliance
Connect incidents to playbooks and threat feeds
sources: FortiSIEM 7.6.1 User Guide: Analytics and advanced search (pp. 1312–1367), machine learning (p. 1368)
FortiSIEM 7.6.1 User Guide: Dashboards (p. 1413+), Reports (pp. 900–924), Playbooks (pp. 1005–1052)

units.title: Asking questions of the data
units.body:
An analytics search has three parts:

1. **Filters**: event type, attributes, time range (`srcIpAddr = 10.20.10.66`, last 24 hours).
2. **Display / group by**: which attributes to show, or counts per attribute ("top users by failed logons").
3. **Time**: real-time or historical.

Typical investigation searches:

| Question | Search |
|---|---|
| Everything this IP did | `srcIpAddr = X` in the incident window, sorted by time |
| Which accounts were tried? | event type = failed logon, group by `user` |
| Who talked to the C2? | `destIpAddr = <C2>`, group by `srcIpAddr` |

Saved searches become report templates and dashboard widgets.

:::recall
Q: How do you list every machine that contacted 185.220.101.47 yesterday?
A: Filter destIpAddr = 185.220.101.47, yesterday's time range, group by srcIpAddr.
:::

units.title: Baselines and machine learning
units.body:
Rules catch known patterns; **baselines** catch "unusual for this entity": a user logging in at 3 a.m. for the
first time, a server suddenly sending ten times its normal traffic.

FortiSIEM builds statistical profiles and offers **machine-learning** anomaly detection models; release 7.x added,
for example, a Gaussian model that flags values with a low occurrence probability (pp. 305, 1368). **UEBA**
focuses on user and entity behavior. Entity **risk scores** add up incidents per user or host so analysts see
who is most at risk.

:::pitfall
Anomaly detection needs a clean learning period: if the attacker was already active while the model learned,
their behavior is "normal". Combine ML with rules.
:::

units.title: Dashboards, reports and automation
units.body:
- **Dashboards** for operations: incidents by severity, top sources, data-collection health (sources that went
  silent are an incident in themselves).
- **Reports** scheduled for management and compliance (PCI, ISO 27001…), built from saved searches.
- **Threat feeds** (FortiGuard, STIX/TAXII, custom lists) enrich events and power rules like "traffic to a
  known malicious IP".
- **Playbooks** (FortiSOAR) automate response: enrich an IP, open a ticket, block on the FortiGate, disable an
  account, with human approval where needed.

:::ps
The most valuable dashboard in a new SIEM is "sources that stopped sending". A FortiGate that went quiet after a
change is a blind spot nobody notices until the incident review.
:::

cards.back: Filters, display/group-by, time range.

cards.back: Filter destIpAddr = IP, group by srcIpAddr.

modules.title: FortiEDR architecture and deployment
objectives: Describe Collector, Aggregator, Core, Central Manager, Threat Hunting Repository and the cloud service
Explain what each component exchanges with the Collector and what autonomous mode is
Plan a Collector rollout and verify connectivity
sources: FortiEDR 7.2.5 Admin Guide: Introducing FortiEDR (pp. 10–21)
FortiEDR 7.2.5 Admin Guide: Deploying FortiEDR, installing Collectors (pp. 22–76)

units.title: The components
units.body:
| Component | Job |
|---|---|
| **Collector** | Agent on each endpoint; collects OS metadata and enforces decisions |
| **Aggregator** | Receives Collector registration, health and security events; sends configuration (pp. 14, 28) |
| **Core** | Analyzes connection metadata to decide block/allow (when not autonomous); receives activity data for threat hunting and communication control (p. 14) |
| **Central Manager** | The console: policies, events, forensics, inventory |
| **Threat Hunting Repository** | Stores activity events for hunting |
| **FortiEDR Cloud Service (FCS)** | Cloud classification and verdicts that drive playbooks (p. 17) |

In the SaaS model, everything except the Collectors runs in Fortinet's cloud; on-premises deployments use the
separate On-Premise Deployment Guide (p. 25).

:::recall
Q: Which component does a new Collector register with?
A: The Aggregator, over SSL (port 8081 is the Aggregator port asked for during installation).
:::

units.title: How protection works
units.body:
FortiEDR focuses on what malware must **do** to cause damage: connect out, encrypt, exfiltrate, tamper. The
Collector intercepts these actions (for example a connection establishment request), checks them locally and/or
with the Core, and blocks or allows (pp. 16–17).

- If all Cores are unreachable, the Collector switches to **autonomous mode** after about a minute and keeps
  protecting with local analysis (p. 14).
- Policies start in a mode that **logs** out of the box; you choose when to move each to prevention (p. 18).

:::why
Q: Why does FortiEDR still protect a laptop on a hotel Wi-Fi with no path to the Core?
A: The Collector falls back to autonomous mode and analyzes locally.
:::

units.title: Rolling out Collectors
units.body:
1. Prepare: registration password, Aggregator address and port 8081, installer per OS; check exclusions needed
   by other security software.
2. Open the network: Collectors → Aggregator (8081) and → Core; through every firewall on the path, including
   branch FortiGates and VPNs.
3. Pilot a group, review events in simulation, add exceptions.
4. Deploy in waves with your software distribution tool; watch **Inventory** for Disconnected or Degraded
   collectors.
5. Move policies to prevention per group once noise is handled.

:::pitfall
A Collector that can't reach the Aggregator looks fine to the user and sends nothing to the console. Alert on
disconnected collectors from day one.
:::

cards.back: Endpoint agent: collects OS metadata, enforces decisions.
Collector registration, health and security events; sends configuration. Port 8081.
Analyzes connection metadata for block/allow; gets activity data for hunting and communication control.
Collector analyzes locally when no Core is reachable (after about a minute).
Stop the malicious actions (connect, encrypt, exfiltrate), not just recognize files.
Prepare → open network → pilot in simulation → waves → prevention per group.

labs.title: Collector rollout checklist
labs.goal: Write the rollout checklist for 600 endpoints in two sites.

worked.config:
# Network: allow endpoints → Aggregator TCP 8081 and → Core on every FortiGate in the path (HQ, branch, VPN)
# Pilot:   IT + 20 users per department, simulation mode, 2 weeks
# Review:  events daily; exceptions for business apps; document each
# Waves:   100 endpoints/day via software distribution; Inventory check after each wave
# Monitor: alert on Disconnected/Degraded collectors
# Enforce: prevention per group after 2 clean weeks
notes: Servers last, with app owners present.

scenarios.title: Half the branch is missing
scenarios.situation:
After deploying Collectors to the Cali branch, only 3 of 40 appear as Running; the rest are Disconnected. HQ is
fine.
scenarios.ask: What do you check?
right_thinking: Path from branch to Aggregator: VPN selectors, routes, FortiGate policy for 8081
The 3 that work: are they on a different VLAN or VPN?
Test with tnc to the Aggregator port from a branch PC
scenarios.what: A network-path fix, verified.
scenarios.why: EDR rollout problems are usually network problems.
scenarios.model_answer:
"If HQ is fine and the branch isn't, it's the path. I'd test from a branch PC to the Aggregator on 8081, then
check the branch FortiGate policy and the VPN selectors for that traffic. The 3 working collectors probably sit in
a VLAN already covered. Fix the policy, then watch Inventory turn Running."
scenarios.best_way: Compare, test, fix, verify.

interview.question: Walk me through FortiEDR's architecture.
interview.model_answer:
"Collectors on endpoints register with the Aggregator, which handles health, events and configuration. The Core
analyzes connection metadata and gets activity data for threat hunting. The Central Manager is the console, the
Threat Hunting Repository stores activity, and the cloud service gives classifications. If the Core is
unreachable, collectors keep protecting in autonomous mode."
interview.best_way: Follow the data.

modules.title: FortiEDR security policies, exceptions and exclusions
objectives: Explain the security policies (execution, exfiltration, ransomware, device control) and their rules
Choose simulation vs prevention per policy and collector group
Handle false positives with narrow exceptions instead of weakening policies
sources: FortiEDR 7.2.5 Admin Guide: Profiles and security policies (pp. 203–263), Exception Manager (p. 213)
FortiEDR 7.2.5 Admin Guide: Event Viewer action values (p. 92)

units.title: The policies
units.body:
| Policy | Stops |
|---|---|
| **Execution Prevention** | Malicious files and unconfirmed executables from running |
| **Exfiltration Prevention** | Malicious outbound connection establishment |
| **Ransomware Prevention** | Malware that blocks users from their own systems/files (encryption) |
| **Device Control** | USB and other external devices |

(p. 204). Each policy has **rules** (e.g. "File Encryptor" under Ransomware Prevention) that can be enabled
individually, and policies are assigned to **collector groups**.

:::recall
Q: A payload encrypts files on a share and calls home. Which two policies apply?
A: Ransomware Prevention (the encryption) and Exfiltration Prevention (the outbound connection).
:::

units.title: Simulation vs prevention
units.body:
- **Simulation**: FortiEDR detects and reports what it **would** have blocked. In the Event Viewer the action
  reads "Simulated Block": the policy was in simulation, so the attempt was not blocked (p. 92).
- **Prevention**: matching actions are blocked.

Out of the box, policies log; you move groups to prevention once you've reviewed the events and added exceptions
(p. 18). Do it per group: IT and pilot users first, servers last.

:::pitfall
Leaving policies in simulation for months is the most common EDR deployment failure: the dashboards fill with
"would have blocked" while nothing is blocked.
:::

units.title: Exceptions done right
units.body:
When a legitimate application triggers a rule:

1. Confirm it's legitimate: signer, path, parent process, hash reputation, the vendor's documentation.
2. Create an **exception** in the Exception Manager (p. 213) scoped as narrowly as possible: this process (path or
   hash), this rule, these groups or collectors.
3. Classify the event (Likely Safe / Safe) so the history is clear.
4. Never fix a false positive by switching the whole policy back to simulation.

Exclusions for other security products (and vice versa) are part of deployment hygiene, agreed with the other
vendors' guidance.

:::ps
Keep an exception register: event, process, rule, scope, who approved, review date. Auditors and the next
engineer will ask.
:::

cards.back: Execution, Exfiltration, Ransomware Prevention; Device Control.
File Encryptor.
Detects and reports what it would block (Simulated Block), blocks nothing.
Per group, after reviewing events and adding exceptions.
This process, this rule, these groups/collectors.

cards.front: Wrong fix for a false positive
cards.back: Switching the whole policy to simulation.

quiz.stem: The Event Viewer shows 'Simulated Block'. What happened?

options.text: The policy was in simulation; the action was not blocked
The action was blocked in a sandbox

quiz.explanation: Simulation reports, doesn't block.

quiz.stem: A signed vendor updater is blocked by 'Unconfirmed Executable' every night. Best fix?

quiz.explanation: Narrow exception.

options.text: That the vendor documents the behavior

quiz.explanation: Evidence that it's legitimate.

labs.title: From simulation to prevention
labs.goal: Plan the move to prevention for a 3-group deployment.

worked.config:
# Week 1-2 all groups simulation; review events daily
# For each event: legit? → exception (process+rule+group) + classify Likely Safe; malicious? → incident
# Week 3 IT group → prevention (all four policies)
# Week 4 Office users → prevention
# Week 6 Servers → prevention after app-owner sign-off; maintenance window
# Ongoing: exception register reviewed monthly
notes: Keep a rollback: a group can return to simulation quickly if something critical breaks.
