scenarios.title: "Turn it off, it's blocking production"
scenarios.situation:
At 7 a.m. the plant manager calls: FortiEDR blocks the label-printing app on all packing stations. He wants
FortiEDR uninstalled.
scenarios.ask: What do you do?
right_thinking: Restore production fast with a narrow exception (or that group to simulation temporarily)
Verify the app is legitimate
Follow up: root cause, permanent exception, communication
scenarios.what: Production restored in minutes without losing protection elsewhere.
scenarios.why: Speed and precision keep the customer trusting the tool.
scenarios.model_answer:
"I'd open the event, confirm the label app's signer and path, and create an exception for that process and rule
on the packing group. That restores printing in minutes. If I can't confirm quickly, I'd put only the packing
group in simulation for the day. Then I explain what happened and make the exception permanent after the vendor
confirms the behavior."
scenarios.best_way: Narrow and fast, then verify.

interview.question: How do you handle EDR false positives?
interview.model_answer:
"I verify the process is legitimate: signer, path, parent, hash reputation, vendor docs. Then I create the
narrowest exception, that process and that rule, for the affected group, classify the event as likely safe, and
record it with an owner and a review date. I never put a policy back into simulation to silence one app."
interview.best_way: Evidence, then narrow.

modules.title: FortiEDR incidents, forensics and threat hunting
objectives: Triage security events by classification and action
Use the investigation view and flow analyzer to reconstruct the attack chain
Remediate (kill, delete, registry) and isolate devices
Hunt for other affected hosts
sources: FortiEDR 7.2.5 Admin Guide: Incidents and Event Viewer (pp. 87–127), classifications (p. 91), isolating a device (p. 104)
FortiEDR 7.2.5 Admin Guide: Forensics and threat hunting (pp. 128–173)

units.title: Reading an event
units.body:
Each security event carries:

- **Classification** (p. 91): Malicious, Suspicious, PUP, Inconclusive, Likely Safe, Safe.
- **Action**: Blocked, Simulated Block (policy in simulation), Log, Post Detection…
- Device, process, path, hash, signer, policy and rule, destinations.

Triage order: Malicious first, then Suspicious; anything blocked still deserves a look at **how it got there**.

:::recall
Q: An event says Malicious, Simulated Block. Is the host clean?
A: No: the policy was in simulation, so the action ran. Investigate and remediate.
:::

units.title: Investigation and flow analyzer
units.body:
The **investigation view** and **flow analyzer** show the process chain: who started what, with command lines,
files written and network destinations (pp. 94–127). From it you answer:

1. **Entry**: which parent launched the payload (OUTLOOK.EXE → attachment, browser → download, a service →
   lateral movement)?
2. **Behavior**: encryption, injection, persistence, credential access?
3. **Communication**: which IPs/domains (C2) did it contact?

Then **hunt**: search the Threat Hunting Repository for the hash, the file name, the C2 destination across all
collectors (pp. 128–173).

:::why
Q: Why hunt for the hash and the C2 IP after remediating one host?
A: Campaigns hit many users; other hosts may have run it without triggering the same rule.
:::

units.title: Containment and remediation
units.body:
- **Isolate the device** (p. 104): blocked from communicating with the outside world, sending and receiving,
  while staying connected to FortiEDR for investigation and remediation.
- **Remediate**: terminate the process, delete the file, clean registry persistence.
- **Network**: block the C2 on the FortiGate (address + deny, or a threat feed), so hosts without a collector are
  covered too.
- **Identity**: if credentials may be stolen, reset them.
- Release isolation only after the host is clean (or reimaged).

:::ps
Write the incident summary as you go: entry vector, affected hosts, C2, actions taken with times. The customer's
management and insurer will ask for exactly that.
:::

cards.back: Malicious, Suspicious, PUP, Inconclusive, Likely Safe, Safe.
The malicious action ran: investigate and remediate.

cards.front: Three questions for the flow analyzer
cards.back: Entry, behavior, communication.
The hash, file name and C2 across all collectors.
Device can't communicate with the outside, but stays connected to FortiEDR.
Terminate process, delete file, clean registry.

scenarios.title: Ransomware in simulation mode
scenarios.situation:
FortiEDR shows a Malicious File Encryptor event on a finance PC, action Simulated Block. Files on a share are
being renamed.
scenarios.ask: Your next five minutes.
right_thinking: Isolate the PC now
Kill/delete via remediation
Check the share, block C2, switch ransomware policy to prevention
scenarios.what: Containment first, then the rest.
scenarios.why: Minutes matter with encryption.
scenarios.model_answer:
"Isolate the PC immediately from FortiEDR so the encryption stops reaching the share, then kill the process and
delete the file. Block the C2 on the FortiGate and switch Ransomware Prevention to prevention for everyone. Then
I tell the file-server team which folder to restore and start the investigation and hunt."
scenarios.best_way: Contain first.

interview.question: An EDR flags ransomware on a laptop. What do you do?
interview.model_answer:
"Isolate the device so it can't reach shares or its C2, kill the process and quarantine the file. Then I read the
process chain for the entry point and the C2, hunt for the same hash and destination on other hosts, block the
C2 at the firewall, reset credentials if needed, restore affected files and reimage. Finally, if policies were in
simulation, move them to prevention."
interview.best_way: The IR lifecycle, concretely.

modules.title: FortiEDR communication control, playbooks and Fabric integration
objectives: Use communication control to manage which applications may talk to the network
Configure playbooks for automatic notification and remediation
Integrate FortiEDR with FortiGate, FortiAnalyzer/FortiSIEM and other tools
Explain multi-tenancy for MSSP deployments
sources: FortiEDR 7.2.5 Admin Guide: Communication control and host firewall (pp. 174–202)
FortiEDR 7.2.5 Admin Guide: Integrations (pp. 264–313), Playbooks (pp. 314–321), Multi-tenancy (pp. 422–451)

units.title: Communication control
units.body:
**Communication control** lists the applications that communicate on your endpoints, with reputation and
vulnerability information, and lets you allow or deny them per policy (pp. 174–202). Uses:

- Block outdated or vulnerable versions of applications from reaching the network.
- Deny unapproved remote-access tools or unknown communicating software.
- A **host firewall** controls traffic on the endpoint itself.

:::recall
Q: How do you stop an old, vulnerable version of a remote-access tool from connecting out on every endpoint?
A: Communication control: deny that application/version in the policy.
:::

units.title: Playbooks
units.body:
**Playbooks** define automatic actions per event classification (pp. 314–321): notify (email, syslog, ticket),
investigate, remediate (terminate, delete, clean persistence), isolate the device, or trigger integrations. Their
remediation actions rely on the **FCS** final determination (p. 17).

Typical policy:

| Classification | Actions |
|---|---|
| Malicious | Notify, isolate, remediate, block on firewall |
| Suspicious | Notify, open ticket |
| PUP | Notify, ticket to IT |
| Likely Safe | No automatic action; review |

:::pitfall
Automatic isolation on servers can take a business service down on a false positive. Use separate playbooks per
collector group and require approval for servers.
:::

units.title: Fabric and multi-tenancy
units.body:
**Integrations** (pp. 264–313) connect FortiEDR to other tools so an endpoint verdict becomes a network action:

- **FortiGate**: block the malicious IP or quarantine the host at the network.
- **FortiAnalyzer / FortiSIEM**: send events for correlation with firewall, identity and server logs.
- **FortiSandbox**, threat intelligence and ticketing tools.

**Multi-tenancy** (pp. 422–451): an MSSP runs one FortiEDR with **organizations** per customer, each with its own
collectors, policies and administrators.

:::ps
The integration story sells the Fabric: "the laptop was isolated by FortiEDR, the C2 was blocked on every
FortiGate, and FortiSIEM correlated it with the VPN login an hour earlier". Design the integrations in the HLD, not
as an afterthought.
:::

cards.back: Lists communicating applications with reputation/vulnerabilities; allow or deny per policy.
Event classification (FCS final determination).
Notify, investigate, remediate, isolate, trigger integrations.
Servers: separate playbook, approval required.
Endpoint verdict → block IP or quarantine host on the firewall.
Organizations per customer with own collectors, policies, admins.

quiz.stem: You want unapproved remote-access tools unable to connect out from endpoints. Which feature?
quiz.explanation: Communication control governs applications' network access.

quiz.explanation: Contain, clean, tell.

quiz.stem: An MSSP wants each customer's admins to see only their own endpoints. FortiEDR feature?
quiz.explanation: Organizations.

solo.notes: Plus ticketing and threat intelligence.

scenarios.title: Auto-isolation took down the ERP
scenarios.situation: A playbook auto-isolated the ERP server after a Suspicious event that turned out to be a backup agent.
scenarios.ask: What do you change?
right_thinking: Separate playbooks for servers; no auto-isolation on Suspicious
Exception for the backup agent
Approval step for server isolation
scenarios.what: A safer automation design.
scenarios.why: Automation must match business impact.
scenarios.model_answer:
"Automatic isolation should only fire on Malicious, and never automatically on critical servers. I'd split the
ERP and other servers into their own group with a playbook that notifies and waits for approval before isolating,
add an exception for the backup agent after verifying it, and review the other playbooks the same way."
scenarios.best_way: Match automation to impact.

interview.question: How does FortiEDR fit into the Fortinet Security Fabric?
interview.model_answer:
"FortiEDR detects and stops malicious actions on the endpoint, then shares that: events to FortiAnalyzer or
FortiSIEM for correlation, and actions to FortiGate to block the C2 or quarantine the host on the network. With
playbooks the whole chain can run in seconds, with approval where impact is high."
interview.best_way: Endpoint, then network, then SOC.

modules.title: FortiAnalyzer devices, log forwarding, fetching and HA
objectives: Add and authorize devices and check that logs arrive
Choose between forwarding and aggregation modes for log forwarding
Use log fetching for historical investigations
Explain FortiAnalyzer HA and its purpose
sources: FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Device Manager (pp. 95–111)
FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Log Forwarding (pp. 573–584), Log Fetching (p. 585), SIEM Collector (p. 534)

units.title: Devices and log arrival
units.body:
A FortiGate pointed at FortiAnalyzer (`config log fortianalyzer setting`) appears in **Device Manager** as
unauthorized; you authorize it into an ADOM, and only then are its logs stored and indexed (pp. 95–111).

Checks when logs don't arrive:

- On the FortiGate: `diagnose log test`, `get log fortianalyzer setting`, the source IP and route to the FAZ
  (`source-ip` matters over VPNs).
- On the FortiAnalyzer: device authorized? In the right ADOM? Disk quota not exhausted?

:::recall
Q: Logs from a branch FortiGate over IPsec never reach the FortiAnalyzer, though the HQ FortiGate's do. First suspect?
A: The source IP: logs leave from the WAN interface unless source-ip is set to an address covered by the tunnel.
:::

units.title: Forwarding and aggregation
units.body:
FortiAnalyzer can forward logs to another FortiAnalyzer, a syslog server or a CEF server, or through output
plugins to public cloud services, and always keeps its local copy (p. 573). Two modes:

| | Forwarding (default) | Aggregation |
|---|---|---|
| When | Real time (max ~5 min delay) | Once a day at a set time |
| To | FortiAnalyzer, syslog, CEF, plugins | FortiAnalyzer only |
| Configured | GUI or CLI, client side only | CLI; the server must accept |
| Filters | Device and log filters, field exclusion, masking | Device filter |

(pp. 573–574). Typical use: forward security logs in real time to a SIEM (FortiSIEM or a third-party SIEM via
syslog/CEF), aggregate daily to a central FortiAnalyzer for long retention.

:::pitfall
Forwarding everything to a third-party SIEM multiplies its licence cost. Use log filters on the forwarding rule
to send what the SIEM's use cases need.
:::

units.title: Fetching, HA and collector mode
units.body:
- **Log fetching** retrieves archived logs for a device and time period from one FortiAnalyzer to another, which
  indexes them for queries and reports: useful for forensics on old data. Both units must run the same firmware,
  and only one fetching session runs at a time between two units (p. 585).
- **Collector mode** FortiAnalyzers receive and forward logs (typically to an analyzer-mode FortiAnalyzer); the
  analyzer does the analytics.
- **HA**: a FortiAnalyzer cluster keeps logging available when a unit fails and synchronizes logs and
  configuration between members.

:::ps
For a regulated customer, write the log path end to end in the design: source → FortiAnalyzer (retention X
months) → SIEM (security subset) → archive (aggregation, Y years). Auditors ask exactly that.
:::

cards.back: The device is authorized in Device Manager (into an ADOM).

cards.front: Branch logs over VPN don't arrive: suspect
cards.back: Source IP (set source-ip so the tunnel carries them).
Forwarding (real time) and aggregation (daily, FAZ to FAZ only).
FortiAnalyzer, syslog, CEF, output plugins to cloud services.

cards.front: Does the forwarding FAZ keep its logs?
cards.back: Yes, it keeps a local copy.
Both FortiAnalyzers on the same firmware; one session at a time between two units.

quiz.stem: You need logs in a third-party SIEM within minutes. Which FortiAnalyzer mode?
quiz.explanation: Forwarding is near real time.

quiz.stem: Which are true of aggregation mode? Select all that apply.

options.text: Runs at a set time each day

quiz.explanation: Daily FAZ-to-FAZ.

quiz.stem: An investigator needs last year's logs that live on an archive FortiAnalyzer. Feature?
quiz.explanation: Fetch, index, query.

labs.title: The log path for a regulated customer
labs.goal: Design retention and forwarding for a bank branch network.

# FAZ-HQ → FortiSIEM: forwarding mode, filter: UTM, denies, VPN, admin events (security use cases)
# FAZ-HQ → FAZ-ARCHIVE: aggregation daily 02:00, 7 years
# Investigations on old data: log fetching from FAZ-ARCHIVE
# Branch FortiGates: source-ip = LAN IP so logs ride the IPsec tunnel
notes: Size disk quotas per ADOM from measured log rates.

solo.prompt: Name the three FortiAnalyzer features for moving logs, one per line: real-time out, daily FAZ-to-FAZ, historical retrieval.
solo.solution:
log forwarding (forwarding mode)
log forwarding (aggregation mode)
log fetching
solo.notes: The local copy stays on the client.

scenarios.title: The SIEM bill doubled
scenarios.situation: After enabling log forwarding from FortiAnalyzer to the customer's cloud SIEM, its monthly ingestion bill doubled.
scenarios.ask: What do you propose?
right_thinking: Identify which log types dominate (traffic accept logs)
Filter the forwarding rule to the SIEM's use cases; exclude fields
Keep full logs in FortiAnalyzer for investigations
scenarios.what: Lower cost without losing detections.
scenarios.why: SIEM cost follows volume.
scenarios.model_answer:
"Most of that volume is likely accepted-traffic logs, which the SIEM's rules rarely use. I'd filter the
forwarding rule to UTM events, denies, VPN and admin events, exclude fields the SIEM doesn't need, and keep the
full logs in FortiAnalyzer, where storage is cheap and investigations can still reach them."
scenarios.best_way: Use cases decide what crosses.

interview.question: How would you send FortiGate logs to both FortiAnalyzer and a SIEM?
interview.model_answer:
"FortiGates log to FortiAnalyzer, which keeps everything for investigations and reports. FortiAnalyzer then
forwards a filtered subset to the SIEM in real time via syslog or CEF, so the SIEM gets what its rules need
without paying for every accepted session."
interview.best_way: One collection point, filtered forwarding.

modules.title: FortiAnalyzer reports, datasets and charts
objectives: Create and schedule reports per ADOM
Write a simple dataset query and troubleshoot empty reports
sources: FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Reports (pp. 465–515)

units.title: Building blocks
units.body:
| Block | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Dataset** | An SQL query over a log type (traffic, UTM, event…) |
| **Chart** | A table or graph built from a dataset |
| **Macro** | A single value from a dataset placed in text ("Total threats: 1,204") |
| **Template / layout** | Cover page, chapters, charts, macros, text |
| **Report** | A template run for a time period, devices and ADOM, on demand or scheduled |

The logs used are determined by the datasets in the charts and macros (p. 465). Predefined templates, charts and
macros cover common needs; you clone and adapt them. Reports are per **ADOM**, and Fabric ADOMs can use datasets
on the SIEM database (p. 466).

:::recall
Q: A report needs the number "1,204 threats blocked" inside a sentence. Which block?
A: A macro.
:::

units.title: Datasets
units.body:
A dataset is SQL with FortiAnalyzer's log-table macros, for example (simplified):

:::cli
select srcip, count(*) as sessions
from $log
where $filter and action='deny'
group by srcip
order by sessions desc
:::

- `$log` is the log table for the dataset's log type; `$filter` applies the report's time range and device
  filters.
- Test a dataset against a device and time range before using it in a chart.

:::pitfall
An empty report usually means: wrong ADOM, devices not selected, a time range with no logs, or a dataset over a
log type the devices don't send (no UTM logs because policies don't log them). Check in Log View first.
:::

units.title: Reports people read
units.body:
- **Schedule** recurring reports (weekly security summary, monthly compliance) and email them.
- Keep executive reports short: trends and a few numbers; keep detailed reports for operations.
- Generation can take long on large datasets; schedule outside peak hours. Reports aren't available while the SQL
  database rebuilds (p. 465).

:::ps
Deliver a "first-week report" at the end of every FortiGate project: top applications, top threats blocked,
top users by bandwidth. It proves value in the customer's own data, and it's built from predefined templates in
minutes.
:::

cards.back: SQL query over a log type that feeds charts and macros.
A single value from a dataset placed in report text.
Per ADOM; time period and devices chosen per run.
$log: the log table; $filter: report time range and device filters.
Wrong ADOM, no devices, empty time range, log type not sent.

quiz.explanation: Datasets are the queries.

modules.title: FortiManager Device Manager: adding devices, ZTP, scripts and templates
objectives: Add existing FortiGates and model devices (zero-touch provisioning)
Use provisioning templates (system, IPsec, SD-WAN, CLI) to standardize device settings
Run CLI scripts against devices, the device database or ADOM database safely
Manage firmware with templates
sources: FortiManager 7.6.8 Admin Guide: Device Manager (pp. 93–378)

units.title: Getting devices in
units.body:
- **Existing FortiGate**: point it at FortiManager (`config system central-management`) or add it from
  FortiManager with credentials; authorize it; **import** its policies and objects into a policy package.
- **Model device** (zero-touch): pre-create the device in FortiManager with its serial number and templates.
  When the real FortiGate comes online and contacts FortiManager (FortiGate Cloud/FortiZTP or DHCP/manual), it
  matches the serial and receives its full configuration.

:::recall
Q: A new branch FortiGate will be cabled by a non-technical person. How do you avoid sending an engineer?
A: A model device with the serial number and templates in FortiManager (zero-touch provisioning).
:::

units.title: Provisioning templates
units.body:
Templates apply standard settings to many devices:

| Template | Covers |
|---|---|
| System template | DNS, NTP, admin settings, alert email, log settings |
| IPsec tunnel template | Branch tunnels to hubs |
| SD-WAN template | Members, zones, health checks, rules |
| Static route template | Common routes |
| CLI template | Anything else, with per-device variables (metadata) |
| Firmware template | Target firmware per device group |

**Metadata variables** (e.g. `$(branch_lan)`) let one template fill in per-device values.

:::pitfall
Templates are applied in a fixed order before the policy package during install; a CLI template that changes an
interface a policy depends on can break the install. Preview every install.
:::

units.title: Scripts
units.body:
CLI scripts run against:

- the **device** directly (changes the FortiGate; then FortiManager retrieves),
- the **device database** (changes FortiManager's copy; installed later),
- the **ADOM database** (objects and policies, for some script types).

Prefer database targets so changes flow through install previews and revisions. Use direct device scripts for
diagnostics (`get`, `diagnose`) across many devices.

:::ps
For a 200-branch change, test the script on two branches' device databases, preview the install, install those
two, verify, then roll out in waves. Keep the script and preview in the change record.
:::

Authorize it and import its policies/objects into a package.

modules.title: FortiManager operations: FortiGuard, FortiSwitch Manager, HA and troubleshooting
objectives: Use FortiManager as a local FortiGuard distribution server and manage firmware
Manage FortiSwitches centrally
Explain FortiManager HA and backups
Troubleshoot FGFM connectivity and install failures
sources: FortiManager 7.6.8 Admin Guide: FortiGuard (pp. 912–969), FortiSwitch Manager (pp. 970–1024), System Settings and HA (p. 1037+)
FortiManager 7.6.8 Admin Guide: Key concepts (pp. 48–65)

units.title: Local FortiGuard and firmware
units.body:
FortiManager can act as a **local FortiGuard Distribution Server (FDS)**: it downloads AV/IPS updates and
answers web filter and other rating queries for managed devices (pp. 912–969). Benefits: less Internet traffic,
updates for devices without direct Internet access (closed networks), central control of versions.

**Firmware**: FortiManager stores images and upgrades devices by template or on demand, following the upgrade path;
upgrade a pilot group first.

:::recall
Q: An OT network has no Internet but its FortiGates need IPS updates. Option?
A: FortiManager as local FDS (fed manually or from a connected FortiManager if fully offline).
:::

units.title: FortiSwitch Manager and HA
units.body:
**FortiSwitch Manager** manages FortiLink switches of many FortiGates centrally: switch templates, VLANs, port
profiles, firmware (pp. 970–1024). It turns per-site switch configuration into reusable templates.

**FortiManager HA** keeps a secondary unit synchronized with the primary's databases, so management survives a
failure. FortiGates keep working when FortiManager is down; you just can't manage centrally. Always schedule
configuration backups of FortiManager itself, stored off-box.

:::pitfall
FortiManager down is not an outage, until someone needs an emergency change and edits FortiGates directly,
creating drift that the next install has to reconcile.
:::

units.title: Troubleshooting
units.body:
| Symptom | Check |
|---|---|
| Device offline / no tunnel | FGFM TCP 541 path, `central-management` settings on the FortiGate, `fmg-source-ip` over VPNs |
| Status "modified" or out of sync | A change on the FortiGate: retrieve or reinstall after review |
| Install fails | Install log: missing dynamic mapping, object conflicts, unsupported settings for the firmware |
| Install preview shows deletions | Unused objects removed, or a mapping problem: read before installing |

FortiManager's key concept: ADOM database → device database → FortiGate, with revisions at each install
(pp. 55–63).

:::ps
After every rollout wave, check Device Manager for any device not "synchronized". Drift found the same day is a
5-minute fix; found three months later, it's a project.
:::

cards.back: Distributes FortiGuard updates and answers rating queries for managed devices.
Stored images, firmware templates, pilot first, upgrade path.
Central FortiLink switch templates, VLANs, port profiles, firmware.
None; only central management stops.
TCP 541.

scenarios.situation: FortiManager is down for hardware replacement. An urgent block rule is needed on 30 FortiGates now.

right_thinking: Make the change directly (scripted, consistent) with a change record

Verify sync status

When FortiManager is back, I add the same rule to the policy package and reinstall, or retrieve from the devices,
so the databases match again, and confirm every device shows synchronized."

interview.question: A FortiManager install fails on some devices. How do you troubleshoot?
interview.model_answer:
"I open the install log for the failed devices: usually a missing dynamic mapping for an object or interface, a
conflict with a local change, or a setting the device's firmware doesn't support. I fix the mapping or
reconcile the change, preview again, and reinstall only those devices."
interview.best_way: The log tells you.

modules.title: Security Fabric and automation
objectives: Build a Security Fabric with root and downstream FortiGates and connected Fortinet devices
Use security rating, topology views and fabric connectors
Design automation stitches with triggers and actions
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Fortinet Security Fabric (pp. 4814–5339)

units.title: What the Fabric is
units.body:
The Security Fabric interconnects Fortinet products to detect, monitor, block and remediate across the network
(p. 4814):

- **Root FortiGate**: usually the edge; shows the whole Fabric in physical and logical topology views.
- **Downstream FortiGates**: internal segmentation firewalls (ISFW) joined to the root.
- **FortiAnalyzer** (logging for the Fabric), FortiManager, FortiSwitch, FortiAP, FortiClient EMS, FortiSandbox,
  FortiEDR and others join it.
- FortiGate models with 2 GB RAM (40F, 50G, 60F series) can authorize up to five devices as Fabric root; a
  maximum of 35 downstream FortiGates is recommended (p. 4814).

:::recall
Q: Why do downstream FortiGates join the root's Fabric instead of standing alone?
A: Shared visibility (topology, logs to one FortiAnalyzer), security rating across all, and Fabric-wide automation.
:::

units.title: Security rating and connectors
units.body:
- **Security rating** checks the Fabric configuration against best practices and highlights vulnerabilities and
  improvements (p. 4814). Run it before and after a project: it's a measurable outcome.
- **Fabric connectors** integrate SDN, cloud and partner platforms (AWS, Azure, VMware, Kubernetes, ITSM…) so
  dynamic addresses follow workloads without manual updates.

:::why
Q: Why use an SDN connector address (e.g. by cloud tag) instead of static IPs for cloud servers?
A: Cloud IPs change; the connector keeps the address object in sync, so policies stay correct.
:::

units.title: Automation stitches
units.body:
An **automation stitch** pairs a **trigger** with one or more **actions** (p. 4814).

| Triggers (examples) | Actions (examples) |
|---|---|
| Compromised host (IOC), event log, HA failover, config change, high CPU, low memory, license near expiry, FortiAnalyzer event, incoming webhook, IPS/virus logs | Email, alert, ban IP, quarantine (FortiSwitch/FortiClient/FortiNAC), CLI script, diagnose script, webhook, Slack/Teams notification, cloud functions |

Example: "IPS critical log from an internal host → quarantine the host on FortiSwitch + Teams message to the SOC".

:::cli
config system automation-trigger
    edit "ips-critical"
        set event-type ips-logs
    next
end
:::

:::pitfall
Automation that bans or quarantines on a noisy trigger causes self-inflicted outages. Start with notify-only
stitches, review a week of triggers, then add blocking actions.
:::

cards.back: Root: edge, full Fabric view. Downstream: internal segmentation firewalls joined to the root.
35 (2 GB RAM roots: up to five devices).
Checks the Fabric against best practices and shows improvements.
SDN/cloud/partner integrations that keep dynamic objects in sync.
Trigger + one or more actions.
Notify first, review triggers, then add blocking actions.

modules.title: Threat prevention at scale: IPS, custom signatures, overrides, offload
objectives: Tune IPS sensors for performance and accuracy
Write custom IPS/application signatures for specific needs
Use web filter and application overrides safely
Explain NP/CP offload and what it means for inspection
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: IPS (p. 2812+), custom signatures (p. 3092+), overrides (p. 3104+)

units.title: IPS that doesn't hurt
units.body:
An **IPS sensor** selects signatures by filters (severity, target OS, application, protocol) and actions
(pass, monitor, block, reset, quarantine). Tuning principles:

- Protect what you have: filter by the OS and applications behind that policy (a Linux web farm doesn't need
  Windows client signatures).
- Start critical/high in **block**, medium in **monitor**, review, then tighten.
- Use per-policy sensors: Internet → DMZ servers is different from users → Internet.
- Watch CPU and sessions after changes; the IPS engine works per session.

:::recall
Q: Why not apply "all signatures, block" to every policy?
A: More signatures cost CPU and raise false positives on irrelevant traffic; filtering to the protected assets is faster and more accurate.
:::

units.title: Custom signatures and overrides
units.body:
**Custom signatures** (p. 3092): you can create application groups, application signatures and IPS signatures,
and apply them in policies. Typical uses: detect an internal app's traffic, block a specific exploit pattern
before an official signature exists, or match a header used by malware.

**Overrides** (p. 3104): web filter and application overrides let specific users or groups temporarily bypass a
block (for example, a manager allowed a blocked category for an hour), and signature overrides change the action
of a single IPS signature in a sensor.

:::pitfall
Custom signatures run on every session the sensor inspects; a careless pattern (very short, unanchored) costs CPU
and false positives. Anchor on protocol and context.
:::

units.title: Hardware acceleration
units.body:
FortiGates use **SPUs**: **NP** (network processors) offload firewall sessions, IPsec and NAT after the first
packets are inspected; **CP** (content processors) accelerate crypto and pattern matching.

- Offloaded sessions don't pass through the CPU, so some features (certain logging, per-packet inspection,
  debug flow after the first packets) don't see them.
- Disabling offload (`set auto-asic-offload disable` on a policy) is a troubleshooting tool, not a fix: it moves
  load to the CPU.
- IPS and proxy-based inspection need the CPU/CP path; sizing must account for which policies use them.

:::ps
When sizing, ask for "threat protection throughput" (IPS + app control + malware) from the datasheet, not
firewall throughput. Customers buy the box for the inspection they'll actually enable.
:::

cards.back: Filter signatures to the protected OS/apps; block high severity, monitor the rest first.
Pass, monitor, block, reset, quarantine.
Application groups, application signatures, IPS signatures.
Lets specific users/groups bypass a block temporarily.
NP: offloads sessions/IPsec/NAT. CP: crypto and pattern matching.

cards.front: Disabling ASIC offload on a policy
cards.back: Troubleshooting aid; moves load to CPU.

scenarios.title: "IPS made everything slow"
scenarios.situation: After enabling IPS with all signatures on every policy, CPU is at 95 % and users complain.
scenarios.ask: What do you do?
right_thinking: Roll back to the previous state if business impact is high
Per-policy sensors filtered to assets; trusted east-west flows may not need IPS
Check sizing vs threat protection throughput
scenarios.what: Performance back with protection kept where it matters.
scenarios.why: Security that breaks the business gets removed.
scenarios.model_answer:
"First stabilize: revert the busiest policies to the previous sensors. Then build per-policy sensors filtered to
the servers and clients behind each, keep critical and high in block, and remove IPS from trusted high-volume
flows like backups if the risk is accepted. If CPU is still high, compare traffic with the model's threat
protection throughput: it may be undersized for the inspection they want."
scenarios.best_way: Stabilize, tune, then size.

interview.question: How do you deploy IPS on a busy FortiGate without hurting performance?
interview.model_answer:
"Per-policy sensors filtered to the assets behind each policy, critical and high in block, the rest monitored and
promoted after review. I phase it in policy by policy, watch CPU and sessions, and size against threat protection
throughput. Confirmed false positives get signature overrides, not a disabled sensor."
interview.best_way: Targeted and phased.

modules.title: Central management at scale: FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer together
objectives: Run change management through FortiManager (workspace, preview, revisions)
Use FortiAnalyzer evidence before and after changes
sources: FortiManager 7.6.8 Admin Guide: Policy & Objects, install and revisions (pp. 379–635)
FortiAnalyzer 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Incidents, alerts and reports (pp. 222–515)

units.title: Changes through one door
units.body:
At scale, every change goes through FortiManager:

1. **Workspace/lock** the ADOM or package (no two admins editing the same thing).
2. Edit the package or templates; use **policy blocks** and **dynamic mappings** to keep one package for many
   sites.
3. **Install preview**: read it; it's the exact diff the FortiGates receive.
4. Install in waves; FortiManager keeps **revisions** of each device, so rollback is "install the previous
   revision".
5. Verify on devices and in FortiAnalyzer.

:::recall
Q: What is the single most important document of a FortiManager change?
A: The install preview: the exact diff that will be applied.
:::

units.title: Evidence from FortiAnalyzer
units.body:
FortiAnalyzer turns changes into evidence-based decisions:

- **Before**: "Who uses this rule?" Log View filtered by policy ID shows real traffic. Rules with zero hits for 90
  days are clean-up candidates.
- **After**: denies on the new rule's path, error spikes, application traffic per site.
- **Incident-driven**: an alert (IPS, IOC) leads to a FortiManager change (block address, update sensor) installed
  to all sites, then FortiAnalyzer confirms no further hits.

:::why
Q: Why check FortiAnalyzer before deleting a "legacy" policy?
A: Logs show whether anything still matches it; zero hits over a long period is evidence, not a guess.
:::

units.title: Operating rhythm
units.body:
| Cadence | FortiManager | FortiAnalyzer |
|---|---|---|
| Daily | Devices not synchronized, failed installs | High-severity alerts, sources that stopped logging |
| Weekly | Pending changes, firmware waves | Top threats, policy hit review |
| Monthly | Unused objects, package clean-up | Compliance reports, retention vs quota |

:::ps
Offer customers this rhythm as part of the handover: it's the difference between a tool they own and a tool they
have.
:::

cards.back: Lock, edit, install preview, install in waves, verify; revisions for rollback.
Install the previous device revision.
Policy hits in FortiAnalyzer over a long period.
FAZ alert → FMG change to all sites → FAZ confirms.
Unsynced devices/failed installs; high alerts/silent log sources.

scenarios.title: "Just delete everything older than 2020"
scenarios.situation: A new CISO wants all policies created before 2020 deleted this weekend to "reduce risk".
scenarios.ask: How do you respond?
right_thinking: Agree with the goal
Age isn't usage: use hit evidence
Disable-then-delete plan with dates
scenarios.what: Risk reduction without outages.
scenarios.why: Evidence beats age.
scenarios.model_answer:
"Reducing rule sprawl is the right goal. Age doesn't tell us if a rule is still used, though: some 2018 rules may
carry payroll. I'd pull 90 days of hits from FortiAnalyzer, disable the zero-hit rules this weekend through
FortiManager, and delete them in a month if nothing breaks. Low-hit rules go to their owners for review."
scenarios.best_way: Same goal, evidence-based path.

interview.question: How do FortiManager and FortiAnalyzer work together in operations?
interview.model_answer:
"FortiManager is the single door for changes, with previews and revisions; FortiAnalyzer is the evidence. Before
a change I check real usage in the logs, after it I confirm the effect, and when FortiAnalyzer raises an incident
the fix goes out through FortiManager to every site and FortiAnalyzer confirms it worked."
interview.best_way: Change and evidence loop.

modules.title: Troubleshooting master: packet flow, resources and sessions
objectives: Walk a packet through the FortiGate end to end and know where each feature acts
Diagnose conserve mode, high CPU and memory problems
Analyze sessions and offload issues
Run an efficient, evidence-based troubleshooting session with a customer
sources: FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: Network diagnostics (p. 1143), Troubleshooting (pp. 5544–5616)
FortiOS 8.0.2 Admin Guide: memory thresholds (system global, conserve mode) and SPU offload (as referenced in M8.04)

units.title: The packet's journey
units.body:
A simplified order for a new session through a FortiGate:

1. Ingress interface, DoS policies, **local-in** check (traffic to the FortiGate itself).
2. **Destination NAT** (VIP) decided.
3. **Routing**: policy routes/SD-WAN rules, then the routing table; **RPF** check.
4. **Firewall policy** match (first match, top to bottom), identity, schedule.
5. **Source NAT**.
6. **Security profiles** (flow or proxy), possibly offloaded afterwards to the NP.
7. Egress, with the session installed for the reply direction.

`diagnose debug flow` shows steps 2–5 with the policy ID and reason; the **sniffer** shows the packet on the wire on
each interface; the **session table** shows what was installed.

:::recall
Q: Debug flow says "reverse path check fail". Which step failed?
A: Routing (RPF): no route back to the source through the incoming interface.
:::

units.title: Resources: CPU, memory, conserve mode
units.body:
When memory runs low, FortiOS enters **conserve mode** to protect itself. The thresholds are in `config system
global`: by default **red 88 %** (enter conserve mode), **extreme 95 %** (drop new sessions), **green 82 %**
(leave conserve mode). While in conserve mode, content inspection may stop: `av-failopen` decides whether
traffic needing inspection passes (default **pass**) or is blocked.

Commands: `get system performance status`, `diagnose sys top` (processes), `diagnose sys session full-stat`,
`get system status`.

Common causes: too many sessions (attack, scan, missing session timers), memory-heavy features (proxy inspection
on a small model), logging to disk on low-end models, memory leaks fixed in later builds.

:::pitfall
Raising the thresholds hides the symptom. Find what consumes memory: sessions, a process, or a feature mismatched
to the model.
:::

units.title: Sessions, offload and method
units.body:
- `diagnose sys session filter …` then `diagnose sys session list`: protocol state, policy ID, NAT, the
  interface pair, and whether the session is **offloaded** (NP flags).
- Asymmetric paths, expired sessions and offload issues all show up here.
- `diagnose sys session clear` (with a filter!) after a routing or policy change, so new sessions take the new
  path.

**Method** for any problem (the one interviewers listen for):

1. Define: who, what, since when, what changed.
2. Reproduce with a known test (source, destination, port).
3. Follow the packet: sniffer on ingress and egress, debug flow, session list.
4. Change one thing at a time; verify; document.

:::ps
On a customer call, narrate the method: "I'll capture on both interfaces while you reproduce." It shows control,
and the evidence ends the "it's the firewall" debate in minutes.
:::

cards.back: DNAT (VIP) → routing (+RPF) → policy match → SNAT.
Sniffer, debug flow, session list.
Red 88 %, extreme 95 %, green 82 %.
pass: traffic needing inspection passes uninspected in conserve mode.
get system performance status; diagnose sys top; diagnose sys session full-stat.
Set diagnose sys session filter first, then clear.
Define, reproduce, follow the packet, change one thing and verify.

scenarios.title: "The firewall is slow"
scenarios.situation:
Monday 9:00, the customer says "everything is slow since the weekend". The FortiGate shows 70 % memory and normal
CPU.
scenarios.ask: Your first questions and commands?
right_thinking: Define: what is slow, for whom, since when, what changed
Reproduce one slow flow; check sessions, routing, SD-WAN state
Follow the packet; don't blame the box without evidence
scenarios.what: A focused, evidence-driven start.
scenarios.why: Vague problems need structure.
scenarios.model_answer:
"First questions: which applications, which sites, all users or some, and what changed this weekend. Then I pick
one slow flow and follow it: SD-WAN member health and which link it uses, the session entry, a sniffer on both
interfaces for retransmissions or latency. Memory at 70 % isn't the problem yet, so I'd look at the path before
the box."
scenarios.best_way: Narrow first.

interview.question: Walk me through how a packet is processed by a FortiGate.
interview.framework: Ingress → DNAT → route → policy → SNAT → inspection → egress
interview.model_answer:
"On ingress, DoS and local-in checks; then destination NAT if a VIP matches; then routing, with policy routes and
SD-WAN rules first and an RPF check; then the first matching firewall policy, with identity and schedule; then
source NAT; then security profiles, and the session may be offloaded to the NP afterwards. Debug flow shows those
steps with the policy ID, so it's my first tool when traffic is dropped."
interview.best_way: In order, with the tool.
